explanation.summary: Long-term lithium therapy requires routine surveillance for the three classical organ effects: chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism, and primary hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcaemia. Australian Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic recommend a steady-state trough lithium level plus electrolytes, eGFR, corrected calcium, and TSH every 6 months once a patient has been stable for at least 6 months, continued lifelong. Earlier monitoring (every 1 to 3 months) is reserved for initiation, dose change, or intercurrent illness with dehydration or new interacting medication.
key_points: Lifelong 6-monthly lithium, U+E, eGFR, corrected calcium, and TSH once stable.
Lithium can cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and chronic interstitial nephritis.
Hypercalcaemia from primary hyperparathyroidism is increasingly recognised on long-term lithium.
explanation.pearls: Any new interacting medication (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides) or intercurrent illness with vomiting warrants a check at 5 to 7 days because lithium toxicity can develop in days.

options.rationale: Routine surveillance must continue regardless of symptoms because lithium nephrotoxicity and thyroid dysfunction are insidious. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)
Monitoring lithium without checking eGFR, TSH, and calcium misses the very organ effects routine review is designed to detect. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)
Hypercalcaemia from lithium-induced hyperparathyroidism is a recognised complication that is missed without routine calcium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)
Six-monthly is the recommended frequency for the panel when stable; staggering creates gaps in detection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)
Australian Therapeutic Guidelines specify 6-monthly lithium, U+E, eGFR, calcium, and TSH once stable, lifelong. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Second-generation antipsychotics, especially olanzapine and clozapine, drive weight gain, dyslipidaemia, and impaired glucose tolerance, often within the first 3 months. The RANZCP and Australian Therapeutic Guidelines schedule recommends measuring weight and waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose or HbA1c, and a lipid panel at baseline, 6 weeks, 12 weeks, 6 months, and annually thereafter. Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic risk; lurasidone and aripiprazole carry the lowest.
key_points: 12 week monitoring includes weight, waist, BP, fasting glucose or HbA1c, and lipid panel.
Olanzapine and clozapine are the highest-risk antipsychotics for metabolic syndrome.
Switch to a lower-risk agent if HbA1c crosses 6.0 percent or weight gain exceeds 7 percent of baseline.
explanation.pearls: If HbA1c rises by more than 0.5 percent at 12 weeks, prompt a switch consideration rather than waiting for diabetes to develop on top of stable psychotic illness.

options.rationale: RANZCP recommends fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids, weight, waist, and blood pressure at 12 weeks and then at least annually on second-generation antipsychotics. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)
Lipid abnormalities can emerge within 12 weeks of olanzapine and are part of routine monitoring at this visit. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)
Twelve week metabolic monitoring is part of the AU schedule precisely because olanzapine commonly causes early metabolic change. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)
Insulin resistance can develop early with olanzapine and screening at 12 weeks is recommended. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)
Routine 12 week ECG and prolactin are not standard unless symptomatic; tardive dyskinesia surveillance starts later in treatment. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)

explanation.summary: Nausea affects roughly a third of patients taking varenicline, is dose-related, usually mild and tends to settle with continued treatment. The management is to take each dose after food with a full glass of water and, if it persists, reduce to 0.5 mg twice daily rather than stop; other common effects are vivid or abnormal dreams and insomnia, managed by taking the evening dose earlier. Treatment is stopped for agitation, depressed mood, hostility or suicidal thoughts, or for a hypersensitivity or serious skin reaction. In context: varenicline is the most effective single cessation agent, and most treatment failures in practice are premature cessation of the drug rather than true non-response, so dose adjustment is the default response to tolerable adverse effects.
key_points: Nausea is dose-related and usually settles; take doses after food with water
Reduce to 0.5 mg twice daily before abandoning treatment
Vivid dreams and insomnia respond to taking the evening dose earlier
Stop for new agitation, depressed mood or suicidal thoughts, or severe skin reaction
explanation.pearls: An abstinent patient at day twelve has already passed the highest-risk window for relapse; keeping them on treatment at a reduced dose is worth more than a clean adverse effect profile.

options.rationale: Nausea is the commonest varenicline adverse effect, is dose-related and usually settles; halving the dose and taking it after food with a full glass of water keeps an abstinent patient on effective treatment. (Source: AMH: Varenicline)

Switching to replacement is right when varenicline causes intolerable effects despite dose reduction, or when mood or suicidal symptoms emerge. Abandoning effective treatment for mild nausea risks relapse. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

An antiemetic is justified for nausea from a treatment that cannot be dose-reduced, such as chemotherapy. Here it adds extrapyramidal risk when a simple dose reduction solves the problem. (Source: AMH: Metoclopramide)

Behavioural support runs alongside pharmacotherapy rather than replacing it; it would be the sole treatment only if he declined or could not tolerate all medicines. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

A shortened course would apply only if treatment had to be ceased for an adverse effect; the standard course runs 12 weeks, and stopping at four weeks markedly increases relapse. (Source: AMH: Varenicline)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis under DSM-5 requires at least five inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (out of nine each), childhood onset before age 12, persistence, impairment in at least two settings, and no better explanation. First-line treatment in Australia is a long-acting stimulant such as lisdexamfetamine 30 mg daily or methylphenidate ER, titrated weekly. Pre-treatment workup includes cardiovascular assessment with resting ECG. Patients must be advised that driving may be impaired during titration or dose changes, and to defer driving until they know their response; ongoing disclosure to the licensing authority is required only if a clinician judges fitness to drive is affected.
key_points: Long-acting stimulant is first-line for adult ADHD in Australia.
Baseline ECG and cardiovascular history are required before initiation.
Patients should not drive during titration or for 2 weeks after each dose change until response is known.
explanation.pearls: Document that the patient understands driving restrictions during titration and the obligation to self-report to the licensing authority if symptoms compromise safe driving; this is a recurrent medicolegal pitfall.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Atomoxetine is reasonable when stimulants are contraindicated or declined but is not the routine first-line in adult ADHD. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guideline)
CBT augments treatment of adult ADHD but is not curative as monotherapy when stimulants are appropriate. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guideline)
DSM-5 adult ADHD is established; first-line is a long-acting stimulant with driving restriction during titration per AU prescribing advice. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guideline)
Immediate release methylphenidate requires multiple daily doses and AU prescribing still advises driving caution during titration. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guideline)
PHQ-9 of 4 and GAD-7 of 6 are not above thresholds that would defer ADHD treatment in this presentation. (Source: RANZCP adult ADHD guideline)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressants sit in the small group of agents where one adult tablet can be lethal to a small child, alongside agents such as sustained release calcium channel blockers, sulfonylureas and opioids. A 25 mg tablet in a 13 kg child is close to 2 mg/kg, and toxicity in children is reported from around 5 mg/kg, but the dose history in an exploratory ingestion is never reliable and the missing tablet may not be the only one. All of these children are referred for a monitored observation period with serial electrocardiograms, and a normal tracing with a normal conscious state at six hours identifies the child who can go home. In context: tricyclic poisoning causes sodium channel blockade, seizures and antimuscarinic delirium, and the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26 provides national advice around the clock.

sources.label: Toxicology Handbook (Murray, Little, Cadogan, Daly), Elsevier Australia
RACGP: Handbook of Non-Drug Interventions and preventive activities

options.rationale: A single adult tricyclic tablet can reach a toxic dose in a toddler, and deterioration is delayed. Australian poisons advice is transfer for assessment with continuous cardiac monitoring and serial electrocardiograms for at least six hours after ingestion.

Home observation is appropriate for a genuinely non-toxic exposure, such as an oral contraceptive pill or a small amount of paracetamol elixir well below the threshold dose. Waiting for drowsiness in a tricyclic ingestion means waiting for cardiotoxicity.

Charcoal is considered in hospital for a recent potentially serious ingestion with a protected or cooperative airway. Administering it at home to an unmonitored toddler risks aspiration and delays transfer.
source_refs: Toxicology Handbook (Murray, Little, Cadogan, Daly), Elsevier Australia

options.rationale: A practice review suits a low-risk exposure needing a second look. General practice cannot deliver the continuous cardiac monitoring and resuscitation capability this ingestion may require.
source_refs: RACGP: Handbook of Non-Drug Interventions and preventive activities

options.rationale: A single delayed tracing would miss the window in which the QRS widens. Serial electrocardiography has a role, but during a monitored hospital observation period beginning now.
source_refs: Toxicology Handbook (Murray, Little, Cadogan, Daly), Elsevier Australia

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a treatable syndrome of motor and behavioural features (mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, echolalia or echopraxia, negativism, stereotypy) recognised by Bush-Francis scoring. The lorazepam challenge with 1 to 2 mg IM is both diagnostic and therapeutic: marked improvement within 30 minutes supports the diagnosis and warrants regular lorazepam (often 4 to 16 mg daily in divided doses). Electroconvulsive therapy is second-line if lorazepam fails or for malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis). Antipsychotics may worsen catatonia and are generally avoided in the acute phase.
key_points: Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IM as the standard catatonia challenge.
Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia in the acute phase.
ECT is second-line, and first-line in malignant catatonia with autonomic instability.
explanation.pearls: Catatonia plus fever, autonomic instability, and rising CK should be treated as malignant catatonia and referred for urgent ECT rather than persisting with benzodiazepines.

options.rationale: Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IM is the standard catatonia lorazepam challenge: rapid improvement supports diagnosis and confirms first-line treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)
Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia, particularly malignant catatonia, and are not first-line here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)
ECT is highly effective in catatonia but is second-line after a trial of lorazepam unless features are life-threatening. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)
Bromocriptine is used in neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which is excluded here by normal temperature, normal CK, and no rigidity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)
Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia and are not the diagnostic or therapeutic step at this stage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: psychotropic)

explanation.summary: DSM-5 schizoaffective disorder requires (a) an uninterrupted period of illness during which there is a major mood episode (depressive or manic) concurrent with Criterion A of schizophrenia; (b) at least 2 weeks of delusions or hallucinations during the lifetime of illness in the absence of a major mood episode; (c) mood episodes present for the majority of the total duration of illness; (d) not better explained by substance use or other medical condition. Persistent psychosis during 12 cumulative euthymic months distinguishes schizoaffective disorder from bipolar I with psychotic features.
key_points: Schizoaffective bipolar type requires at least 2 weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms in the lifetime.
Mood symptoms must be present for the majority of total illness duration.
Bipolar I with psychotic features confines psychosis to mood episodes.
explanation.pearls: Document the timing of psychosis relative to mood episodes carefully across the lifetime course; the diagnosis hinges on whether psychotic symptoms outlast mood episodes by at least 2 weeks.

options.rationale: Persistent psychotic symptoms across 12 cumulative months between mood episodes excludes simple bipolar I with psychotic features. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)
DSM-5 schizoaffective disorder requires at least 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms in the absence of major mood symptoms during the lifetime of illness. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)
Clear discrete manic episodes meeting bipolar criteria favour schizoaffective bipolar type over schizophrenia plus depression. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)
Delusional disorder requires functioning outside the delusion to be relatively preserved and excludes prominent hallucinations. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)
Urine drug screen is negative and the symptoms persist outside any substance use, excluding this diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP schizophrenia guideline)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate has the highest teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk of any mood stabiliser: approximately 10% major congenital malformations (notably neural tube, cardiac, and craniofacial) and 30 to 40% rate of neurodevelopmental disability including reduced IQ and autism spectrum disorder. Australian and TGA pregnancy prevention requirements mean valproate should not be used in women of childbearing potential unless no alternative works. When unplanned pregnancy occurs, cross-titrate to a safer agent (quetiapine, lamotrigine if not on valproate, or lithium balancing first trimester Ebstein risk against later trimester safety) over 2 to 4 weeks, increase folate to 5 mg daily, arrange dating ultrasound, and refer to perinatal psychiatry.
key_points: Valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy unless no alternative exists.
Cross-titrate over 2 to 4 weeks to avoid relapse; quetiapine and lamotrigine are commonly substituted.
Increase folate to 5 mg daily for 12 weeks of pregnancy on any anticonvulsant.
explanation.pearls: If valproate truly cannot be substituted, the patient must be counselled about the residual risk and offered detailed morphology scanning at 18 to 20 weeks plus paediatric neurodevelopmental follow-up.

options.rationale: Valproate carries 10% major congenital malformation and 30 to 40% neurodevelopmental disability rates and is contraindicated in pregnancy unless no alternative. (Source: RANZCP perinatal mood disorder guideline)
Abrupt cessation of valproate without substitution carries about 50 percent risk of relapse in the first trimester. (Source: RANZCP perinatal mood disorder guideline)
Valproate carries 10% major malformation risk and 30 to 40% neurodevelopmental risk; substitution by a safer mood stabiliser is recommended. (Source: RANZCP perinatal mood disorder guideline)
Lithium during organogenesis carries a small Ebstein anomaly risk and is generally avoided in the first trimester if a safer alternative exists. (Source: RANZCP perinatal mood disorder guideline)
Valproate strongly inhibits lamotrigine clearance, doubling Stevens-Johnson syndrome risk; combining the two during titration is unsafe. (Source: AMH antiepileptic interactions)

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium causes chronic interstitial nephritis in a minority of users, often slowly progressive after 10-15 years. Sustained eGFR decline below 60 mL/min/1.73m2 (CKD G3a) on confirmatory repeat warrants joint nephrology and psychiatry review. Continuing lithium is sometimes the best option for a patient with no alternative mood stabiliser tolerated, but the conversation must occur. Dose reduction does not reverse established nephropathy. Abrupt cessation carries high relapse risk and is contraindicated.
key_points: Lithium nephropathy: progressive interstitial nephritis over 10+ years
Sustained eGFR under 60 mL/min/1.73m2 triggers nephrology/psychiatry joint review
Lithium cessation, if undertaken, is gradual over months
explanation.pearls: The decision to continue lithium with CKD weighs relapse risk (high) against rate of further renal decline (often modest) - shared decision making with both teams is the standard.

options.rationale: Sustained eGFR decline below 60 mL/min/1.73m2 on confirmatory repeat with otherwise unexplained chronic kidney disease in a long-term lithium user prompts joint nephrology and psychiatry review to discuss switching. RANZCP recommends collaborative decision-making with the patient. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG 2020)
Lower lithium dose does not reverse established interstitial nephritis and risks relapse if the level falls below the therapeutic window. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG 2020)
Confirmed eGFR decline to under 60 mL/min/1.73m2 requires escalation in monitoring frequency and consideration of switch, not routine annual review. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG 2020)
Abrupt lithium cessation carries a high relapse risk and valproate is teratogenic; switching is a planned discussion, not an emergency. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG 2020)
Amiloride is used for lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, not for chronic interstitial nephropathy with falling eGFR. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG 2020)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is contraindicated in pregnancy and in women planning pregnancy because of a roughly 10% major malformation rate and a 30-40% rate of neurodevelopmental impairment. The TGA pregnancy prevention program requires effective contraception, annual review, and documented counselling. For bipolar maintenance in women planning pregnancy who do not tolerate lithium, lamotrigine is the preferred switch, cross-titrated gradually with continued contraception until stable, and combined with high-dose folate 5 mg daily preconception.
key_points: Valproate: 10% major malformation rate, 30-40% neurodevelopmental impairment
TGA pregnancy prevention program mandates documented annual review
Lamotrigine is the preferred bipolar maintenance in pregnancy planning
explanation.pearls: Folate 5 mg daily preconception is for women on enzyme-inducing antiepileptics or those at high neural tube defect risk - not just 0.5 mg.

options.rationale: Valproate exposure in early pregnancy carries about 10% major congenital malformation rate and about 30-40% neurodevelopmental impairment. It is contraindicated in pregnancy and in women planning pregnancy unless no alternative. (Source: TGA valproate pregnancy prevention program)

Lamotrigine is the preferred maintenance mood stabiliser in women planning pregnancy who have not tolerated lithium. Cross-titration with valproate is gradual, contraception is continued until stabilisation, and high-dose folate 5 mg daily is added preconception. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG 2020)
Severe tremor at therapeutic level was previously intolerable and is not cosmetic; lamotrigine is the more rational option here. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG 2020)
Untreated bipolar I disorder relapse rate without prophylaxis is high, particularly during pregnancy and postpartum. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG 2020)
Adding a second agent does not solve the teratogenicity problem; the issue is valproate itself, not the level of cover. (Source: RANZCP mood disorders CPG 2020)

explanation.summary: Long-acting stimulants (lisdexamfetamine or extended-release methylphenidate) are first-line for adult ADHD per the Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline 2022. Lisdexamfetamine is a lysine prodrug, requiring intestinal conversion to active dexamfetamine, which reduces abuse potential. Baseline cardiovascular assessment (history, blood pressure, pulse, ECG when indicated) is required before initiation. Atomoxetine and guanfacine are second/third-line.
key_points: Long-acting stimulant first-line in adult ADHD in Australia
Baseline BP, pulse, and cardiovascular history are required
Atomoxetine reserved for stimulant intolerance or substance use concerns
explanation.pearls: Most state stimulant prescribing rules require a paediatrician or psychiatrist for initiation; GPs continue care under shared care arrangements.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022

options.rationale: Long-acting preparations are preferred first-line in adult ADHD to reduce diversion and improve adherence; immediate release is reserved for top-up. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022

options.rationale: Atomoxetine is second-line; reserved for stimulant intolerance, contraindication, or substance use disorder concern. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022

options.rationale: Long-acting stimulant (lisdexamfetamine or extended-release methylphenidate) is first-line in adult ADHD in Australia. Lisdexamfetamine has a low abuse potential due to lysine prodrug structure. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022

options.rationale: Guanfacine is third-line in adults and primarily used in children/adolescents. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022

options.rationale: Bupropion is not first-line for ADHD; reserved for selected cases or co-existing nicotine dependence. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD 2022

explanation.summary: Catatonia is recognised on the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale and includes mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, and posturing. The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV or IM) is diagnostic and therapeutic; response within minutes supports scheduled benzodiazepine. Antipsychotic medication is paused because of NMS risk. ECT is reserved for lorazepam failure or for malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis). Thiamine is supportive for nutrition but does not treat catatonia.
key_points: Lorazepam challenge 1-2 mg IV/IM is diagnostic and first-line treatment
Pause antipsychotic medication to avoid NMS precipitation
ECT reserved for lorazepam failure or malignant catatonia
explanation.pearls: If response to first lorazepam dose is partial, a second 2 mg dose 30 minutes later is given before declaring failure - catatonia is benzodiazepine-responsive in roughly 70% of adults.

options.rationale: ECT is highly effective in catatonia but is reserved for failure of lorazepam or for malignant catatonia; lorazepam challenge precedes ECT. (Source: RANZCP psychosis CPG 2016)
There is no fever, no rigidity, and normal creatine kinase. NMS is unlikely and dopamine agonists are not the first move in catatonia without NMS. (Source: RANZCP psychosis CPG 2016)

Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia (and may precipitate NMS); the standard is to pause the antipsychotic and use scheduled lorazepam. Oral diazepam is also slower acting than IV/IM lorazepam in this acute context. (Source: RANZCP psychosis CPG 2016)

A lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV or IM, sometimes followed by a second dose) is both diagnostic and the first-line treatment for catatonia in adults. Response within 5-15 minutes confirms catatonia and supports scheduled benzodiazepine therapy. (Source: RANZCP psychosis CPG 2016)
Although IV thiamine is appropriate in any unwell, malnourished patient (and should be considered here for nutrition), it does not treat catatonia. (Source: RANZCP psychosis CPG 2016)

explanation.summary: TCA overdose causes sodium-channel blockade (widened QRS, right axis deviation, terminal R in aVR) plus anticholinergic features. QRS above 100 ms or aVR R-wave above 3 mm triggers IV sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg boluses, repeated until QRS narrows below 100 ms and pH reaches 7.50-7.55. Flumazenil is contraindicated. Phenytoin worsens cardiotoxicity. Lipid emulsion is reserved for refractory toxicity. Activated charcoal is only useful within an hour and only if airway is protected.
key_points: QRS above 100 ms in TCA overdose triggers IV sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg
Target arterial pH 7.50-7.55 and QRS below 100 ms
Phenytoin contraindicated; flumazenil contraindicated
explanation.pearls: In TCA overdose, a terminal R wave of 3 mm or more in aVR is a sensitive early marker of cardiotoxicity - check aVR before relying on QRS duration.

options.rationale: Charcoal is considered within one hour of ingestion in alert co-operative patients; at three hours with reduced GCS and seizure risk it is not appropriate. (Source: Toxicology Wiki Calvey TCA 2024)
Flumazenil is contraindicated in TCA co-ingestion because it lowers the seizure threshold; she has already seized. (Source: Toxicology Wiki Calvey TCA 2024)

Phenytoin is a class IB agent and worsens TCA cardiotoxicity by adding to sodium-channel blockade. Levetiracetam is the preferred second seizure agent if needed. (Source: Toxicology Wiki Calvey TCA 2024)
Lipid emulsion is reserved for refractory cardiotoxicity (cardiac arrest, persistent shock) after sodium bicarbonate; it is not first-line. (Source: Toxicology Wiki Calvey TCA 2024)

QRS above 100 ms in TCA overdose indicates sodium-channel blockade requiring sodium bicarbonate. Boluses of 1-2 mmol/kg are repeated until QRS narrows below 100 ms and arterial pH reaches 7.50-7.55. (Source: Toxicology Wiki Calvey TCA 2024)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder requires (a) an uninterrupted period of illness during which a major mood episode is concurrent with criterion-A schizophrenia symptoms, (b) at least two weeks of delusions or hallucinations in the absence of a major mood episode during the same lifetime illness, and (c) mood-episode symptoms present for the majority of the active and residual periods. The bipolar subtype applies when manic episodes occur; the depressive subtype applies when only depressive episodes do.
key_points: Schizoaffective: a two-week period of psychosis without mood symptoms distinguishes it from bipolar with psychotic features
Bipolar subtype if any lifetime manic episode
Substance use and primary medical causes must be excluded
explanation.pearls: Most psychiatrists capture the 'two weeks of pure psychosis' criterion with a detailed week-by-week longitudinal chart of the illness, not a single cross-sectional interview.

options.rationale: Psychosis persisting for at least two weeks without mood symptoms during the same illness distinguishes schizoaffective from bipolar with mood-congruent psychosis. (Source: DSM-5-TR text revision)

Schizoaffective disorder requires a major mood episode concurrent with active-phase schizophrenia symptoms PLUS at least 2 weeks of psychosis without prominent mood symptoms during the same lifetime episode. The bipolar subtype applies because manic episodes have occurred. (Source: DSM-5-TR text revision)
Two clear manic episodes preclude a schizophrenia plus MDD construction; the affective component meets bipolar criteria. (Source: DSM-5-TR text revision)
Brief psychotic disorder lasts less than one month and does not capture the longitudinal pattern with manic and depressive episodes. (Source: DSM-5-TR text revision)
Repeated negative urine drug screens and an established pattern over 18 months argue against a substance-induced diagnosis. (Source: DSM-5-TR text revision)

explanation.summary: Modern ECT is performed under general anaesthetic with muscle relaxation, and remains the most effective treatment for severe depression. The most common adverse effect is cognitive: transient confusion immediately post-treatment, then anterograde and retrograde amnesia mostly for events around the treatment period. Most patients recover baseline cognition within weeks to months. Mortality is comparable to general anaesthetic alone (approximately 2 per 100,000 treatments). Headache and muscle ache occur in around 25%.
key_points: Memory effects are the dominant ECT adverse effect
Mortality is comparable to GA alone
Cognitive recovery typically within months
explanation.pearls: Bilateral ECT has greater cognitive impact than right unilateral; many AU services begin with right unilateral and switch only for non-response after 6 treatments.

options.rationale: Memory disturbance is the most common ECT side effect and the one most relevant to consent; it usually improves but may persist for some events around treatment. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement 2022)
Persistent global cognitive impairment is uncommon; baseline cognition typically returns by 6 months. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement 2022)
There is no evidence of structural brain damage from ECT on MRI or histopathology. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement 2022)
ECT mortality is approximately 2 per 100,000 treatments, similar to general anaesthetic alone. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement 2022)
Seizure threshold does rise over a course but is managed by adjusting stimulus dose; ketamine substitution is for specific resistant cases. (Source: RANZCP ECT Position Statement 2022)

explanation.summary: Borderline personality disorder is best managed with structured evidence-based psychotherapy. AU NHMRC and RANZCP guidelines list DBT, mentalisation-based therapy, schema-focused therapy, and transference-focused psychotherapy as effective. Pharmacotherapy is not first-line; specific target symptoms (impulsivity, mood instability) may be treated symptomatically with short courses. Brief admissions are appropriate for crisis stabilisation but prolonged admissions are not recommended.
key_points: Structured psychotherapy is primary BPD treatment
Medications are symptom-targeted, not core
Avoid prolonged admissions
explanation.pearls: DBT skills training in groups reduces self-harm and emergency presentations by approximately 50% within 12 months when completed.

options.rationale: AU NHMRC and RANZCP guidelines specify structured psychotherapy as the primary treatment for BPD; medications have limited role and are not first-line. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)
Lithium does not have an evidence base for BPD as monotherapy; psychotherapy is primary. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)
Prolonged inpatient care for BPD is associated with regression and dependence; structured outpatient psychotherapy is preferred. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)
Antipsychotics have only short-term and symptom-targeted role in BPD; long-term use is not recommended. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)
Supportive management alone is not sufficient when structured psychotherapy is available; AU guidance specifies psychotherapy as primary. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guideline)

explanation.summary: Functional neurological disorder is a positive diagnosis based on internal inconsistency of neurological signs (Hoover sign for leg weakness, tremor entrainment, give-way power, distractibility). It is not a diagnosis of exclusion. Patients are typically distressed and concerned. Malingering and factitious disorder differ by conscious symptom production; only malingering has external incentive. Treatment is multidisciplinary including physiotherapy, psychoeducation, and CBT.
key_points: FND is a positive diagnosis using internal inconsistency
Malingering needs external incentive
Factitious is conscious for sick role
explanation.pearls: Naming the diagnosis clearly using positive signs (Hoover) reduces healthcare utilisation more than ambiguous explanations - patients often improve when given the diagnosis and a referral to FND physiotherapy.

sources.label: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus

options.rationale: Positive Hoover sign and inconsistent neurology with patient distress and no external incentive support a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder. (Source: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus)
source_refs: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus

options.rationale: Malingering requires an external incentive (avoiding work, financial gain, legal); none is present here. (Source: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus)
source_refs: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus

options.rationale: Factitious disorder requires conscious symptom fabrication for the sick role; clinical pattern here is involuntary distress without fabrication. (Source: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus)
source_refs: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus

options.rationale: Hoover positive and distractibility are not stroke findings; normal MRI within hours of presentation does not exclude stroke but inconsistent power on distraction is functional. (Source: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus)
source_refs: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus

options.rationale: MS would not produce Hoover positive findings or distractibility; MRI is normal. (Source: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus)
source_refs: DSM-5-TR; UK Functional Neurological Disorder consensus

explanation.summary: Adult ASD diagnosis, especially in women, requires a structured assessment to overcome masking and camouflaging. The AU National Guideline recommends use of the ADOS-2 plus a developmental history (ADI-R or 3Di-Adult) by a clinician experienced in adult presentations. Self-report screens (AQ-50, RAADS-R, CAT-Q) are valuable indicators but cannot replace assessment. Diagnosis enables NDIS access and reframes prior misdiagnoses such as social anxiety or BPD.
key_points: Structured ADOS-2 + developmental history is the gold standard
Self-report screens do not diagnose
Female presentation often masks - require experienced clinician
explanation.pearls: Women diagnosed in adulthood have higher rates of co-occurring depression and PTSD than men, and benefit from autism-specific therapy rather than generic CBT.

sources.label: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018

options.rationale: AU national autism guideline mandates a structured diagnostic assessment using validated tools by an experienced clinician for adult diagnosis, especially given the masking presentation. (Source: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018)
source_refs: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018

options.rationale: Adult diagnosis can provide identity, access to NDIS supports, and adjustment of treatment; dismissing the request is not consistent with AU guidance. (Source: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018)
source_refs: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018

options.rationale: Self-report screens cannot make a diagnosis; structured clinician-administered assessment is required. (Source: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018)
source_refs: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018

options.rationale: Chromosomal microarray is offered after diagnosis when there are features of syndromic autism; it does not precede clinical diagnostic assessment. (Source: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018)
source_refs: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018

options.rationale: Risperidone is reserved for severe irritability and aggression in ASD, not core social features; it is never started before diagnosis. (Source: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018)
source_refs: NHMRC National Guideline for Autism Diagnosis 2018

explanation.summary: Refugees presenting with somatic complaints commonly have underlying PTSD, depression, or anxiety. Confidential history-taking with a professional (preferably gender-matched) interpreter is essential; family interpreters miss disclosure and may pose safety risks. Australian specialist refugee trauma services (STARTTS NSW, Foundation House VIC, ASeTTS WA, QPASTT QLD) provide trauma-focused therapy with culturally appropriate care. Benzodiazepines worsen PTSD outcomes and are not first-line.
key_points: Refugee somatic complaints can mask PTSD
Professional interpreter required, not family
Refer to specialist refugee trauma service
explanation.pearls: Refugees on temporary protection visas have restricted Medicare and may have no access to PBS-subsidised medications; check eligibility before prescribing.

options.rationale: Refugee somatic complaints often mask PTSD; trauma history requires a professional interpreter without family present, and AU refugee trauma services (e.g. STARTTS, Foundation House) are the appropriate referral pathway. (Source: ASID and Australian Refugee Health Practice Guide)
Somatic complaints in refugees often signal underlying PTSD; reassurance alone misses the diagnosis. (Source: Australian Refugee Health Practice Guide)
Family interpreters compromise confidentiality, miss disclosure, and create harm; a professional interpreter is mandated. (Source: Australian Refugee Health Practice Guide)
Benzodiazepines worsen PTSD outcomes and carry dependence risk; they are not first-line. (Source: Australian Refugee Health Practice Guide)
Generic services may lack interpreters and trauma-specific therapies; specialist refugee services are the correct AU pathway. (Source: Australian Refugee Health Practice Guide)

explanation.summary: Community treatment orders authorise mental health services to follow up, assess, and enforce treatment in the community for patients with severe mental illness who would otherwise relapse. When a carer reports concern, the AU response is direct clinical assessment, usually by home visit with appropriate safety planning. Police may attend if there is risk of harm. Involuntary admission requires mental state examination demonstrating the criteria. Family information is taken seriously but does not replace clinical assessment.
key_points: CTO authorises home visit assessment
Police only if safety risks
Family report is a trigger to assess, not to admit
explanation.pearls: Most AU jurisdictions require a clinical review within 2-3 working days of CTO breach to either restore adherence or escalate to inpatient assessment; document the timeline in clinical notes.

sources.label: RANZCP Mental Health Legislation Position Statement

options.rationale: CTOs in AU jurisdictions authorise community follow-up and assessment; the first step in suspected relapse is direct clinical assessment, with police only if safety risks. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)
An inpatient order requires direct assessment of mental state and risk; second-hand report from family does not substitute. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)
Waiting risks deterioration; the relapse pattern of medication non-adherence followed by admission is well-documented for this patient. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)
Non-contact is a sign for follow-up, not for discharge; revoking a CTO without assessment leaves no legal framework for community care. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)
Breach administration without clinical assessment is not appropriate; the CTO authorises hands-on review. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)

explanation.summary: When de-escalation and oral medication fail in acute severe behavioural disturbance, NSW Health GL2015_007 gives droperidol 10 mg IM as the first parenteral dose, a second 10 mg if the patient has not settled in 15 minutes, and a maximum of 20 mg per event. Third-line options are midazolam 5 to 10 mg IM/IV or, after senior medical consultation, ketamine 4 to 5 mg/kg IM. IM olanzapine is an alternative but has a 2 hour labelled minimum before a repeat 10 mg dose and should not be combined with a parenteral benzodiazepine. Every sedated patient needs continuous observation and monitoring in line with the ANZCA guideline for sedated ABD patients.
key_points: NSW first parenteral agent: droperidol 10 mg IM, repeat once at 15 minutes, maximum 20 mg
Third line: midazolam, or ketamine after senior medical consultation
IM olanzapine repeats sooner than 2 hours are unevaluated; do not combine it with a parenteral benzodiazepine
Monitor every sedated patient continuously
explanation.pearls: GL2015_007 describes droperidol QT prolongation as rarely clinically significant: an Australian study of 1009 patients given 10 mg or more found no torsades de pointes, so a pre-dose ECG is not required.

sources.label: NSW Health GL2015_007: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments
ANZCA guideline on care of sedated ABD patients (RANZCP-endorsed)

options.rationale: IM olanzapine is an option, but the label states that 10 mg injections given more often than 2 hours after the first dose have not been evaluated, so a 30 minute repeat is outside labelled use. It is not the NSW first-line parenteral agent. (Source: Zyprexa IntraMuscular product label; NSW Health GL2015_007)
source_refs: NSW Health GL2015_007: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

options.rationale: The manufacturer does not recommend giving IM olanzapine with a parenteral benzodiazepine because of excessive sedation and cardiorespiratory depression. (Source: Zyprexa IntraMuscular product label)

The NSW adult algorithm gives droperidol 10 mg IM as the first parenteral dose and a second 10 mg IM or IV if the patient has not settled in 15 minutes, to a maximum of 20 mg per event. Droperidol causes fewer adverse events and less need for repeat sedation than midazolam, and GL2015_007 does not require an ECG before the first dose. (Source: NSW Health GL2015_007)
source_refs: NSW Health GL2015_007: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

options.rationale: This is a UK combination (NICE). It is not part of the NSW GL2015_007 adult algorithm, which starts with droperidol and keeps midazolam or ketamine for the third line. (Source: NSW Health GL2015_007)
source_refs: NSW Health GL2015_007: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

options.rationale: NSW lists ketamine 4 to 5 mg/kg IM as a third-line ED agent after senior medical consultation, not as the first parenteral dose. (Source: NSW Health GL2015_007)
source_refs: NSW Health GL2015_007: Management of patients with acute severe behavioural disturbance in emergency departments

explanation.summary: Severe anorexia with bradycardia, electrolyte abnormalities, and a low BMI requires medical admission. Refeeding syndrome (phosphate, potassium, magnesium drop, thiamine depletion, cardiac decompensation) historically led to ultra-low starting calories. Current AU MARSIPAN and ANZAED guidance favours higher starting calories (1400-2000 kcal/day) combined with proactive electrolyte replacement and thiamine 100 mg IV or oral prior to any carbohydrate load. Cardiac monitoring is required during the first week.
key_points: Higher start (1400-2000 kcal/day) with electrolyte and thiamine cover
Thiamine before any carbohydrate
Cardiac monitoring during first week
explanation.pearls: Phosphate below 0.5 mmol/L is the strongest predictor of refeeding-related arrhythmia; replace IV with 9 mmol over 4-6 hours and recheck.

options.rationale: AU MARSIPAN and ANZAED guidance now favour higher starting calorie ranges (1400-2000 kcal/day) with proactive electrolyte and thiamine cover, rather than the historic 500-1000 kcal/day. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Practice Standards 2022)

Historic 500 kcal/day under-feeds severe AN and prolongs starvation; current AU guidelines support higher calorie start with electrolyte cover. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Practice Standards 2022)
Feeding without replacement of phosphate and other electrolytes precipitates refeeding syndrome with arrhythmia and seizures. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Practice Standards 2022)
Dextrose without prior thiamine in malnourished patients precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy; thiamine must precede any carbohydrate load. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Practice Standards 2022)
Bradycardia, electrolyte abnormalities, prolonged QTc, and BMI 13.5 are medical admission criteria; outpatient is unsafe. (Source: ANZAED Eating Disorders Practice Standards 2022)

explanation.summary: Substance-induced psychotic disorder by DSM-5 is a time-limited diagnosis that resolves within approximately one month of abstinence. Persistence beyond this point shifts the formulation toward a primary psychotic illness, with cannabis having acted as a precipitant in a vulnerable individual. Cannabis use approximately doubles schizophrenia risk in vulnerable individuals; high-potency forms further increase risk. Long-term antipsychotic treatment and early psychosis service involvement are recommended.
key_points: Substance-induced psychosis resolves within ~4 weeks of abstinence
Persistence beyond shifts diagnosis to primary disorder
Cannabis is precipitant in vulnerable people
explanation.pearls: Schizophreniform is a provisional 1-6 month placeholder; reserve for cases where you genuinely cannot predict whether the episode will remit, and re-formulate at 6 months.

options.rationale: Substance-induced psychosis is expected to resolve with abstinence; persistence at 12 weeks with confirmed abstinence and ongoing functional decline shifts the diagnosis to a primary psychotic disorder. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Early Psychosis)
Substance-induced psychosis by DSM-5 resolves within 4 weeks of abstinence; 12 weeks of persistent psychosis with confirmed abstinence excludes this. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Early Psychosis)
Brief psychotic disorder is by definition under 1 month with full return to baseline; this case has lasted 3 months with ongoing impairment. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Early Psychosis)
Schizoaffective requires a major mood episode concurrent with psychosis; no mood episode is described. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Early Psychosis)

Schizophreniform is the correct provisional label between 1 and 6 months only when the clinician cannot yet exclude full schizophrenia trajectory; at 3 months with marked functional decline a schizophrenia diagnosis is increasingly likely. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Early Psychosis)

explanation.summary: Postpartum psychosis affects 1-2 per 1000 deliveries but recurrence risk in bipolar I with a prior postpartum episode is 25-50%. Stopping mood stabilisers around delivery increases relapse risk substantially. Admission to a mother-baby unit allows treatment while preserving attachment, with antipsychotic plus benzodiazepine as the first pharmacological step. Lithium can be restarted with monitoring, and ECT is reserved for severe or treatment-resistant cases. Prominent confusion mandates organic workup including thyroid, infection, and consideration of autoimmune encephalitis.
key_points: PPP in bipolar I is high-risk: mood stabiliser at delivery prevents relapse
MBU admission preserves mother-infant attachment
Antipsychotic + benzodiazepine is the typical first regimen
explanation.pearls: Postpartum psychosis with prominent confusion warrants exclusion of NMDA receptor encephalitis - send anti-NMDA antibodies and consider EEG.

sources.label: COPE Australian Perinatal Mental Health Guideline

options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency requiring inpatient care, preferably MBU; antipsychotic plus benzodiazepine is first-line, and confusion mandates exclusion of organic mimic. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health 2023)
Outpatient management of postpartum psychosis is unsafe given infanticide and suicide risks; admission is required. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health 2023)
Baby blues do not present with delusions, hyperactivity, sleeplessness, or confusion; this is psychosis. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health 2023)
Many psychotropics are compatible with breastfeeding; cessation is a separate decision balanced with treatment needs, not a prerequisite. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health 2023)

ECT is rapidly effective in postpartum psychosis but is reserved for severe cases or non-response after a short pharmacological trial; antipsychotic plus benzodiazepine is the typical first step. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health 2023)

explanation.summary: Antenatal antidepressant decisions weigh untreated maternal depression risks (preterm birth, low birth weight, postnatal depression, impaired attachment) against medication risks. The Australian RANZCP perinatal guideline supports continuing an effective SSRI through pregnancy where the woman has a history of recurrent depression. Sertraline is the preferred first-line SSRI in pregnancy; paroxetine is avoided where possible. Fluoxetine is acceptable when already effective but is more associated with neonatal adaptation syndrome. Multidisciplinary perinatal mental health follow-up is standard.
key_points: Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in pregnancy with the largest AU evidence base.
Paroxetine has a small first-trimester cardiac malformation signal; avoid if alternatives.
Stopping in recurrent depression: 60-70% relapse within 6 months.
Multidisciplinary perinatal mental health surveillance is standard.
explanation.pearls: Sertraline is the preferred AU pregnancy SSRI; paroxetine is avoided due to first-trimester cardiac malformation signal.

sources.label: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023
COPE Perinatal Mental Health National Guideline

options.rationale: Mirtazapine has less pregnancy safety data than sertraline and is not preferred when a patient is already responding well to a first-line SSRI. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023

options.rationale: Paroxetine is associated with a small increased risk of cardiac malformations in first-trimester exposure and is not preferred when other SSRIs are options. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023

options.rationale: Fluoxetine has a long half-life and active metabolite that increases neonatal adaptation syndrome risk; sertraline is preferred when already effective. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023

options.rationale: Stopping a well-controlled SSRI in recurrent depression carries a 60-70% relapse risk within 6 months, with associated obstetric morbidity and infant outcomes. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023

options.rationale: Sertraline has the most extensive AU pregnancy evidence base and is the preferred SSRI antenatally; continuing an effective regimen avoids relapse, which is itself a fetal and maternal risk. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Clinical Practice Guideline 2023

explanation.summary: Lithium toxicity precipitates in dehydration, renal impairment, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors or thiazide diuretics, low-salt diet, and intercurrent illness. Mild toxicity (1.5-2.0 mmol/L) presents with tremor, ataxia, dysarthria and gastrointestinal symptoms; moderate (2.0-2.5) adds confusion and myoclonus; severe (>2.5) brings seizures, coma, and arrhythmia. Withhold lithium, measure serum level and UEC, treat the underlying volume loss, and arrange admission if symptomatic or level high. Haemodialysis indicated for level >2.5, neurological compromise, or renal failure.
key_points: Lithium toxicity precipitants: dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, thiazides.
Therapeutic 0.6-1.0; toxicity at 1.5+ mmol/L.
Mild: tremor, ataxia, dysarthria. Severe: seizures, coma, renal failure.
Dialysis: level >2.5, severe neurological features, or renal failure.
explanation.pearls: Mild lithium toxicity at 1.5-2.0 mmol/L presents with tremor, ataxia and dysarthria; gastroenteritis is a classic precipitant.

options.rationale: Acute illness with volume loss reduces lithium clearance and precipitates toxicity; the AU step is to withhold the dose and measure both lithium and renal function immediately because clinical features alone underestimate risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
Continuing full-dose lithium in dehydration risks progressive toxicity; oral fluids without dose adjustment or measurement are inadequate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Empirical dose halving without a serum level and renal function is unsafe; lithium has a narrow therapeutic window and the level may already be in toxic range. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Permanent cessation after a single episode of suspected toxicity is excessive; lithium is generally restarted at a reduced dose after the acute illness resolves and renal function recovers. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Haemodialysis is reserved for levels >2.5 mmol/L, severe neurological features, or renal failure; you cannot triage to dialysis without measuring the lithium level. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes sodium-channel blockade (wide QRS, terminal R in aVR, hypotension), antimuscarinic effects (mydriasis, urinary retention, ileus), seizures, and CNS depression. The cornerstone of cardiotoxic management is intravenous sodium bicarbonate, indicated when QRS >100 ms, terminal R wave in aVR >3 mm, refractory hypotension, or ventricular arrhythmia. Target QRS <120 ms and serum pH 7.50-7.55. Class IA, IC, and III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated. Refractory cases may require lipid emulsion or VA-ECMO.
key_points: TCA cardiotoxicity: QRS >100 ms, aVR terminal R >3 mm, refractory hypotension.
Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg IV bolus, repeat to target QRS <120 ms.
Target serum pH 7.50-7.55.
Avoid class IA, IC, III antiarrhythmics; avoid physostigmine.
explanation.pearls: TCA overdose: sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg when QRS >100 ms or terminal R in aVR >3 mm.

options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not tricyclic antidepressants; it is also contraindicated in TCA co-ingestion because it lowers the seizure threshold. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate seizures and asystole; it is reserved for isolated pure antimuscarinic toxidromes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

TCA cardiotoxicity from sodium-channel blockade is reversed by sodium bicarbonate boluses; an indication is QRS >100 ms or features such as terminal R wave in aVR >3 mm or refractory hypotension. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Activated charcoal in TCA overdose is considered only within 1 hour of ingestion and in an airway-protected patient; at 90 minutes the cardiotoxicity is the priority and bicarbonate should not be delayed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Class IB antiarrhythmic alone does not address the underlying sodium-channel blockade; lidocaine is a second-line option for ventricular arrhythmias after bicarbonate, not first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Atypical antipsychotic metabolic burden ranges from clozapine and olanzapine (highest) through quetiapine and risperidone (intermediate) to aripiprazole, lurasidone and ziprasidone (lowest). Monitor weight, waist, lipids, glucose and prolactin at baseline, 4 weeks, 12 weeks, and annually. When metabolic syndrome develops on olanzapine in a stable patient, the AU preferred switch is to aripiprazole, with a cross-taper over 2-4 weeks because abrupt change risks relapse. Lifestyle interventions, metformin for glycaemic concern, and statin therapy when indicated complement the switch.
key_points: Metabolic burden: clozapine/olanzapine > quetiapine/risperidone > aripiprazole.
Cross-taper olanzapine to aripiprazole over 2-4 weeks.
Add metformin for glycaemic concerns; statin if indicated by AbsCVD risk.
Baseline, 4-week, 12-week, then annual metabolic monitoring.
explanation.pearls: Aripiprazole has the lowest metabolic burden of the atypicals and is the preferred switch when olanzapine causes metabolic syndrome.

options.rationale: Risperidone has intermediate metabolic burden and high prolactin elevation; aripiprazole offers a better metabolic profile while preserving efficacy. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Maintenance Guideline 2022)

Dose reduction may modestly help but a substantial proportion of metabolic burden persists even at lower doses; switching is the AU recommendation when metabolic syndrome is established. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Maintenance Guideline 2022)

Metformin addition helps offset weight gain but does not address the dyslipidaemia or the overall metabolic profile; switching to a lower-burden antipsychotic is preferred when relapse risk allows. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Maintenance Guideline 2022)

Aripiprazole has the lowest metabolic burden among atypicals and is the AU preferred switch for olanzapine-related metabolic syndrome in stable patients with relapse risk balanced by partial dopamine agonism. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Maintenance Guideline 2022)

Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failed 2 antipsychotics at adequate dose); this patient is well controlled on olanzapine and clozapine has worse metabolic burden anyway. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Maintenance Guideline 2022)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder is distinguished from bipolar disorder with psychotic features by the requirement of at least 2 weeks of criterion A psychotic symptoms in the ABSENCE of prominent mood symptoms during the lifetime course of illness. Mood episodes must also be present for the majority of the total illness duration. Bipolar with psychotic features confines all psychotic symptoms to the mood episode. Schizoaffective subtype is bipolar type if any manic episode has occurred, depressive type otherwise. Treatment combines a mood stabiliser or antipsychotic with episode-specific care.
key_points: Schizoaffective requires ≥2 weeks of psychosis WITHOUT mood symptoms.
Bipolar with psychotic features: psychosis only during mood episodes.
Schizophrenia: mood episodes brief relative to total illness duration.
Schizoaffective subtype is bipolar type if any manic episode.
explanation.pearls: Schizoaffective vs bipolar with psychotic features: ≥2 weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms indicates schizoaffective disorder.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizoaffective and Related Disorders

options.rationale: DSM-5 schizoaffective disorder requires a mood episode concurrent with criterion A psychosis AND at least 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms without prominent mood symptoms; the 3 weeks of pure psychosis here separates it from bipolar with psychotic features. (Source: DSM-5-TR American Psychiatric Association 2022)

Bipolar I with psychotic features confines psychosis to the mood episode; the 3 weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms in this patient excludes this diagnosis. (Source: DSM-5-TR American Psychiatric Association 2022)

Schizophrenia requires criterion A symptoms for at least 6 months and mood episodes are time-limited relative to total illness duration; the prominence of mood episodes here makes schizoaffective the better fit. (Source: DSM-5-TR American Psychiatric Association 2022)

MDD with psychotic features confines psychosis to mood episodes and excludes manic episodes; this patient has clear manic features with elevated mood and reduced sleep need. (Source: DSM-5-TR American Psychiatric Association 2022)

Brief psychotic disorder is by definition less than 1 month and resolves with return to premorbid functioning; this patient has been symptomatic for 6 weeks with prior mood episodes. (Source: DSM-5-TR American Psychiatric Association 2022)

explanation.summary: Smoking in pregnancy increases miscarriage, IUGR, placental abruption, stillbirth and SIDS. Behavioural support is first-line; pharmacotherapy should be considered when behavioural alone fails. Intermittent NRT (lozenges, gum, inhaler) is preferred to patches because it allows lower total nicotine dose and self-titration. Varenicline and bupropion are contraindicated in pregnancy due to safety data gaps. Electronic cigarettes are not recommended. Partner cessation, nicotine replacement counselling, and ongoing CO breath monitoring increase quit success.
key_points: First-line: behavioural support and brief intervention.
Pharmacotherapy: intermittent NRT (lozenges, gum) preferred over patches.
Varenicline and bupropion contraindicated in pregnancy.
Electronic cigarettes not recommended.
explanation.pearls: AU pregnancy NRT: intermittent lozenges or gum over patches because self-titration reduces total fetal nicotine exposure.

options.rationale: Bupropion is contraindicated in pregnancy because of seizure threshold effects and insufficient safety data; intermittent NRT is the AU pregnancy first-line. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline 2021)

Varenicline is contraindicated in pregnancy due to insufficient safety data and a signal for neuropsychiatric effects; AU guidance does not use it antenatally. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline 2021)

RACGP and RANZCOG guidance prefers intermittent (not patch) NRT in pregnancy because lozenges and gum allow self-titration to minimum effective dose; varenicline and bupropion are contraindicated in pregnancy. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline 2021)

AU guidance does not recommend electronic cigarettes in pregnancy because of inhalation product safety concerns and unregulated nicotine doses. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline 2021)

Continuous patches give sustained nicotine that crosses the placenta; AU pregnancy guidance prefers intermittent dosing to minimise fetal nicotine exposure. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline 2021)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a clinical syndrome (not a discrete diagnosis) characterised by mutism, negativism, posturing, waxy flexibility, stupor or excitement. It is most commonly secondary to mood disorders (especially depression and bipolar), then schizophrenia, then medical causes (autoimmune encephalitis, NMS, drug withdrawal, electrolyte disturbances). The Bush-Francis lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV with reassessment in 10-15 minutes) is diagnostic and often therapeutic. Failure of response or malignant features (fever, autonomic instability, rigidity, raised CK) trigger ECT consideration. Avoid antipsychotics during active catatonia because they worsen rigidity and risk NMS.
key_points: Bush-Francis lorazepam challenge: 1-2 mg IV, reassess in 10-15 minutes.
Antipsychotics worsen catatonia and risk NMS - avoid during the syndrome.
Malignant features (fever, instability, rigidity, raised CK) escalate to ECT.
Causes: mood disorders > schizophrenia > medical (autoimmune, electrolytes).
explanation.pearls: Lorazepam 1-2 mg IV is the Bush-Francis challenge for catatonia; response at 10-15 minutes confirms diagnosis and starts treatment.

options.rationale: Dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia; malignant catatonia treatment is benzodiazepines and ECT, not dantrolene, and pre-emptive intubation is not the first step in this stable patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

ECT is the next escalation if benzodiazepines fail or the patient is malignant catatonia, but lorazepam challenge is the diagnostic and first-line therapeutic step. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Antipsychotics in catatonia risk precipitating neuroleptic malignant syndrome and worsening rigidity; they are not first-line and should be avoided until catatonia is treated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Empirical infectious cover is given when meningoencephalitis is plausible, but unblinking stare with waxy flexibility and negativism in a known depression patient is more likely catatonia; CT and clinical picture do not suggest encephalitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

The Bush-Francis lorazepam challenge is the AU first-line approach to catatonia: 1-2 mg IV with response (improved mutism, posturing, rigidity) at 10-15 minutes confirms the diagnosis and informs ongoing therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced neutropenia and agranulocytosis is the highest-risk haematological adverse effect, with risk peaking in the first 18 weeks of treatment. Australian clozapine programs (ClozapineConnect, ClopineConnect) use a traffic-light system: green (neutrophils ≥2.0 × 10^9/L, continue and routine monitoring), amber (1.0-1.5, continue with twice-weekly FBC, infection precautions), red (<1.0 or signs of infection, stop clozapine, urgent haematology, possible G-CSF). Patients with confirmed agranulocytosis are usually permanently de-registered; rechallenge requires specialist haematology and psychiatry input.
key_points: Traffic light: green ≥2.0, amber 1.0-1.5, red <1.0 (×10^9/L).
Amber: continue clozapine, twice-weekly FBC, infection precautions.
Red or febrile: stop clozapine, urgent haematology, possible G-CSF.
Rechallenge after agranulocytosis requires specialist haematology and psychiatry.
explanation.pearls: Clozapine amber alert (neutrophils 1.0-1.5): continue dose with twice-weekly FBC and infection precautions; stop only at <1.0 or febrile.

options.rationale: Australian Clopine and Clozaril protocols classify neutrophils 1.0-1.5 × 10^9/L as 'amber' alert: continue clozapine but switch to twice-weekly FBC until neutrophils recover above 2.0, with infection precautions. (Source: ClozapineConnect Australian Treatment Protocol 2024)

Cessation and G-CSF are reserved for 'red' alerts (neutrophils <0.5 × 10^9/L) or symptomatic patients; an amber-level fall in an asymptomatic patient is managed by enhanced monitoring. (Source: ClozapineConnect Australian Treatment Protocol 2024)

Dose reduction does not improve haematological recovery because clozapine-induced neutropenia is idiosyncratic, not dose-related, and reduction risks symptomatic relapse. (Source: ClozapineConnect Australian Treatment Protocol 2024)

Switching from clozapine in treatment-resistant schizophrenia after an amber alert is premature; the AU protocol allows continuation with enhanced monitoring and saves clozapine for the patient who has responded. (Source: ClozapineConnect Australian Treatment Protocol 2024)

Empirical IV antibiotics are for neutropenic fever or significant infection; this patient is asymptomatic and afebrile, so admission is not indicated. (Source: ClozapineConnect Australian Treatment Protocol 2024)

explanation.summary: EPDS ≥13 plus item 10 endorsement is the AU community threshold for further assessment and intervention. Moderate-to-severe PND benefits from combined pharmacotherapy (sertraline first-line in breastfeeding) and psychological therapy. Suicidal ideation requires a documented safety plan even when passive, and inpatient admission is reserved for active intent, psychosis, or care impairment.
key_points: EPDS ≥13 with item 10 endorsement is the AU community referral threshold
Sertraline is preferred SSRI in breastfeeding because relative infant dose is <2%
Combined SSRI plus psychological therapy beats either alone for moderate-to-severe PND
explanation.pearls: Always screen for bipolar history before starting SSRI in postpartum women - postpartum unmasking of bipolar with SSRI-induced mania is a recognised risk. EPDS item 10 is the suicide-question; any non-zero response warrants safety planning. Paroxetine has higher discontinuation symptoms; fluoxetine has the longest half-life and active metabolite.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health

options.rationale: Benzodiazepines do not treat depression, accumulate in breast milk, may cause infant sedation, and risk maternal dependence. They are not first-line for PND. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health

options.rationale: Fluoxetine is not first-line for the breastfeeding mother because its long half-life and active metabolite norfluoxetine result in higher relative infant dose than sertraline. Stopping breastfeeding is also not required for SSRI initiation. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health

options.rationale: Inpatient mother-baby admission is reserved for severe PND with active suicidal intent or plan, psychotic features, or inability to care for baby. She has passive thoughts of harm without intent or plan and is functioning to a degree; community management with safety planning is appropriate. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health

options.rationale: EPDS 18 with item 10 positive and 4 weeks of melancholic features defines moderate-to-severe postnatal depression. NHMRC and beyondblue guidance is for combined pharmacotherapy plus psychological therapy for moderate-to-severe PND. Sertraline is first-line for breastfeeding because of the lowest relative infant dose (<2%); the AU SAFEMOM database lists it as compatible with breastfeeding. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health

options.rationale: Psychological therapy alone is reasonable for mild-to-moderate PND (EPDS 10 to 13 without item 10 endorsement) but moderate-to-severe disease with passive suicidal ideation benefits from combined treatment. Waiting 2 weeks risks worsening with active suicidal ideation. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline: Perinatal Mental Health

explanation.summary: First-episode psychosis with delirium features (fluctuant attention, autonomic instability, hallucination modality other than auditory) mandates organic workup before functional diagnosis. Sympathomimetic toxidromes (amphetamines, cocaine, synthetic cannabinoids, MDMA) cause acute psychosis with mydriasis, hyperthermia, tachycardia and diaphoresis - treat with benzodiazepines, not antipsychotics, in the acute phase.
key_points: Tactile hallucinations and visual hallucinations are more suggestive of delirium / intoxication than primary psychosis
Sympathomimetic toxidrome treated with benzodiazepines first-line; avoid antipsychotics that worsen hyperthermia and QT
Steroid-induced psychosis usually occurs at >40 mg prednisolone daily and during, not after, the course
explanation.pearls: Always include a structured organic workup in first-episode psychosis: blood ammonia, B12, TSH, syphilis, HIV, autoimmune (anti-NMDA receptor antibody), MRI, EEG, and urine drug screen including synthetic cannabinoids. Ammonia derangement is the missed diagnosis in young men with new psychosis on valproate.

options.rationale: Fluctuant attention, sympathomimetic features (mydriasis, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, warm flushed skin), and tactile hallucinations point to delirium - probably from stimulant use at the music festival, not primary psychosis. RANZCP defines first-episode psychosis with these features as needing organic workup completed before functional diagnosis. Antipsychotics in acute stimulant intoxication may worsen hyperthermia; benzodiazepines are first-line. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

HSV encephalitis is a reasonable differential but he is afebrile with normal CRP, normal MRI, no neck stiffness, no headache, and an alternative cause is more likely from history; he also has the toxidrome of stimulants. Empirical aciclovir is not the most appropriate immediate step unless the LP is showing pleocytosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Encephalitis)

Steroid-induced psychosis usually occurs during steroid therapy and at higher doses (typically above 40 to 60 mg prednisolone daily). The prednisolone course has already finished 3 days ago and the sympathomimetic features are not steroid-induced; this is a misattribution. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

Diagnosing primary psychosis without completing organic workup is the AU sentinel-event lesson learned from missed encephalitis, delirium tropicale and stimulant toxidromes. Olanzapine carries QT prolongation and hyperthermia risk in stimulant toxicity. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

An acutely confused agitated patient with sympathomimetic features and disorientation is not safe for discharge. Acute toxic delirium has a measurable mortality if missed. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Adolescent anorexia nervosa with bradycardia (HR under 50), postural BP drop above 20 mmHg, hypothermia, prolonged QTc above 460 ms, hypoglycaemia, or refeeding-syndrome risk markers (low K, Mg, phosphate) requires medical admission. Refeed cautiously at 20 kcal/kg/day with daily electrolyte checks. Family-based therapy is the longitudinal psychological therapy after medical stabilisation.
key_points: ANZAED admission criteria: HR<50, BP drop>20, hypothermia, QTc>460, BMI<75% expected, refeeding risk
Start refeeding at 20 kcal/kg/day; daily electrolyte and phosphate checks for first 5 to 7 days
SSRIs are ineffective in underweight anorexia - defer pharmacotherapy until weight restoration
explanation.pearls: Phosphate is the most commonly seen refeeding electrolyte to drop; prophylactic thiamine 200 mg IV before glucose load (Wernicke prevention) is standard. Family-based treatment (Maudsley method) is first-line psychological therapy for adolescents.

options.rationale: GCS is preserved but cardiovascular instability (HR 42, postural drop, QTc 480) makes home management with daily GP review unsafe. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)
SSRIs are ineffective in underweight anorexia nervosa because of serotonergic depletion at low weight; antidepressant trial is deferred until weight is restored. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

Olanzapine is not first-line in adolescent anorexia nervosa; weak evidence supports a small weight gain but it does not address the urgent metabolic and cardiac risks. Admission and refeeding are more critical now. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

Outpatient management is contraindicated when medical-admission criteria are met. Family-based therapy is the appropriate longitudinal therapy but begins after medical stabilisation when she meets admission criteria. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

RANZCP eating disorder guidelines and the ANZAED guidelines have defined medical-admission criteria: pulse under 50, postural BP drop above 20 mmHg, hypothermia, prolonged QTc above 460 ms, glucose under 3.5, refeeding-syndrome risk markers (hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia, hypomagnesaemia), and BMI under 75% of expected. She meets multiple. Start refeeding cautiously at 20 kcal/kg/day, correcting electrolytes before increasing calories. (Source: RANZCP Practice Guidelines)

explanation.summary: AU first-line for adult ADHD is long-acting methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine, started by a psychiatrist under Schedule 8 authority. Commercial driving is not contraindicated; Austroads requires stable medication, no impairment, and at least annual clinical review with notification of the medical assessor. SSRI-stimulant combinations are well tolerated; atomoxetine has CYP2D6 interactions with SSRIs.
key_points: Long-acting methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine is AU first-line for adult ADHD
Austroads allows stimulant ADHD therapy with commercial driving subject to medical assessor notification and stability
Atomoxetine has CYP2D6 interactions with SSRIs; titrate slowly
explanation.pearls: Schedule 8 prescribing requires psychiatrist authority in most jurisdictions; check state-based S8 stimulant rules (NSW vs Vic differ). Cardiovascular screening before starting stimulants is mandatory; ECG only required if family history of sudden cardiac death or personal cardiac history.

options.rationale: AU Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive guidance allows commercial driving with stable, supervised stimulant medication for ADHD provided the medication has been stable for at least 4 weeks, the patient is not impaired, and an annual review by the treating psychiatrist confirms ongoing fitness. Long-acting methylphenidate is first-line for adult ADHD in AU. The medical assessor will need to be informed and follow Austroads guidance. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Notifying the medical assessor is part of the driver's and clinician's responsibility in AU under the Austroads framework; failing to notify breaches mandatory reporting requirements for heavy vehicle medical certification. Twice-daily dexamfetamine in a long-haul driver also risks afternoon waning. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

AU practice does not require stopping commercial driving to treat ADHD; treatment may improve safety. The supervised-stable-medication pathway in Austroads is the standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Clonidine is used as adjunct, often for sleep onset or as adjunct to stimulants in children. It is not first-line monotherapy for adult ADHD in AU. It is also sedating and could compromise commercial driving. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Atomoxetine is a second-line agent in ADHD with smaller effect size and slower onset (4 to 6 weeks). It is not contraindicated for commercial driving but stimulants are not blanket-prohibited; the Austroads decision is made on clinical stability rather than drug class.
