Family or personal history of bipolar disorder is the major risk
Admit to mother-baby unit (when available)
Risk of suicide and infanticide remains until resolution
explanation.pearls: Women with a history of postpartum psychosis or bipolar I have approximately 50% risk of relapse in a subsequent pregnancy; prophylactic lithium at delivery is the AU recommended preventive intervention in shared planning.

sources.label: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

options.rationale: This is postpartum psychosis (psychotic features, sleeplessness, mood lability, abrupt onset within the first weeks postpartum), not postnatal depression. SSRI alone does not treat psychosis. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

options.rationale: Outpatient management of postpartum psychosis is unsafe; suicide and infanticide risks are elevated and admission to a mother-baby unit is the AU standard. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

options.rationale: Community management is reserved for mild postnatal mental illness with intact reality testing and adequate supports; psychotic features mandate inpatient mother-baby unit care. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

options.rationale: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency with a significant suicide and infanticide risk; admission to a mother-baby unit allows joint care while ensuring infant safety. An antipsychotic (olanzapine or risperidone) is first-line; lithium has strong evidence for prevention of recurrence and acute treatment, with shared breastfeeding decisions about infant lithium monitoring. ECT is considered for severe or refractory cases or when rapid response is needed. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement; COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

options.rationale: CBT does not treat acute psychosis and outpatient settings cannot guarantee infant safety; this is an emergency. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement)
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Position Statement

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder is differentiated from bipolar I with psychotic features and from schizophrenia by the temporal relationship between mood and psychotic symptoms. DSM-5-TR requires: (1) major mood episode (depressive or manic) concurrent with criterion A of schizophrenia, (2) delusions or hallucinations for at least 2 weeks without a major mood episode at any time in the lifetime of the illness, (3) mood symptoms present for the majority of the total active and residual periods. Subtypes are bipolar type and depressive type. Management combines antipsychotic with mood stabiliser (lithium, valproate, lamotrigine) and structured psychosocial intervention. Longitudinal records and collateral history are essential to differentiate from bipolar I with psychotic features.
key_points: At least 2 weeks of psychosis WITHOUT major mood episode (lifetime) - the distinguishing criterion
Concurrent major mood episode plus criterion A of schizophrenia
Mood symptoms present for the majority of active and residual phases
Subtype by lifetime presence or absence of manic episodes
explanation.pearls: In schizoaffective disorder, mood symptoms occupy the majority of the total active and residual illness; if they occupy a small fraction with chronic psychosis dominating, the diagnosis is schizophrenia with mood episodes.

options.rationale: Bipolar I with psychotic features requires psychotic symptoms occurring only during mood episodes; the documented inter-episode psychosis disqualifies this label. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG; DSM-5-TR)

Schizophrenia requires 6 months of disturbance with at least 1 month of active-phase positive symptoms; the prominent and recurrent mood episodes with mood-congruent psychosis are too prominent for schizophrenia. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

This option correctly identifies the schizoaffective construct but uses imprecise terminology; the DSM-5-TR requires the major mood episodes to be present for the majority of the total active illness duration and at least 2 weeks of psychosis without prominent mood symptoms - the question's diagnostic phrasing differs. The intended best option pairs the bipolar type label with the specific 2-week inter-episode psychosis criterion. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

Delusional disorder requires non-bizarre delusions for at least 1 month without hallucinations or other psychotic features prominent enough to meet schizophrenia criteria; this patient has prominent hallucinations and prior psychotic episodes that exceed that. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type requires (1) an uninterrupted period during which there is a major mood episode (depressive or manic) concurrent with criterion A of schizophrenia, (2) delusions or hallucinations for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a major mood episode during the lifetime of the illness, (3) mood symptoms present for the majority of the active and residual phases. This patient meets all three. The bipolar subtype is assigned because manic episodes have occurred. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG; DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Adult autism in women is frequently identified late because of masking (consciously or unconsciously hiding autistic traits in social settings) and restricted interests aligned with socially accepted domains. Diagnosis is by specialist multidisciplinary assessment with a structured developmental interview (parent-informant if possible) and an observational measure. RANZCP guidance acknowledges the female phenotype and the high comorbidity with anxiety and depression. Management is post-diagnosis and includes psychoeducation, occupational input, sensory environment modification, and concurrent treatment of comorbid anxiety or depression. Late diagnosis often produces relief and improved self-understanding for the person.
key_points: Masking and internalising features common in women with late diagnosis
Multidisciplinary assessment with ADI-R/ADOS-2 (or AU equivalents)
High comorbidity with anxiety and depression
Workplace accommodation under DDA requires assessment first
explanation.pearls: The Autism Quotient (AQ-50) is a self-rated screening tool with a clinical cut-off at 32; sensitivity is reasonable but specificity is modest, so a positive screen prompts referral rather than confirming diagnosis.

options.rationale: Anxiety is a comorbidity and not a substitute for the autism assessment she has requested; anxiety treatment alone misses the developmental diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP CPG ASD; NICE Adult Autism Guideline)
High autonomic load with masking is characteristic of late-recognised autism in women; functional achievement does not exclude autism. (Source: RANZCP CPG ASD)

Adult autism assessment requires multidisciplinary specialist input including a structured developmental interview (ADI-R or equivalent) and an observational assessment (ADOS-2) with attention to female phenotype features (masking, intense restricted interests in socially accepted domains, internalising comorbidity). General practice screening with AQ-50 above threshold supports referral but does not constitute diagnosis. Concurrent anxiety management is appropriate but does not replace the diagnostic pathway. (Source: RANZCP CPG ASD)

Workplace accommodation under the DDA depends on a formal diagnosis being established or the worker self-identifying as having a disability; assessment is the prerequisite. (Source: Australian Human Rights Commission)
Intranasal oxytocin is not a TGA-approved or AU first-line treatment for autism; evidence is mixed and use is restricted to research settings. (Source: TGA)

explanation.summary: Australian guidance ranks varenicline as the first-line single agent for nicotine dependence in adults able to take it. The 2016 EAGLES trial demonstrated comparable neuropsychiatric safety in stable psychiatric patients to non-psychiatric controls, leading to removal of the prior FDA boxed warning. Combination NRT (patch plus oral form) is the alternative first-line for those unable to tolerate varenicline. Bupropion is contraindicated in seizure disorder and bipolar disorder. Behavioural support amplifies pharmacotherapy effect. Smoking cessation increases plasma levels of clozapine, olanzapine, theophylline (CYP1A2 induction by tobacco smoke reverses on cessation) and dose review is required; sertraline is not affected.
key_points: Varenicline first-line; safe in stable depression per EAGLES
NRT combination as first-line alternative
Bupropion contraindicated in seizure disorder
Cessation increases CYP1A2 substrate levels (clozapine, olanzapine, theophylline)
explanation.pearls: Smoking cessation increases plasma clozapine concentration by 50-100% within 2-4 weeks through CYP1A2 de-induction; the clozapine dose is reduced by about 30% at cessation with weekly level monitoring.

options.rationale: Bupropion is contraindicated in active seizure disorder and is best avoided in patients with reduced seizure threshold; varenicline has better cessation outcomes in EAGLES and is no longer considered to worsen neuropsychiatric outcomes. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline)

Combination NRT is reasonable second-line, but varenicline has the highest single-agent cessation success rates in the EAGLES trial population including stable depression. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline)
Nortriptyline is a third-line agent; it has cardiac and anticholinergic effects that are less favourable than varenicline in stable depression. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline)
Clonidine is fourth-line at best and is not the AU first-line; sedation, hypotension, and rebound limit its use. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline)

Varenicline (alpha-4 beta-2 nicotinic partial agonist) is the AU first-line single agent with the highest cessation rates. The 2016 EAGLES trial demonstrated no increase in neuropsychiatric adverse events in patients with stable psychiatric disorders compared with placebo. Stable depression on SSRI is not a contraindication. The 12-week course is started 8 days before the planned quit date with titration to 1 mg twice daily. Smoking cessation does not reduce SSRI efficacy but smoking cessation does increase plasma levels of some psychotropics (clozapine, olanzapine) through CYP1A2; sertraline is unaffected. (Source: RACGP Supporting Smoking Cessation Guideline; EAGLES trial)

explanation.summary: Borderline personality disorder responds best to structured psychological therapy. Australian (NHMRC) guidance lists dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation-based therapy, schema-focused therapy, and transference-focused therapy as first-line. Pharmacotherapy is reserved for clearly defined comorbidities (current major depression, persistent generalised anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder) or short-term crisis use; routine SSRI or antipsychotic use for emotional dysregulation alone is discouraged. A written crisis plan with the patient, a primary treating clinician, and a clear pathway for short focused admissions (commonly under 72 hours) is more effective than reactive long-stay admission. The recovery trajectory is more favourable than once thought, with majority remission of BPD criteria over a decade.
key_points: First-line: DBT, MBT, schema therapy, TFP
Pharmacotherapy reserved for comorbidity or short-term crisis
Brief admission only; long-stay risks worsening
Crisis plan, primary clinician, scheduled review
explanation.pearls: The LABILE trial (Lancet Psychiatry 2018) showed no benefit of lamotrigine over placebo for BPD affective symptoms; AU guidance has reduced routine use of mood stabilisers in this population.

options.rationale: SSRIs are not first-line for BPD core symptoms; the AU guidance reserves psychotropics for clear comorbid depression, anxiety, or short-term crisis use, and removes them for emotional dysregulation alone. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines; RANZCP CPG Personality Disorder)

Inpatient admission is reserved for acute crisis with imminent risk and short stays (commonly under 72 hours); prolonged admission risks worsening BPD outcomes. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines)
Routine as-needed antipsychotic for distress is discouraged; structured psychological therapy with crisis planning is the evidence-based treatment. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines)

Australian NHMRC and RANZCP guidance position structured psychological therapy (DBT, MBT, schema-focused therapy, transference-focused therapy) as the cornerstone of BPD treatment. Pharmacotherapy is reserved for clearly defined comorbidities or short-term crisis use. A written crisis plan, safety planning, and a relationship with one primary treating clinician reduces hospitalisation and improves outcomes. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines; RANZCP CPG Personality Disorder)

Recent trials (LABILE 2018) showed lamotrigine offers no advantage over placebo for BPD affective symptoms; the AU guidance does not recommend it as first-line. (Source: NHMRC BPD Clinical Practice Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder is distinguished from bipolar disorder with psychotic features by the presence of delusions or hallucinations for 2 weeks or more in the ABSENCE of a major mood episode at some point during the illness. Mood symptoms must be present for the majority of the active and residual illness duration (otherwise primary schizophrenia with mood symptoms is the diagnosis). Bipolar subtype includes manic episodes; depressive subtype includes only depressive episodes. Treatment requires both mood stabilisation (lithium, valproate, or atypical with mood stabilising effect such as quetiapine, olanzapine, aripiprazole) and antipsychotic effect, often via the same atypical agent.
key_points: 2+ weeks of psychosis in absence of mood episode at some point
Mood symptoms majority of active/residual illness duration
Bipolar subtype if manic episode present
Treatment: mood stabiliser plus antipsychotic effect
explanation.pearls: The 2-week criterion of psychosis without mood episode most clearly separates schizoaffective disorder from bipolar with psychotic features; a careful longitudinal interval history is essential.

options.rationale: Bipolar I with mood-congruent psychosis has psychosis only during mood episodes; this patient has 2 weeks or more of psychosis during euthymia, which excludes the diagnosis. (Source: DSM-5-TR)
Urine drug screen is negative and the symptom pattern is not time-locked to substance use; substance-induced disorder requires temporal association with substance exposure. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

Recurrent severe major depression with psychosis fits some criteria but does not explain the manic episode, which qualifies the patient for bipolar spectrum or schizoaffective consideration. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

DSM-5-TR schizoaffective disorder requires: (1) major mood episode (depressive or manic) concurrent with criterion A of schizophrenia for an uninterrupted period; (2) delusions or hallucinations for 2 weeks or more in the absence of a major mood episode at some time during the lifetime duration; (3) major mood episode symptoms present for the majority of the active and residual illness duration; (4) not attributable to substance or medical cause. The 2-week euthymic interval with persistent psychosis distinguishes schizoaffective from bipolar with psychosis. Bipolar subtype is used because of the manic episode. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)
Schizophreniform disorder lasts under 6 months; this patient's illness has been at least 1 year and includes prominent mood episodes meeting full criteria. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Differentiating cannabis-induced psychosis from primary schizophrenia in a young user requires longitudinal assessment of symptoms during abstinence. Cannabis-induced psychotic disorder resolves within days to a few weeks of abstinence; persistent symptoms beyond 4 weeks of demonstrated abstinence, sustained negative symptoms, and functional decline support primary schizophrenia. Cannabis is a risk factor for schizophrenia onset, especially when high-potency, daily, and used in adolescence; the odds ratio is approximately threefold in heavy daily users. Treatment uses an atypical antipsychotic (aripiprazole, olanzapine, risperidone) plus structured substance use disorder management; cannabis cessation is the most modifiable risk for relapse.
key_points: Cannabis-induced psychosis: resolves within days-weeks of abstinence
Persistent psychosis beyond 4 weeks abstinence supports primary psychosis
Cannabis is risk factor (OR ~3) for schizophrenia in heavy users
Cessation is the most modifiable relapse risk
explanation.pearls: High-potency cannabis (>=10% THC) used daily in adolescence is associated with a dose-response increase in schizophrenia risk; an Australian young person presenting with first-episode psychosis should be screened with quantitative cannabis history.

options.rationale: Cannabis-induced psychosis resolves within days to weeks of abstinence; persistent psychosis through 4 weeks of abstinence is inconsistent. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)
Schizotypal personality disorder does not include sustained delusions, hallucinations, or thought broadcasting; this patient's presentation fits frank psychotic illness. (Source: DSM-5-TR)
Brief psychotic disorder lasts under 1 month; this patient's psychotic symptoms have been continuous over 8-12 months with negative symptoms and functional decline. (Source: DSM-5-TR)
His PHQ-9 is in the mild-to-moderate range and there is no acute mood episode; cannabis-related psychosis without mood prominence is not depression. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

Continuous psychotic symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, thought broadcasting) through 4 weeks of cannabis abstinence, with functional decline over 12 months, sustained negative symptoms over 8 months, family history, and high-potency cannabis use as a risk factor, fits primary schizophrenia. Cannabis use is causally associated (genetic risk and high-potency THC exposure increase schizophrenia odds ratio approximately threefold) but does not redefine the diagnosis when symptoms persist beyond cannabis clearance. Treatment includes atypical antipsychotic and structured substance use disorder care. (Source: RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia; DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: ECT is the most effective treatment for severe depression with food and fluid refusal, persistent suicidal ideation, catatonia or psychotic features. In pregnancy it is safe with obstetric review, left lateral tilt to avoid aortocaval compression, continuous fetal heart rate monitoring, intubation in the second and third trimesters and short-acting anaesthesia. The second trimester is the lowest-risk window. Consent is the pivot: a voluntary patient with capacity who consents in writing needs no Tribunal involvement in NSW, and certificates from two medical practitioners, at least one a psychiatrist, complete the requirements. A course is typically 6 to 12 treatments given 2 to 3 times weekly.
key_points: ECT in pregnancy is safe with obstetric review and continuous fetal monitoring.
Left lateral tilt avoids aortocaval compression.
Intubate in the second and third trimesters; mask ventilation is inadequate.
A consenting voluntary patient with capacity needs no NSW Tribunal inquiry.
explanation.pearls: In NSW, applying to the Tribunal for a patient who has already given valid written consent is not merely unnecessary, it delays treatment by a week or more while she is not eating or drinking.

sources.label: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy

options.rationale: Food and fluid refusal with active suicidal ideation in pregnancy is an acute risk to mother and fetus, and another drug trial does not address it. (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders)

ECT is safe and effective in pregnancy when depression is severe or refractory or there is food and fluid refusal. The setup is obstetric review, left lateral tilt to avoid aortocaval compression, continuous fetal monitoring, intubation rather than mask ventilation in the second and third trimesters, and short-acting anaesthesia. Consent is already valid: capacity intact, informed, voluntary and in writing. (Source: RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders; RANZCP Position Statement on ECT)

An ECT inquiry is for a detained or involuntary patient, or a person under 16, or a voluntary patient whose capacity is in doubt. She is a voluntary patient with documented capacity who has consented in writing, so the requirement is certificates from two medical practitioners, at least one a psychiatrist. (Source: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy

options.rationale: Lithium carries first-trimester teratogenicity risk, notably Ebstein anomaly, and demands close monitoring through pregnancy and delivery; it is not the first move here. (Source: AMH; RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders)
Ketamine is not TGA approved for major depression in pregnancy and is confined to research or named-patient use, while ECT is the established pathway. (Source: TGA; RANZCP CPG Mood Disorders)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome of motor abnormality with mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, echophenomena, stereotypy, and grimacing. It occurs in primary mood disorders (especially bipolar), schizophrenia spectrum disorders, autoimmune encephalitis (especially anti-NMDAR in young women), medical illness, and substance states. Diagnosis uses the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (2+ of the first 14 items = catatonia). The lorazepam challenge (2 mg IV with reassessment at 5-10 minutes) is both diagnostic and therapeutic; a positive response (50% or greater reduction in BFCRS) confirms catatonia and prompts scheduled lorazepam. Antipsychotics are avoided because they can precipitate NMS. ECT is the next step for failure or malignant catatonia. Autoimmune encephalitis workup proceeds in parallel in young women with no clear psychiatric history.
key_points: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale: 2+ first-14 items = catatonia
Lorazepam challenge 2 mg IV: diagnostic and therapeutic
Avoid antipsychotics while active (risk of NMS)
ECT second-line; immune workup for young women
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis) is indistinguishable from neuroleptic malignant syndrome and is treated with the same urgent withdrawal of antipsychotics, supportive care, and ECT.

options.rationale: Autoimmune encephalitis (e.g. anti-NMDAR) workup is reasonable in young women with catatonia, but the immediate diagnostic and therapeutic step is a lorazepam challenge; immune therapy is reserved once autoimmune cause is established. (Source: BAP catatonia consensus; Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale)

The lorazepam challenge (2 mg IV with reassessment at 5-10 minutes) is both diagnostic and therapeutic for catatonia. A positive response (50% or greater reduction in Bush-Francis Rating Scale) confirms the diagnosis and the patient is then commenced on scheduled lorazepam (typically 6-21 mg/day divided 8-hourly) titrated to response. Antipsychotics are AVOIDED while catatonia is active because they can precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome. ECT is the second-line response if lorazepam fails or for malignant catatonia. (Source: BAP catatonia consensus; RANZCP Position Statement on ECT)

Antipsychotics are AVOIDED in active catatonia because they can precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome and worsen the catatonic state; benzodiazepines are first-line. (Source: BAP catatonia consensus)

ECT is highly effective for catatonia, including malignant catatonia, but the AU sequence trials lorazepam first; ECT is the next step if benzodiazepines fail or for life-threatening features. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement on ECT)

NMS is excluded by normal temperature, normal creatine kinase, normal white cell count, no rigidity, and no recent antipsychotic exposure; the clinical picture is non-malignant catatonia. (Source: BAP catatonia consensus)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is the most teratogenic of all anticonvulsants and mood stabilisers, with a 10% major malformation rate (neural tube defects, cardiac, craniofacial, limb anomalies) and a 30 to 40% neurodevelopmental impairment rate; both rates are dose-dependent above 700 mg/day. The TGA pregnancy prevention program (mirroring the European RMP) requires that women of reproductive potential do not receive valproate unless no alternative is effective, that they use highly effective contraception, and that annual specialist review confirms ongoing need. Cross-titration to lithium, lamotrigine or an atypical antipsychotic is the standard pre-conception plan. Lithium carries a small risk of Ebstein's anomaly (now estimated at <1%) which is acceptable against valproate exposure.
key_points: Valproate teratogenicity: 10% malformation, 30-40% neurodevelopmental
TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program mandates alternatives
Lithium acceptable in bipolar I planning pregnancy (Ebstein risk <1%)
Cross-titrate before conception; do not stop abruptly
explanation.pearls: Valproate confers a 30-40% neurodevelopmental impairment risk (fetal valproate syndrome) and a 10% major malformation rate; lithium's Ebstein's anomaly risk in pregnancy is now estimated at under 1%, making lithium the preferred swap for bipolar I planning conception.

options.rationale: Folic acid 5 mg reduces neural tube defect risk modestly but does not address the broader spectrum of valproate teratogenicity; continuing valproate when alternatives exist breaches the TGA pregnancy prevention program. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program)

Sodium valproate is teratogenic (10% major malformations, 40% neurodevelopmental impairment) and is contraindicated in women planning pregnancy unless no alternative exists; the RANZCP and TGA pregnancy prevention program mandates discontinuation before conception, with lithium an evidence-supported alternative given prior good response in the family. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guidelines; TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program; AMH)

Lower-dose valproate retains teratogenicity (especially neurodevelopmental risk above 700 mg/day) and would also raise relapse risk; dose reduction is not a safe pregnancy strategy. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program)

Lamotrigine has lower teratogenicity than valproate but is more effective for bipolar depression than for mania prevention; given her prior manic episodes lithium is the better-evidenced choice. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guidelines)
Abrupt discontinuation without bridging mood stabiliser carries a high mania relapse risk; supervised cross-titration to a safer agent is the correct approach. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose carries cardiotoxicity (sodium channel blockade causing QRS widening, hypotension, ventricular arrhythmia), CNS depression (drowsiness, seizures), anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, mydriasis, urinary retention, tachycardia) and alpha-blockade (hypotension). ECG markers of severe toxicity are QRS >100 ms, terminal R wave in aVR >3 mm, and rightward axis. Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV is the antidote, working by alkalinisation and sodium loading to displace TCA from cardiac sodium channels; aim for arterial pH 7.50 to 7.55. Hypertonic saline is an alternative when alkalosis is contraindicated. Lipid emulsion is reserved for refractory arrest. Intubation is required for GCS deterioration, seizures or progressive cardiotoxicity to prevent acidaemia worsening sodium channel blockade.
key_points: QRS >100 ms or aVR terminal R >3 mm = severe toxicity
IV NaHCO3 1-2 mmol/kg bolus targeting pH 7.50-7.55
Intubate for progressive CNS depression to prevent acidaemic deterioration
Flumazenil contraindicated in TCA co-ingestion
explanation.pearls: In tricyclic overdose, QRS over 100 ms predicts seizures and QRS over 160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmia; IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg targets QRS narrowing and arterial pH 7.50 to 7.55.

options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose with sodium channel blockade because it can precipitate seizures that worsen acidosis and TCA toxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology)

Charcoal at one hour post-ingestion may have some role in alert patients with intact airway, but in a drowsy patient with progressive QRS it should not delay sodium bicarbonate or airway control. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology)

Torsades is uncommon in TCA overdose; the dominant arrhythmia mechanism is sodium channel blockade, addressed by bicarbonate. Magnesium is reserved for documented torsades or hypomagnesaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology)

QRS prolongation >100 ms with widening trend in TCA overdose is the trigger for IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus to overcome cardiac sodium channel blockade; ongoing CNS depression with rising QRS heralds seizure and arrhythmia and warrants airway control. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology; ANZCOR Toxic Cardiac Arrest)
TCA levels do not correlate well with toxicity and are not used to guide acute management; ECG and clinical features drive treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Adolescent non-suicidal self-injury is common (lifetime prevalence around 17%) and most often reflects emotion regulation rather than suicidal intent, but it is a marker of future suicide risk and warrants structured assessment. The HEEADSSS framework guides psychosocial history. Safety planning is collaboratively constructed with the young person and a parent or trusted adult: it lists warning signs, internal coping strategies, social distractions, people to contact, professional supports and means restriction. Rapid follow up with the local Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service (CAMHS) within 72 hours is the Australian standard. Inpatient admission is reserved for acute suicidal intent with means or plan, severe psychiatric illness needing inpatient treatment, or unsafe home environment.
key_points: NSSI lifetime prevalence in adolescents around 17%
Structured safety plan with means restriction is core
CAMHS rapid follow up within 72 hours
Inpatient admission only for active suicidal intent with plan/means or unsafe home
explanation.pearls: Safety planning in adolescent self-harm follows the Stanley-Brown template: warning signs, internal coping, social distractions, support people, professional contacts and means restriction; rapid CAMHS follow up within 72 hours is the Australian discharge standard.

sources.label: RANZCP CPG: Adolescent Mood and Self Harm

options.rationale: Six week GP review is too long for a first NSSI presentation; structured safety planning plus rapid CAMHS follow up within 72 hours is the standard. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Adolescent Mood and Self Harm)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG: Adolescent Mood and Self Harm

options.rationale: Involuntary admission requires risk of serious harm to self or others not manageable in the community; her chronic NSSI without current intent or plan can be safely managed outpatient with parental support. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Adolescent Mood and Self Harm)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG: Adolescent Mood and Self Harm

options.rationale: Brief paediatric ward admission for chronic NSSI lacks therapeutic structure, can reinforce admission-seeking and is not recommended; outpatient follow up is preferred when risk allows. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Adolescent Mood and Self Harm)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG: Adolescent Mood and Self Harm

options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy is not first-line for adolescent self-harm without a clear major depressive episode; psychological intervention (DBT-informed or CBT) is the first step. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Adolescent Mood and Self Harm)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG: Adolescent Mood and Self Harm

options.rationale: She has chronic non-suicidal self-injury without current suicidal intent or plan, a supportive parent, and willingness to engage; current Australian guidelines support outpatient management with structured safety planning and rapid CAMHS follow up. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Adolescent Mood and Self Harm; eMHPrac)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG: Adolescent Mood and Self Harm

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome of motor immobility, mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, echolalia, echopraxia and stereotypies that may arise in mood disorders, schizophrenia, autism, post-stroke states, drug-induced presentations and medical illness. The Bush Francis Catatonia Rating Scale identifies cases and malignant catatonia adds fever, rigidity, autonomic instability and elevated CK. The lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV) is both diagnostic and therapeutic with response within 10 minutes confirming the syndrome. Maintenance lorazepam 6 to 24 mg/day is titrated to response and ECT is the second-line treatment reserved for non-responders or malignant catatonia. Antipsychotics should be paused as they can worsen non-malignant catatonia.
key_points: Bush Francis Catatonia Rating Scale for diagnosis
IV lorazepam 1-2 mg challenge is first-line; maintenance 6-24 mg/day
Pause antipsychotics during catatonia treatment
Malignant catatonia (fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, raised CK) needs ECT
explanation.pearls: The lorazepam challenge in catatonia: 1 to 2 mg IV with reassessment at 10 minutes; a dramatic response (mute patient who suddenly speaks, eats, moves) is both diagnostic and guides maintenance titration to 6 to 24 mg/day.

options.rationale: Antidepressant rotation does not address acute catatonia; benzodiazepines or ECT are the treatments, and abrupt cessation has its own risks. (Source: RANZCP CPG Catatonia)

Bush Francis positive catatonia in the absence of fever and rigidity is non-malignant catatonia; first-line treatment is a lorazepam challenge 1 to 2 mg IV, with response (often dramatic) confirming diagnosis and guiding maintenance dosing of 6 to 24 mg/day. (Source: RANZCP CPG Catatonia; AMH)
There is no fever, no rigidity and no autonomic instability; NMS is not the syndrome, and dantrolene exposes her to hepatotoxicity without benefit. (Source: RANZCP CPG Catatonia)
Non-convulsive status is worth excluding when investigations are equivocal, but should not delay a lorazepam challenge which is itself anticonvulsant and diagnostic. (Source: RANZCP CPG Catatonia)

ECT is highly effective and is the second-line treatment if lorazepam fails; in current Australian practice the lorazepam challenge is offered first because of its diagnostic yield and lower invasiveness. (Source: RANZCP CPG Catatonia)

explanation.summary: Smoking cessation in Australia follows a stepped approach: brief intervention with the 5As (Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange), behavioural support and pharmacotherapy. First-line agents are varenicline (12 weeks, dose escalation in week 1), combination nicotine replacement (long-acting patch plus short-acting form), and bupropion. Varenicline has the highest absolute quit rate. The EAGLES trial demonstrated no excess cardiovascular or neuropsychiatric events with varenicline, dispelling earlier concerns and supporting its use in patients with stable cardiovascular and mental health comorbidity. Nicotine vaping is restricted to prescription-only and is positioned as second-line by the TGA. Cardiac rehab is the ideal cessation window post-MI.
key_points: Varenicline = highest absolute quit rate (NNT ~8)
EAGLES trial: no excess CV or neuropsychiatric events
Combination NRT outperforms single NRT
Nicotine vaping is prescription-only, second-line in Australia
explanation.pearls: Varenicline post-ACS is safe per EAGLES and AHA secondary-prevention statements; the dose escalation (0.5 mg daily x 3 days, 0.5 mg twice daily x 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily for 11 weeks) is the standard 12-week course.

options.rationale: Combination NRT outperforms single NRT, but varenicline retains the highest single-agent efficacy; combination NRT is the preferred next-line when varenicline is contraindicated or not tolerated. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

Bupropion is effective but has roughly half the absolute quit rate of varenicline; it is also contraindicated in patients with seizure risk and lowers seizure threshold. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

Varenicline is the most effective single agent for smoking cessation (NNT approximately 8 versus placebo) and the EAGLES trial confirmed no excess cardiovascular or neuropsychiatric events; it is preferred over single-agent NRT, particularly after failed NRT alone. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines; EAGLES trial; AMH)

Nortriptyline has demonstrated efficacy in smoking cessation but is third-line in Australia given anticholinergic burden and TCA cardiotoxicity, particularly post-MI. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

Nicotine vaping is available in Australia by prescription as a second-line cessation aid when first-line pharmacotherapies have failed; first-line varenicline should be offered first. (Source: TGA Nicotine Vaping Products; RACGP Smoking Cessation Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder in refugee and asylum-seeker populations has a prevalence of 30-50% depending on conflict exposure and post-migration stressors. First-line treatment is trauma-focused psychological therapy: TF-CBT, EMDR, or cognitive processing therapy. Therapy should be delivered in a culturally appropriate way, often with an accredited interpreter familiar with mental health vocabulary. Pharmacotherapy (SSRIs such as sertraline or paroxetine) is second-line and useful when therapy is unavailable, declined or when comorbid major depression is severe. Benzodiazepines are NOT recommended (worsen PTSD outcomes). Post-migration stressors (housing, finances, family reunion, immigration status) must be addressed as social determinants alongside symptom-focused care.
key_points: First line PTSD: trauma-focused CBT, EMDR, or cognitive processing therapy
SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine) are second-line
Benzodiazepines avoided
Address post-migration stressors as part of care
explanation.pearls: Phoenix Australia guidelines place trauma-focused psychological therapy (TF-CBT, EMDR, cognitive processing therapy) as first-line for PTSD across populations; benzodiazepines are explicitly discouraged because they worsen long-term outcomes.

options.rationale: Peer support is a valuable adjunct in refugee settings but is not a substitute for evidence-based trauma-focused therapy in established PTSD. (Source: RACGP Refugee Health)
SSRIs are second-line for PTSD when trauma-focused therapy is not available or declined; her preference and clinic access favour therapy first. (Source: Phoenix Australia ASD/PTSD Guidelines)
Atypical antipsychotics are not first-line for PTSD and carry metabolic risk; sleep hygiene plus trauma-focused therapy is preferred. (Source: Phoenix Australia ASD/PTSD Guidelines)

Six months of established PTSD symptoms in a refugee with high PCL-5 score warrants active trauma-focused treatment; passive monitoring delays recovery. (Source: Phoenix Australia ASD/PTSD Guidelines)

Trauma-focused psychological therapy (TF-CBT, EMDR, or cognitive processing therapy) is the first-line treatment for PTSD across all guidelines, and is preferred over medication unless not available; cultural and language-appropriate delivery is essential. (Source: Phoenix Australia ASD/PTSD Guidelines; RACGP Refugee Health)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome and neuroleptic malignant syndrome both present with autonomic instability, altered mental status and elevated temperature, but their neuromuscular phenotypes differ critically. Serotonin syndrome is dominated by hyperreflexia, clonus (especially lower limb), myoclonus, agitation and dilated pupils, develops within hours of a serotonergic addition or dose change, and resolves rapidly when offending agents are stopped. NMS is dominated by lead-pipe (axial) rigidity, bradyreflexia, severe hyperthermia, marked CK elevation (often >1000 U/L) and autonomic instability, develops over days to weeks of antipsychotic exposure or dose change, and resolves more slowly. The Hunter Criteria for serotonin toxicity require ingestion of a serotonergic agent plus one of: spontaneous clonus, inducible clonus plus agitation or diaphoresis, ocular clonus plus agitation or diaphoresis, tremor plus hyperreflexia, or hypertonia plus T >38 °C plus ocular or inducible clonus.
key_points: Serotonin syndrome: clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, agitation; hours after serotonergic change
NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, marked CK rise, days-weeks after antipsychotic change
Tramadol plus SSRI is a classic serotonin syndrome trigger
Cyproheptadine reserved for severe/refractory serotonin syndrome
explanation.pearls: Lower-limb-dominant hyperreflexia with sustained ankle clonus plus agitation plus T >38 °C after a serotonergic addition (especially tramadol or linezolid added to an SSRI) is the highest-specificity bedside picture for serotonin syndrome by the Hunter Criteria.

sources.label: RANZCP CPG NMS vs Serotonin Syndrome

options.rationale: Without meningism, focal neurology or CSF features and with classical serotonin toxicity from a new tramadol prescription, broad spectrum antibiotics and LP are not the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

NMS would be expected to show lead-pipe rigidity (axial dominant) with bradyreflexia and develops over days to weeks with antipsychotic exposure or dose change; absent these features and given new tramadol introduction the diagnosis is serotonin syndrome, not NMS. (Source: RANZCP CPG NMS vs Serotonin Syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG NMS vs Serotonin Syndrome

options.rationale: Paracetamol does little for centrally driven hyperthermia in serotonin syndrome (active cooling and benzodiazepines work) and admission without serotonergic cessation does not address the cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology)

Bromocriptine is an NMS adjunct, not a serotonin syndrome treatment; pushing dopaminergic activity does not address the syndrome and delays the correct withdrawal of serotonergic agents. (Source: RANZCP CPG NMS vs Serotonin Syndrome)
source_refs: RANZCP CPG NMS vs Serotonin Syndrome

options.rationale: The Hunter Toxicity Criteria are met (clonus plus agitation plus diaphoresis plus hyperthermia in a serotonergic context) and the addition of tramadol to escitalopram and mirtazapine is the precipitant; serotonin syndrome management is rapid serotonergic withdrawal, supportive care including aggressive cooling and benzodiazepines, with cyproheptadine reserved for severe or refractory cases. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology; Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria)

explanation.summary: Bipolar disorder in pregnancy carries high recurrence risk if mood stabiliser is stopped, particularly in women with multiple prior episodes. Lithium continuation in pregnancy is supported by RANZCP for high relapse risk women: the absolute risk of Ebstein anomaly is approximately 1 to 2 per 1000 (relative risk doubled but small absolute increase) and is detectable on fetal echocardiography at 18 to 20 weeks. Lithium clearance rises in pregnancy and falls sharply at delivery so dose adjustment and frequent serum monitoring (monthly first and second trimester, fortnightly third) are essential. Valproate is contraindicated in women of childbearing potential. The postpartum period carries up to 50% relapse risk in bipolar disorder and lithium prophylaxis around delivery is highly protective.
key_points: Discontinuation: approximately 50% relapse risk pregnancy and postpartum
Lithium Ebstein anomaly absolute risk approximately 1 in 1000
Fetal echocardiography at 18 to 20 weeks
Valproate contraindicated in women of childbearing potential
explanation.pearls: Postpartum lithium relapse prophylaxis is highly protective for bipolar disorder; the postpartum period has approximately 50% mood recurrence risk untreated in bipolar disorder per RANZCP perinatal guidance.

options.rationale: Interrupted dosing increases relapse risk and the absolute Ebstein anomaly risk on lithium is small (around 1 in 1000); continuous prophylaxis is preferred in high recurrence risk women. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health)

For high recurrence risk bipolar disorder, continuation of lithium across pregnancy with serum monitoring (more frequent in third trimester) and 18 to 20 week fetal echocardiography is preferred to discontinuation; the absolute risk of Ebstein anomaly is only about 1 in 1000. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health; SOMANZ)

Valproate is contraindicated in women of childbearing potential because of high teratogenicity (neural tube defects, dysmorphic features, neurodevelopmental impairment); this is the wrong move. (Source: AMH; RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health)

Lamotrigine is preferred for bipolar depression maintenance rather than mania prevention; a stable patient on effective lithium should not switch without strong indication. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health)

Discontinuation of lithium is associated with approximately 50% relapse risk in pregnancy and postpartum; unmedicated bipolar pregnancy in a woman with prior admissions exposes mother and fetus to greater risk than continued lithium. (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health; SafeScript)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic-associated cardiometabolic disease is the leading cause of premature mortality in schizophrenia. Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic risk; aripiprazole, ziprasidone and lurasidone carry the lowest. The RANZCP and eTG-Psychotropic standard schedule is: weight at every visit; baseline plus 12 weeks plus 12 months then yearly fasting lipids and glucose; ECG and prolactin at baseline plus annually; QTc check after dose change on QT-prolonging drugs. Switching antipsychotic to a metabolically safer agent should be considered when weight gain exceeds 5 to 7% of baseline, fasting glucose rises above 5.6 mmol/L, or lipids fall outside target. Smoking cessation, exercise and dietetic input are part of the package.
key_points: Standard: weight at every visit; fasting lipids and glucose 12 weeks then yearly
Plus ECG and prolactin baseline and yearly
Switch to metabolically safer agent if weight gain over 5 to 7%
Olanzapine and clozapine highest metabolic risk; aripiprazole lowest
explanation.pearls: Olanzapine causes the largest mean weight gain (around 4 kg over 12 weeks) and the largest glucose change of standard antipsychotics; switching to aripiprazole 15 mg or lurasidone 40 mg is the most metabolically favourable single-step option per RANZCP.

options.rationale: Reactive monitoring misses asymptomatic metabolic syndrome which is the major cause of premature death in schizophrenia; routine monitoring schedule is required. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Monitoring; eTG: Psychotropic)
Monthly fasting bloods are unnecessarily intensive and reduce adherence; the RANZCP standard is 12 weeks then yearly. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Monitoring)

The RANZCP early psychosis monitoring schedule is weight at every visit, BMI plus waist circumference, fasting lipids and glucose at 12 weeks then 12 months then yearly while on antipsychotic; this catches early metabolic syndrome which is the main cardiovascular risk on antipsychotics. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Monitoring; eTG: Psychotropic)
HbA1c can miss rapid onset olanzapine-induced diabetes; the RANZCP standard uses fasting glucose because of the speed of glycaemic change on olanzapine. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Monitoring)
OGTT is reserved for borderline fasting glucose; routine OGTT screening on antipsychotic is not the recommended schedule. (Source: RANZCP Antipsychotic Monitoring)

explanation.summary: Delirium tremens is the most severe alcohol withdrawal syndrome, typically peaking 48 to 96 hours after the last drink, with mortality up to 15% if untreated. Wernicke encephalopathy is a separate but co-occurring thiamine deficiency syndrome of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia; only one feature is required for clinical diagnosis. The Australian standard is parenteral thiamine 300 mg three times daily for 3 days before any glucose-containing fluid because glucose precipitates Wernicke in deficient patients. Delirium tremens is treated with intravenous diazepam (Australian preference) titrated to CIWA, with magnesium replacement, prevention of falls, and treatment of co-existing infection. Antipsychotics are avoided because they lower seizure threshold.
key_points: Wernicke triad: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia (one feature enough)
Parenteral thiamine 300 mg three times daily for 3 days, before glucose
DT: diazepam titrated to CIWA, plus magnesium and infection workup
Avoid antipsychotics in withdrawal: lower seizure threshold
explanation.pearls: Untreated Wernicke encephalopathy progresses to Korsakoff dementia in approximately 80% within weeks; only one of the triad features is required to mandate parenteral thiamine 300 mg three times daily per AMH and eTG-Substance Use.

options.rationale: Restraint without pharmacotherapy is unsafe and unethical; delirium tremens has a mortality up to 15% if untreated, and Wernicke encephalopathy is preventable with timely thiamine. (Source: NHMRC Alcohol Guidelines)

Antipsychotics are contraindicated in alcohol withdrawal because they lower seizure threshold; glucose without prior parenteral thiamine precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy in deficient patients. (Source: NHMRC Alcohol Guidelines; eTG: Substance Use)
Oral dosing in delirium tremens with CIWA 24 has unreliable absorption and is too slow; suspected Wernicke needs parenteral high-dose thiamine, not oral. (Source: NHMRC Alcohol Guidelines)

Wernicke encephalopathy is suggested by the triad of confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia in an alcohol-dependent patient; treatment is parenteral thiamine 300 mg three times daily for 3 days (Australian high-dose Pabrinex equivalent) given before any glucose load, plus benzodiazepine for delirium tremens and magnesium replacement. (Source: NHMRC Alcohol Guidelines; eTG: Substance Use; AMH)
Chlormethiazole is rarely used in Australia due to respiratory depression and dependence risk; diazepam or lorazepam are preferred. Oral thiamine is inadequate in suspected Wernicke. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Clozapine is the only TGA-approved antipsychotic for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and produces neutropenia in approximately 3% and agranulocytosis in approximately 0.8% of patients, with highest risk in the first 18 weeks. Australian patients are mandatorily registered with the Clozapine Patient Monitoring Service (CPMS) for full blood count surveillance: weekly for 18 weeks, then 4 weekly. Result categories are green (ANC over 2.0), amber (1.5 to 2.0, twice weekly FBC) and red (ANC under 1.5, mandatory cessation). Cessation is permanent unless a haematologist confirms a benign ethnic neutropenia variant with separate CPMS rules. Suspected agranulocytosis with infection symptoms requires hospital admission, reverse barrier nursing and treatment with broad spectrum antibiotics with consideration of G-CSF.
key_points: CPMS thresholds: green over 2.0; amber 1.5-2.0; red under 1.5 x10^9/L
Red zone: mandatory cessation, daily FBC, CPMS notification
Highest risk window: first 18 weeks
Resumption requires haematologist confirmation of benign variant
explanation.pearls: Benign ethnic neutropenia is recognised in CPMS Australia and may allow clozapine continuation with separate thresholds (ANC under 1.0 cessation rather than 1.5), but requires haematologist confirmation of the variant rather than informal assumption based on ethnicity.

options.rationale: Lithium augmentation of neutrophil count is not a recognised CPMS response and cannot be used to bypass the cessation rule; clinical safety requires stopping clozapine. (Source: CPMS Australia)
ANC under 1.5 x10^9/L is the Australian CPMS red zone for which clozapine must be ceased; continuing risks agranulocytosis. (Source: CPMS Australia; AMH)
Filgrastim is reserved for confirmed agranulocytosis under haematology supervision; it is not used to keep a patient on clozapine in the red zone. (Source: HSANZ Position Statement)
There is no dose reduction step in the Australian CPMS protocol; the response to a red ANC is mandatory cessation and daily monitoring. (Source: CPMS Australia)

An ANC under 1.5 x10^9/L is the CPMS red zone; mandatory cessation of clozapine with daily monitoring until counts recover above 2.0 x10^9/L and registry notification within 24 hours protects against fatal agranulocytosis. (Source: CPMS Australia; AMH)

explanation.summary: Gamma hydroxybutyrate (GHB) and its precursors GBL and 1,4-butanediol are GABA-B agonists; dependent users dose every 2 to 4 hours around the clock and withdrawal is often severe by 6 to 12 hours after the last dose. The syndrome resembles sedative-hypnotic withdrawal with delirium, autonomic instability, agitation and seizures, but distinguishes itself by being relatively benzodiazepine resistant. Australian protocols escalate diazepam or midazolam aggressively in inpatient settings; if symptoms remain refractory, baclofen 10 mg three times daily is added because it acts at the same GABA-B receptor. Refractory cases may require phenobarbital or ICU admission with propofol and airway protection. Discharge planning includes engagement with drug and alcohol services for relapse prevention.
key_points: GHB withdrawal: severe at 6 to 12 hours, often benzodiazepine resistant
First-line: escalating IV diazepam or midazolam with airway monitoring
Add baclofen for refractory cases; phenobarbital if still refractory
Antipsychotics contraindicated: lower seizure threshold
explanation.pearls: Severe GHB withdrawal in Australia is best managed in a unit with intensive care backup because total benzodiazepine doses required can exceed 200 mg diazepam equivalent over 24 hours, with airway protection becoming the rate-limiting safety concern.

sources.label: NSW Drug and Alcohol GHB Withdrawal

options.rationale: GHB withdrawal is frequently benzodiazepine resistant requiring rapid dose escalation; Australian Drug and Alcohol Services protocols escalate intravenous midazolam in 5 mg aliquots every 5 minutes with airway monitoring until agitation settles. (Source: NSW Drug and Alcohol GHB Withdrawal; eTG: Substance Use)
source_refs: NSW Drug and Alcohol GHB Withdrawal

options.rationale: Baclofen is an adjunct for refractory GHB withdrawal but the acute presentation requires inpatient management with parenteral sedation, not outpatient oral taper. (Source: NSW Drug and Alcohol GHB Withdrawal)
source_refs: NSW Drug and Alcohol GHB Withdrawal

options.rationale: Propofol requires intubation and intensive care monitoring at sedative doses; it is reserved for benzodiazepine failure with airway protection in ICU, not as initial escalation. (Source: NSW Drug and Alcohol GHB Withdrawal)
source_refs: NSW Drug and Alcohol GHB Withdrawal

options.rationale: GHB is not a registered medication in Australia and substitution therapy is not part of any approved protocol; benzodiazepines are the standard withdrawal agent. (Source: NSW Drug and Alcohol GHB Withdrawal)
source_refs: NSW Drug and Alcohol GHB Withdrawal

options.rationale: Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold and are contraindicated in sedative-hypnotic withdrawal syndromes such as GHB; benzodiazepines are the correct class. (Source: eTG: Substance Use; AMH)

explanation.summary: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia is defined as inadequate response to at least 2 different antipsychotic trials at therapeutic doses for at least 6 weeks each, with confirmed adherence (concentration monitoring or directly observed therapy). Approximately 30% of people with schizophrenia meet this criterion. Clozapine has superior efficacy in TRS, is the only TGA-approved indication, and is associated with reduced all-cause mortality, suicide risk and hospital admission. Initiation requires mandatory CPMS registration, baseline FBC, ECG, fasting lipids and glucose, and prolactin. Titration is slow over weeks with weekly FBC and clinical review for the first 18 weeks. Side effects include hypersalivation, constipation (which can cause ileus and death), tachycardia, weight gain, glucose dysregulation, myocarditis (first 4 weeks) and rarely agranulocytosis.
key_points: TRS: two adequate antipsychotic trials at therapeutic doses with adherence confirmed
Clozapine is the only TGA-approved option for TRS
Mandatory CPMS registration and weekly FBC for first 18 weeks
Watch myocarditis in first 4 weeks and constipation throughout
explanation.pearls: Clozapine-induced myocarditis presents in the first 4 weeks of treatment with tachycardia, fever, fatigue or raised troponin; routine weekly troponin and CRP for 4 weeks during initiation is recommended in Australian initiation protocols per RANZCP.

options.rationale: Lithium augmentation has only modest evidence in schizophrenia and is not a substitute for clozapine in treatment-resistant disease; he meets criteria for TRS and should be offered clozapine. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia; eTG: Psychotropic)

Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (inadequate response to two adequate trials of different antipsychotics) is the only TGA-approved indication for clozapine, which is more effective than any alternative for TRS; CPMS registration is mandatory in Australia. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia; CPMS Australia; eTG: Psychotropic)
Antipsychotic polypharmacy has limited evidence and increases extrapyramidal and metabolic side effects; clozapine monotherapy is the evidence-based step in TRS. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia)
Long-acting injection addresses adherence problems; this patient's adherence has been confirmed, so the limiting issue is drug efficacy not adherence. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia)
ECT is sometimes used adjunctively in TRS but is not first-line after two failed antipsychotic trials; clozapine remains the first step. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia)

explanation.summary: Catatonia complicates major depressive disorder, bipolar affective disorder, schizophrenia and a wide range of medical conditions (autoimmune encephalitis, post infectious, metabolic). Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale stratifies severity; mutism, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism and stupor are common features. First-line is a lorazepam challenge: 1 to 2 mg IV with response within hours; some patients require ongoing lorazepam 8 to 12 mg per day. Failure to respond after 48 to 72 hours at adequate dose is an indication for ECT, which has response rates over 80% in catatonia regardless of underlying diagnosis. Antipsychotics can precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome in catatonic patients and should be avoided until catatonia resolves. Refractory catatonia carries 10 to 20% mortality from dehydration, immobility complications, and venous thromboembolism.
key_points: First-line: lorazepam challenge 1 to 2 mg IV, escalate to 8 to 12 mg/day
Lorazepam failure at 48 to 72 hours: ECT
Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia resolves
Refractory catatonia mortality 10 to 20% from immobility complications
explanation.pearls: In Australian practice, refractory catatonia patients receive ECT under a Mental Health Act treatment authority when capacity is compromised; involuntary ECT requires Mental Health Tribunal authorisation in most jurisdictions and is an emergency safeguard.

options.rationale: Continued lorazepam escalation without response delays definitive treatment; catatonia not responding to adequate lorazepam after 48 to 72 hours is an indication for ECT. (Source: RANZCP ECT; Royal Children's Hospital ECT Guidelines)
Amytal interview is now considered historical and not standard practice; investigations and EEG already exclude organic causes and the priority is treatment escalation. (Source: RANZCP ECT)

Refractory catatonia after adequate lorazepam challenge is a class I indication for ECT; bilateral ECT three times weekly under substitute consent (treatment authority) is the standard Australian path. (Source: RANZCP ECT; Mental Health Act)
Clozapine is not delivered intravenously and is not indicated in acute catatonia; ECT is the proven escalation after lorazepam failure. (Source: AMH; RANZCP Schizophrenia)

Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia and risk progression to neuroleptic malignant syndrome; they are contraindicated in active catatonia until catatonia resolves. (Source: RANZCP ECT; AMH)

explanation.summary: Severe chronic lithium toxicity (level above 2.5 mmol/L with neurological impairment or AKI, or any level above 4 mmol/L) requires haemodialysis. Saline diuresis is inadequate at this severity. Lithium is not bound by activated charcoal and benefits from extracorporeal clearance, with a rebound level expected 6 hours after dialysis due to intracellular redistribution.
key_points: Haemodialysis criteria (EXTRIP): level above 4 mmol/L; or above 2.5 with severe symptoms or AKI; or rising despite saline.
Charcoal does not bind lithium; whole bowel irrigation for sustained-release acute on chronic only.
Expect rebound rise 6 hours after dialysis from intracellular redistribution.
SILENT (syndrome of irreversible lithium-effectuated neurotoxicity) is the long-term consequence of delayed treatment.
explanation.pearls: A chronic lithium level of 3.6 mmol/L with confusion and ataxia is a renal unit call, not just a saline drip; the level rebounds at 6 hours, so it must be rechecked.

options.rationale: EXTRIP and Australian poisons guidance recommend haemodialysis for serum lithium above 2.5 mmol/L with severe neurological impairment or renal impairment; haemodialysis efficiently clears lithium and must be followed by re-measurement due to redistribution rebound. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Saline diuresis alone is inadequate at a level of 3.6 mmol/L with renal impairment and severe neurological features; relying on it delays definitive treatment and risks ongoing toxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)
Activated charcoal does not bind lithium and is ineffective for lithium toxicity; saline alone is insufficient at this severity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Ceasing the drug without active removal at a level of 3.6 mmol/L with neurological features and renal impairment carries a high risk of permanent neurotoxicity (SILENT syndrome). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Whole bowel irrigation is reserved for sustained-release lithium ingestion (acute on chronic) with no neurological features; in this severe chronic case it has minimal yield and delays haemodialysis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced myocarditis peaks during weeks 2 to 6 of titration and presents with fever, tachycardia, malaise, and often pleuritic chest pain. The Australian recommended response is immediate cessation, troponin, BNP, CRP, ECG, and echocardiogram. The neutrophil count is not the key marker for myocarditis; that monitoring system addresses agranulocytosis, not cardiac inflammation.
key_points: Clozapine myocarditis risk peaks weeks 2 to 6 of titration.
Cease clozapine on suspicion; troponin, BNP, CRP, ECG, echocardiogram.
ANC monitoring is for agranulocytosis, separate from myocarditis.
Rechallenge after myocarditis is specialist-led and rarely undertaken.
explanation.pearls: Fever plus tachycardia in week 3 of clozapine is myocarditis until disproven by troponin and BNP; do not blame a viral illness without ruling it out.

sources.label: RANZCP CALC Clinical Practice Guideline for Clozapine

options.rationale: Clozapine-induced myocarditis peaks during weeks 2 to 6 of titration; missing it carries high mortality, and the picture of fever, tachycardia, and pleuritic chest pain mandates immediate cardiac workup. (Source: RANZCP CALC Clinical Practice Guideline for Clozapine)
source_refs: RANZCP CALC Clinical Practice Guideline for Clozapine

options.rationale: The constellation of fever, tachycardia, and pleuritic chest pain during weeks 2 to 6 of clozapine titration is the textbook presentation of clozapine-induced myocarditis; AU practice is immediate cease, troponin and BNP, ECG, CRP, and echocardiogram. (Source: RANZCP CALC Clinical Practice Guideline for Clozapine)
source_refs: RANZCP CALC Clinical Practice Guideline for Clozapine

options.rationale: Increasing the dose during suspected myocarditis worsens the inflammation; the immediate step is cease and investigate, not titrate up. (Source: RANZCP CALC Clinical Practice Guideline for Clozapine)
source_refs: RANZCP CALC Clinical Practice Guideline for Clozapine

options.rationale: Continuing clozapine at any dose during suspected myocarditis is inappropriate; valproate adds metabolic burden without addressing the cardiac risk. (Source: RANZCP CALC Clinical Practice Guideline for Clozapine)
source_refs: RANZCP CALC Clinical Practice Guideline for Clozapine

options.rationale: Switching antipsychotic during acute clozapine myocarditis workup risks confounding the picture and adds anticholinergic and metabolic load; stabilise the cardiac issue before reintroducing antipsychotic. (Source: RANZCP CALC Clinical Practice Guideline for Clozapine)
source_refs: RANZCP CALC Clinical Practice Guideline for Clozapine

explanation.summary: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is managed by ceasing the offending antipsychotic, aggressive supportive care (IV fluids, cooling), and specific pharmacotherapy with dantrolene for muscle rigidity or bromocriptine as a dopaminergic agent. Severity is graded by temperature, CK, and autonomic instability. ICU admission is appropriate for severe presentations.
key_points: NMS specific agents: dantrolene 1-2.5 mg/kg IV (rigidity) or bromocriptine 2.5 mg orally TDS (dopamine agonist).
Cyproheptadine is for serotonin syndrome, not NMS; the two differ in muscle tone, reflexes, and trigger drug.
Aggressive cooling and IV fluids to limit rhabdomyolysis and renal failure.
Reintroduction of any antipsychotic is delayed at least 2 weeks after resolution and specialist-led.
explanation.pearls: Lead-pipe rigidity with haloperidol exposure is NMS (dantrolene), not serotonin syndrome (cyproheptadine); reflexes are reduced or absent in NMS but brisk in serotonin syndrome.

options.rationale: Continuing the precipitating antipsychotic in NMS perpetuates the syndrome and risks fatal hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, and arrhythmia; cessation is the foundational step. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Benzodiazepines are an adjunct but not a definitive treatment for NMS; the priority is to cease the antipsychotic, cool, hydrate, and add specific therapy (dantrolene or bromocriptine) for severe cases. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Severe NMS with rigidity, hyperthermia above 38.5 °C, and rhabdomyolysis is managed by ceasing the antipsychotic, aggressive cooling, IV fluids, dantrolene for muscle rigidity, and ICU admission; bromocriptine is an alternative dopaminergic agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Switching antipsychotic during active NMS is contraindicated; reintroduction of any antipsychotic is delayed until full resolution and is specialist-led. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Cyproheptadine is a serotonin antagonist for serotonin syndrome and has no role in NMS; the picture of haloperidol exposure and lead-pipe rigidity points to NMS, not serotonin syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Valproate is the most teratogenic mood stabiliser and is contraindicated in women planning pregnancy or of reproductive potential unless other options are ineffective. Lamotrigine has the most favourable perinatal profile and is the preferred alternative for a stable patient with bipolar I disorder. Lithium remains an option in selected cases but carries the small risk of Ebstein anomaly and requires close level monitoring across pregnancy.
key_points: Valproate teratogenicity is dose-dependent and not abolished by folate.
Lamotrigine is preferred for cross-titration before conception when patient is stable.
Lithium remains an option if lamotrigine inadequate; level monitoring intensifies in pregnancy.
Pre-conception planning includes contraception continuation until cross-titration complete.
explanation.pearls: Stable bipolar I on valproate planning pregnancy: cross-titrate to lamotrigine before stopping contraception, not after conception.

options.rationale: Folate does not abolish the dose-dependent neurodevelopmental and neural tube defect risk of valproate; valproate carries the highest teratogenic burden of mood stabilisers and AU practice avoids it in women planning pregnancy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic, perinatal section)
Carbamazepine is also teratogenic (neural tube defects, cardiac, urinary) and not preferred over lamotrigine or lithium in bipolar pregnancy planning. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Lithium is a reasonable option in pregnancy for bipolar I prophylaxis (especially if previously responsive) but lamotrigine has a more favourable teratogenic profile; lithium is not the universally preferred next agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Lamotrigine has the most favourable perinatal safety profile among mood stabilisers and is preferred for cross-titration before conception in stable bipolar disorder; valproate is avoided in women of reproductive age due to teratogenicity and neurodevelopmental impact. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Ceasing prophylaxis in bipolar I with previous severe mania and postnatal depression carries an unacceptably high relapse risk; a safer pregnancy-compatible agent should be substituted. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: TCA cardiotoxicity is identified by QRS prolongation above 100 ms, terminal R wave in aVR above 3 mm, and hypotension. The specific intervention is intravenous sodium bicarbonate boluses to alkalinise and overcome sodium channel block. Seizures, hypotension, and ventricular arrhythmias are the principal causes of death.
key_points: Sodium bicarbonate dose: 1-2 mmol/kg boluses, repeat to QRS under 120 ms and arterial pH 7.45-7.55.
ECG markers of toxicity: QRS above 100 ms, R wave aVR above 3 mm, R:S ratio aVR above 0.7.
Hypokalaemia worsens arrhythmia risk; correct to normal but expect intracellular shifts with bicarbonate.
Lipid emulsion considered in refractory cardiotoxicity after toxicology advice.
explanation.pearls: QRS above 100 ms with a terminal R wave in aVR after TCA overdose is the cue for sodium bicarbonate, not benzodiazepines.

options.rationale: Sedation does not reverse TCA cardiotoxicity; the priority is sodium bicarbonate for QRS prolongation and seizure prophylaxis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)
Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose or unknown overdose due to seizure risk, and does not reverse TCA toxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Charcoal is of limited value beyond 1 hour post-ingestion and does not reverse established cardiotoxicity; sodium bicarbonate addresses the immediate life-threatening QRS prolongation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)
Whole bowel irrigation has no role in TCA overdose; sodium bicarbonate is the cardiotoxicity-specific intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

TCA cardiotoxicity (QRS above 100 ms, terminal R in aVR above 3 mm, hypotension) is treated with IV sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg bolus, titrated to QRS narrowing and pH 7.45 to 7.55; the alkalinisation increases protein binding and the sodium load overcomes the sodium channel block. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: For an involuntary patient in NSW, ECT requires an ECT administration inquiry before the Mental Health Review Tribunal. The Tribunal determines capacity and consent first. If the person is incapable of giving informed consent, or is capable but has refused, or has neither consented nor refused, the Tribunal goes on to determine whether ECT is a reasonable and proper treatment and necessary or desirable for the person's safety or welfare, on evidence from two medical practitioners of whom at least one is a psychiatrist. Senior sign-off, substitute consent and common law necessity are all outside the statutory scheme.
key_points: A capable refusal by an involuntary patient does not stop a Tribunal determination.
A capable refusal by a voluntary patient does stop ECT while they remain voluntary.
Substitute consent by a carer has no standing for ECT in NSW.
The Tribunal must take the patient's own views into account.
explanation.pearls: The voluntary and involuntary pathways diverge exactly here: a voluntary patient with capacity who refuses cannot be given ECT, so reclassifying a refusing patient as voluntary to avoid a hearing removes the only lawful route to treatment.

sources.label: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy
NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers
NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: involuntary patient orders

options.rationale: In NSW the Tribunal first determines whether an involuntary patient can give informed consent and has given it. Where the patient is capable but has refused, the Tribunal must then determine whether ECT is a reasonable and proper treatment and is necessary or desirable for the patient's safety or welfare. Retained capacity therefore does not end the matter for a detained patient, which is where NSW differs from several other states. (Source: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy

options.rationale: Two practitioners, at least one a psychiatrist, must certify that ECT is reasonable and proper, but their certificates are evidence for the Tribunal, not an authorisation in themselves. (Source: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: electro convulsive therapy

options.rationale: Administering ECT otherwise than in accordance with the Act is an offence attracting civil and criminal penalties, so necessity is not available where the Act sets out a pathway. (Source: NSW Mental Health Act 2007)

A designated carer is entitled to notice of the ECT application and to information, and may apply for her discharge, but cannot consent to treatment on her behalf. (Source: NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers)
source_refs: NSW Health: designated carers and principal care providers

options.rationale: She remains a mentally ill person at risk of serious harm with no less restrictive care available, so the grounds for her involuntary order are unchanged and discharge would breach the duty of care. (Source: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: involuntary patient orders)
source_refs: NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal: involuntary patient orders

explanation.summary: Catatonia is treated with a lorazepam challenge as both diagnostic and therapeutic step, regardless of the underlying cause (psychiatric, medical, or autoimmune). A partial response within minutes to hours confirms the diagnosis; ongoing benzodiazepine and parallel ECT planning are appropriate as ECT is the definitive treatment for refractory or malignant catatonia. Antipsychotics can precipitate NMS and must be avoided.
key_points: Lorazepam 1-2 mg IV is the AU first-line challenge for catatonia.
Avoid antipsychotics during active catatonia (NMS risk).
ECT is the definitive treatment if lorazepam fails or in malignant catatonia.
Investigate underlying cause in parallel (anti-NMDA, medical, structural).
explanation.pearls: Posturing plus waxy flexibility plus fever and elevated CK without neuroleptic exposure is malignant catatonia; the answer is lorazepam now and ECT next, not haloperidol.

options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome; they are not the diagnostic or therapeutic tool of choice for suspected catatonia. (Source: RANZCP Practice Resources: Catatonia)

Lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV) is both diagnostic (rapid partial response within minutes to hours) and therapeutic for catatonia, regardless of underlying cause; parallel ECT planning is appropriate as ECT is the definitive treatment for refractory catatonia. (Source: RANZCP Practice Resources: Catatonia)
Propofol is not used for catatonia treatment; lorazepam challenge is the AU recommended first-line diagnostic-therapeutic approach. (Source: RANZCP Practice Resources: Catatonia)
There is no neuroleptic exposure, so NMS is unlikely; bromocriptine is for NMS-specific management and is not first-line for catatonia of any cause. (Source: RANZCP Practice Resources: Catatonia)
CSF is bland and there is no meningoencephalitis evidence; empirical antibacterial cover is not justified and does not address the catatonia itself. (Source: RANZCP Practice Resources: Catatonia)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome from a MAOI plus tramadol is managed by ceasing offending agents, supportive care with IV benzodiazepines, aggressive cooling and IV fluids, with cyproheptadine reserved as an oral adjunct in moderate to severe non-responders. Antipsychotics are avoided as they may worsen hyperthermia and confuse the clinical picture with NMS. Hyperreflexia (especially lower limbs) and clonus distinguish it from NMS, which shows rigidity and reduced reflexes.
key_points: Distinguishing features: serotonin syndrome causes hyperreflexia and clonus (lower limb predominant); NMS causes lead-pipe rigidity and reduced reflexes.
Cyproheptadine is oral only in Australia; no IV preparation.
Antipsychotics worsen serotonin syndrome and risk diagnostic confusion with NMS.
MAOIs plus serotonergic agents (SSRI, SNRI, tramadol, pethidine, linezolid) are the highest-risk combinations.
explanation.pearls: Lower limb clonus with diaphoresis after a MAOI plus tramadol is serotonin syndrome; the answer is benzodiazepines and cooling, with oral cyproheptadine as a backup.

options.rationale: Haloperidol increases the risk of NMS and worsens hyperthermia in serotonin syndrome; antipsychotics should be avoided in the acute setting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)
Dantrolene is used in NMS or malignant hyperthermia, not as first-line in serotonin syndrome; benzodiazepines and supportive care are the AU first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

AU management of serotonin syndrome is cessation of the offending agents, IV benzodiazepines as first-line for agitation and hyperthermia, aggressive cooling and IV fluids; cyproheptadine (PO only, no IV preparation in Australia) is reserved as adjunct in moderate-severe non-responders. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)
