There is no parenteral cyproheptadine available in Australia; oral or NG cyproheptadine is the only route, and benzodiazepines come first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)
Tramadol and phenelzine together cause serotonin syndrome, not sodium channel block; sodium bicarbonate has no role here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate has the worst teratogenic and neurodevelopmental profile of all antiepileptics and mood stabilisers (major malformation rate 10%; 30-40% neurodevelopmental impact). The TGA has issued a black-box restriction on valproate in women of childbearing potential without a Pregnancy Prevention Program. For bipolar with predominantly manic episodes, lithium is the AU first-line alternative for women planning pregnancy because of superior anti-manic prophylaxis; the absolute Ebstein anomaly risk is around 1 in 1000 (recent data revise the originally cited 1 in 100). Switch is performed under specialist supervision with at least 6 months of stability on lithium before conception, fetal echocardiography at 18-20 weeks, third-trimester lithium dose review, and discussion of breastfeeding (lithium is relatively contraindicated). Lamotrigine is preferred for depression-predominant bipolar.
key_points: Valproate is contraindicated in WOCBP without a Pregnancy Prevention Program (TGA).
Lithium first-line for mania-predominant bipolar planning pregnancy.
Absolute Ebstein anomaly risk on lithium ~1 in 1000.
Confirm 6 months of stability before conception attempts.
Lamotrigine first-line if depression-predominant bipolar.
explanation.pearls: Ebstein anomaly absolute risk on lithium is about 1 in 1000 - the historical 1 in 100 figure overstated risk and modern RANZCP guidance favours lithium over valproate for mania-predominant bipolar in WOCBP.

sources.label: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline
Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Bipolar in pregnancy

options.rationale: Valproate has the highest teratogenic risk (10% major malformation, 30-40% neurodevelopmental impact); folate does not abolish that risk and continuation in WOCBP is contraindicated where alternatives exist. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of valproate in bipolar I with manic-psychotic episodes carries high relapse risk; switch under cover to an alternative agent before stopping, do not leave untreated. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Carbamazepine is also a category D teratogen (neural tube defects, craniofacial defects) and is no safer than valproate in pregnancy; not appropriate first choice. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Olanzapine is acceptable in pregnancy but lithium is the AU first-line for mania-predominant bipolar with planned pregnancy due to superior anti-manic prophylaxis and well characterised pregnancy data. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Lithium is RANZCP first-line for mania-predominant bipolar in WOCBP planning pregnancy; absolute Ebstein anomaly risk is approximately 1 in 1000; switch under cover, confirm stability 6 months before conception, and arrange fetal echocardiography at 18-20 weeks. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP Bipolar Disorder Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: The Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD (AADPA, 2022) recommends, before initiating any stimulant or non-stimulant pharmacotherapy in adults: (1) baseline 12-lead ECG, (2) baseline blood pressure and heart rate, (3) focused personal and family cardiovascular history (syncope, palpitations, exercise intolerance, sudden death <40 years, congenital heart disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, long QT), and (4) cardiac examination. Routine cardiology referral is NOT required unless abnormalities are identified. Stimulants are first-line; methylphenidate and dexamfetamine/lisdexamfetamine are accessed via psychiatrist or appropriately authorised paediatrician/GP under state regulations.
key_points: Baseline 12-lead ECG, BP, HR, focused CV history before stimulant.
Routine cardiology referral NOT required without abnormal findings.
Sudden cardiac death family history <40 years is the relevant family screening question.
Monitor BP and HR at 1 month, then 3 monthly on stimulants.
Stimulants are first-line; atomoxetine and guanfacine are second-line.
explanation.pearls: Family history of late MI (parent over 50) does not require cardiology referral before stimulants - the screening question is sudden cardiac death under 40, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, or long QT syndrome.

sources.label: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: RACGP, AADPA and RANZCP recommend baseline 12-lead ECG plus focused CV history and exam (palpitations, syncope, exercise intolerance, family history of sudden death <40 years) before initiating stimulants; routine cardiology referral is not required without abnormal findings. (Source: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Skipping baseline ECG and CV history is below AU standard for stimulant initiation; baseline ECG is recommended in adults before starting any stimulant. (Source: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Late-onset MI in a parent (mother >50) does not mandate cardiology workup beyond baseline ECG; this is over-investigation that delays treatment without evidence base. (Source: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Stimulants are first-line pharmacotherapy in adult ADHD with strong evidence; CBT is adjunctive. Family CV history alone does not contraindicate stimulants - baseline screen is enough. (Source: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline

options.rationale: Atomoxetine also requires baseline BP and HR (and has its own CV considerations); the appropriate first step is baseline ECG plus screening, not bypassing stimulants. (Source: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: AADPA Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: The NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for Borderline Personality Disorder (Project Air) emphasises that admission for self-harm in BPD without active suicidal intent, psychosis, or severe medical injury is iatrogenic and tends to reinforce maladaptive coping. Community-based crisis management with rapid follow-up by the existing care team (case manager, DBT therapist) is the evidence-based AU standard. Brief admissions (24-72 hours) may be considered for safety stabilisation in carefully selected cases but should not be the default. Pharmacotherapy is symptomatic and adjunct to psychological therapy (DBT, MBT, schema therapy, transference-focused psychotherapy). Compulsory admission is reserved for active suicidality with intent and plan plus inability to engage with safety planning.
key_points: Routine admission for BPD self-harm without active suicidality is iatrogenic.
Community-based crisis support with safety plan review is first-line.
DBT is the primary evidence-based psychotherapy.
Pharmacotherapy is symptomatic only; no specific licensed agent.
Compulsory admission requires active suicidality plus inability to safety plan.
explanation.pearls: For BPD self-harm without intent, planned community follow-up within 72 hours and DBT skills coaching outperforms 72-hour observational admissions, which can reinforce help-seeking via crisis.

explanation.summary: Benzodiazepine choice in alcohol withdrawal is dictated by hepatic function. In NORMAL hepatic function, diazepam (long-acting, self-tapering) is first-line. In SIGNIFICANT hepatic impairment (cirrhosis, Child-Pugh B or C), oxazepam, lorazepam, or temazepam (the LOT drugs) are preferred because they are glucuronidated (phase II metabolism) without prior oxidation - they do NOT accumulate in liver disease. Symptom-triggered dosing (CIWA-Ar guided) reduces total benzodiazepine use, length of stay, and incidence of complications versus fixed-schedule regimens. Thiamine (high-dose IV) must be given before any glucose load to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. Phenobarbital and continuous infusion benzodiazepines are reserved for benzodiazepine-resistant delirium tremens in ICU.
key_points: Cirrhosis: use oxazepam, lorazepam, or temazepam (LOT) - glucuronidated.
Normal liver: diazepam first-line (long-acting, self-tapering).
Symptom-triggered (CIWA-Ar) reduces total dose and complications.
Parenteral thiamine before any glucose to prevent Wernicke.
Phenobarbital / midazolam infusion: ICU-level refractory withdrawal.
explanation.pearls: LOT drugs (lorazepam, oxazepam, temazepam) are glucuronidated and do not accumulate in cirrhosis - choose oxazepam in any patient with Child-Pugh B or C to avoid encephalopathy from diazepam metabolites.

sources.label: RACP Australian guidelines for the treatment of alcohol problems

options.rationale: Diazepam undergoes hepatic oxidation with long-acting active metabolites (desmethyl diazepam); in Child-Pugh B cirrhosis it accumulates causing prolonged sedation and precipitating hepatic encephalopathy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Alcohol withdrawal)

Midazolam infusion is reserved for refractory delirium tremens requiring ICU; first-line is symptom-triggered oral lorazepam or oxazepam; combining with infusion is over-sedation risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Alcohol withdrawal)

Oxazepam undergoes glucuronidation without phase I hepatic oxidation, avoiding accumulation in cirrhosis; symptom-triggered dosing is superior to fixed-schedule in moderate withdrawal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Alcohol withdrawal)

Chlordiazepoxide is hepatically oxidised and accumulates in cirrhosis (similar to diazepam); fixed schedule over-sedates compared with symptom-triggered approach. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Alcohol withdrawal)

Phenobarbital is third-line for benzodiazepine-resistant withdrawal in ICU settings; not first-line in any AU outpatient or general ward setting for alcohol withdrawal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Alcohol withdrawal)

explanation.summary: Refeeding syndrome is a constellation of metabolic disturbances (hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, thiamine deficiency, fluid overload) precipitated by reintroduction of carbohydrate-containing nutrition after prolonged starvation, due to intracellular shifts of phosphate, potassium and magnesium driven by insulin. It occurs within 24-72 hours of refeeding commencement. Detection at the biochemical stage (asymptomatic falling electrolytes) requires slowing of caloric advancement, IV electrolyte replacement, continued high-dose thiamine, and intensive monitoring (6-hourly bloods, continuous ECG). Risk factors: BMI <16, weight loss >15% in 3 months, minimal intake >5 days. Symptomatic refeeding syndrome may cause cardiac arrhythmia, respiratory failure, seizures, rhabdomyolysis, and death.
key_points: Refeeding within 24-72 hours: hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia.
Detection at biochemical stage: reduce calories, IV replacement, continue thiamine.
Continuous ECG monitoring while electrolytes deranged.
Thiamine 300 mg IV before any carb load (Wernicke prevention).
Stopping refeeding entirely is also dangerous in severe malnutrition.
explanation.pearls: Biochemical refeeding syndrome (PO4 dropping below 0.5 on day 2-3) is a slow-the-feed signal - reduce kcal to maintenance, replace PO4/K/Mg IV, keep thiamine going, and monitor every 6 hours.

sources.label: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders

options.rationale: Continuing same calories with falling electrolytes risks symptomatic refeeding syndrome (cardiac arrhythmia, weakness, encephalopathy); reduction of calories AND IV replacement of phosphate, K and Mg are required. (Source: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders)
source_refs: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders

options.rationale: Increasing calories in falling electrolytes accelerates refeeding syndrome; the principle is to slow caloric advancement when biochemistry deteriorates, not accelerate. (Source: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders)
source_refs: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders

options.rationale: Stopping refeeding entirely is not appropriate; the principle is to reduce caloric load, replace electrolytes, and continue nutrition. Stopping in severely malnourished patients carries its own risk of further deterioration. (Source: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders)
source_refs: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders

options.rationale: Biochemical refeeding syndrome (falling K, Mg, PO4 within 72 hours of feeding start) mandates calorie reduction, IV electrolyte replacement, continued thiamine, and 6-hourly monitoring with cardiac telemetry until biochemistry stabilises. (Source: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders)
source_refs: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders

options.rationale: ICU and TPN are not first-line; oral or NG refeeding with monitored electrolyte replacement on the adolescent medicine ward is the AU standard for refeeding syndrome. Intubation is unjustified. (Source: ANZAED Clinical Practice Guideline: Eating disorders)

explanation.summary: Postpartum psychosis (puerperal psychosis) is a rare (1 in 1000 births) but severe psychiatric emergency presenting within 2 weeks of delivery with mood symptoms (most commonly mania, sometimes mixed or depressive), psychotic features, disorganisation and confusion. Women with a history of bipolar I disorder (especially those who discontinue mood stabilisers preconception) are at the highest risk - approximately 1 in 4 will develop puerperal psychosis. Infanticide and suicide risk are high. Management is involuntary admission to a Mother-Baby Unit (or general psychiatric inpatient unit with infant access where MBU unavailable), antipsychotic (olanzapine is well-studied in postpartum), reinstatement of lithium (which is incompatible with breastfeeding, so support cessation), and consideration of ECT for rapid response in severe cases. Long-term plan includes mood stabiliser prophylaxis through any future pregnancies.
key_points: Onset within 2 weeks postpartum; mania most common syndrome.
Bipolar I women off mood stabilisers preconception have ~25% risk.
Involuntary admission to MBU (or adult psych unit) for safety and treatment.
Olanzapine first-line acute; lithium reintroduction once breastfeeding ceased.
ECT considered for severe or refractory presentations within 48-72 hours.
explanation.pearls: Bipolar I women who stop lithium before conception carry a 1 in 4 risk of postpartum psychosis - the priority on representation is MBU admission, antipsychotic, and lithium reintroduction with breastfeeding cessation.

options.rationale: This is postpartum psychosis (psychotic features, mood-incongruent delusions, infant-directed harm risk), not postpartum depression; SSRI alone is inadequate and delays antipsychotic treatment. (Source: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period)

(Source: COPE Mental Health Care in the Perinatal Period)

explanation.summary: Lithium toxicity is graded by neurological features rather than serum level alone because tissue distribution lags serum. Mild toxicity (1.5-2.0 mmol/L) gives tremor and GI symptoms; moderate (2.0-2.5) adds dysarthria, ataxia, clonus, drowsiness; severe (over 2.5 or any level with seizures, coma, severe symptoms) requires dialysis. Precipitants include ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides, NSAIDs, dehydration, and renal impairment. EXTRIP recommends haemodialysis for severe neurological toxicity, level above 4.0 mmol/L (or 2.5 with renal impairment), seizures, or coma. Intermittent haemodialysis is preferred over CRRT for faster lithium removal.
key_points: Tissue lithium lags serum level; neurology guides severity
Precipitants: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides, NSAIDs, dehydration, AKI
Charcoal does not bind lithium; whole bowel irrigation only for massive SR ingestion
EXTRIP threshold for dialysis: severe neurology, level above 4.0 (or 2.5 with AKI), seizures, coma
Stop lithium, IV saline, stop precipitant, dialysis
explanation.pearls: Lithium level alone does not classify severity; coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, drowsiness, and clonus in a chronic user trigger EXTRIP dialysis criteria even at lower levels because tissue lithium lags serum.

options.rationale: Outpatient management is unsafe with neurological toxicity, lithium of 2.4 mmol/L, and AKI; severe lithium toxicity requires admission and IV rehydration with consideration of dialysis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Lithium 2.4 mmol/L with neurological toxicity (drowsiness, ataxia, dysarthria, clonus) and AKI meets EXTRIP criteria for haemodialysis; saline and stopping lithium and the precipitant (ACE inhibitor) are essential immediate steps. (Source: EXTRIP Lithium Workgroup Recommendations; Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Activated charcoal does NOT bind lithium and has no role in lithium toxicity; whole bowel irrigation has a role in massive ingestion of sustained-release lithium only. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Urinary alkalinisation does not enhance lithium elimination; saline rehydration and dialysis are the mainstays. Bicarbonate is used for tricyclic antidepressant and salicylate toxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Acute toxicity is a separate problem from maintenance bipolar therapy; switching to valproate during the toxicity admission is not the priority and is decided by psychiatry after recovery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced myocarditis occurs in around 1% of new initiators and usually presents within the first 4 weeks of treatment. The screening protocol mandates baseline and weekly troponin, CRP, and ECG for the first 4 weeks. Any fever, tachycardia, chest pain, dyspnoea, troponin rise (any value), or CRP above 100 mg/L triggers same-day cardiology referral with echocardiography. Mortality is around 10% without intervention. Clozapine is permanently ceased once myocarditis is confirmed; alternatives include olanzapine or risperidone but neither matches clozapine's efficacy in treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Neutropenia is monitored separately with weekly FBC.
key_points: Clozapine myocarditis usually presents within the first 4 weeks
Screening: weekly troponin, CRP, ECG for 4 weeks
Trigger thresholds: fever, tachycardia, any troponin rise, CRP above 100 mg/L
Mortality 10% without intervention; cardiology and echo same-day
Clozapine permanently ceased once myocarditis confirmed
explanation.pearls: Clozapine-induced myocarditis classically presents within 4 weeks of starting; ANY troponin rise plus fever plus tachycardia is the trigger to refer to ED for echocardiography even when the chest examination is unremarkable.

options.rationale: Onset of fever, tachycardia, and elevated troponin and CRP within 4 weeks of clozapine initiation is the classical clozapine-induced myocarditis triad; the AU clozapine screening protocol mandates urgent ED referral with TTE and cardiology. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement: Clozapine-induced Myocarditis; AMH)

Outpatient observation with rising troponin and CRP during the high-risk first 4 weeks of clozapine misses myocarditis which can progress rapidly to cardiogenic shock; this needs same-day specialist assessment. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement: Clozapine-induced Myocarditis)

Switching antipsychotics does not address the immediate concern of possible myocarditis which needs ED workup; only after exclusion of myocarditis can clozapine be ceased and an alternative discussed. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement: Clozapine-induced Myocarditis)

Neutropenia is a separate clozapine adverse effect; the current concern (fever plus tachycardia plus troponin rise plus CRP rise) is myocarditis, not neutropenia. ANC is currently normal. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement: Clozapine-induced Myocarditis)

Atypical pneumonia is in the differential but troponin rise on a normal chest examination and clear chest x-ray points more strongly to myocarditis; empirical antibiotics alone are inadequate. (Source: RANZCP Position Statement: Clozapine-induced Myocarditis)

explanation.summary: COPE guidelines recommend continuing antidepressants in pregnancy when there has been a prior moderate-severe episode and remission depends on medication; relapse risk on cessation is around 60%. Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in pregnancy and lactation because of low transplacental and breast milk transfer and the largest reassuring evidence base. Paroxetine carries a small first-trimester association with cardiac malformations (especially ventricular septal defects). Fluoxetine has the longest half-life and higher breast milk transfer. Cross-tapering from one SSRI to another over 1-2 weeks is the standard transition method. Non-pharmacological therapies (CBT, IPT) are adjuncts, not substitutes, when relapse risk is high.
key_points: Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in pregnancy and lactation in Australia
Paroxetine first-trimester carries small VSD association
Stopping antidepressants in pregnancy has 60% relapse rate
Cross-taper over 1-2 weeks is the standard transition
ECT reserved for severe perinatal depression with psychosis or imminent risk
explanation.pearls: Sertraline is the preferred SSRI in pregnancy and lactation because of low breast milk transfer (under 2% relative infant dose) and the largest reassuring safety dataset; cross-taper from paroxetine over 1-2 weeks before week 8 of gestation.

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome of motor, behavioural, and autonomic disturbance occurring in primary psychiatric (mood disorders most commonly), neurological (encephalitis, NMDA receptor antibody), and medical (electrolytes, infection) contexts. Diagnostic criteria require 3 or more of 12 features (stupor, catalepsy, waxy flexibility, mutism, negativism, posturing, mannerism, stereotypy, agitation, grimacing, echolalia, echopraxia). Lorazepam 1-2 mg IV is the diagnostic and therapeutic challenge; over 70% respond within 30-60 minutes. ECT is the next-line if lorazepam fails or for malignant catatonia (hyperthermia, autonomic instability). Antipsychotics worsen catatonia and risk NMS; benzodiazepine titration up to 6-8 mg lorazepam daily is often required. The condition is reversible when recognised; missed catatonia carries high morbidity from immobility complications.
key_points: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale is the standard severity tool
Lorazepam 1-2 mg IV is the diagnostic and therapeutic challenge
Over 70% of patients respond within 30-60 minutes
Antipsychotics worsen catatonia and risk NMS
ECT is first-line for lorazepam-non-responsive or malignant catatonia
explanation.pearls: The lorazepam challenge (1-2 mg IV) is both diagnostic and therapeutic in catatonia; over 70% improve within 30-60 minutes, and persistent benzodiazepine cover plus deprescribed antipsychotics is the standard maintenance approach.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.rationale: NMS classically has hyperthermia, autonomic instability, marked CK rise (often above 1000), and altered consciousness; her CK is only 168 and she has no fever or autonomic instability - this points to catatonia, not NMS. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.rationale: ECT is highly effective in catatonia (especially malignant or lorazepam-non-responsive) but the diagnostic lorazepam challenge precedes ECT in most protocols. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Antipsychotic dose escalation in catatonia worsens it and can precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome; antipsychotics are deprescribed and benzodiazepines are first-line. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Lorazepam 1-2 mg IV is the AU and international first-line diagnostic challenge for suspected catatonia; over 70% of patients respond within 30-60 minutes and this is both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders; UpToDate Catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Mood Disorders

explanation.summary: The standard varenicline course is twelve weeks. For a patient who has stopped smoking on treatment, tolerates it, and remains at high relapse risk, a further twelve weeks reduces relapse and is an accepted extension in Australian practice. Relapse risk is highest in the first three months and is driven by cued craving, alcohol, other smokers in the household and low mood, so behavioural support and scheduled review continue alongside the medicine rather than stopping with it. In context: nicotine dependence is chronic and relapsing, and abstinence at twelve weeks is a milestone rather than a cure, which is why the end of a course is a decision point rather than a discharge.
key_points: Standard course is twelve weeks; a further twelve weeks is offered to those who have quit and remain at risk
Extended therapy reduces relapse in patients abstinent at the end of the first course
Behavioural support and scheduled review continue past the end of pharmacotherapy
Cued craving, alcohol and household smoking are the practical relapse triggers
explanation.pearls: Abstinence at twelve weeks predicts long-term success but roughly half of quitters relapse within a year, so the end-of-course consultation is planned rather than incidental.

options.rationale: A second 12-week course is offered to a patient who has quit on treatment, tolerates it and remains at high relapse risk; extended therapy reduces relapse in this group. (Source: AMH: Varenicline)

Short-acting replacement after the course suits a patient who cannot continue varenicline or declines it; it is less effective than extending the agent that has already worked for him. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

Tapering is used at the end of treatment mainly to limit irritability in some patients; it does not address ongoing craving and varenicline does not require a withdrawal taper. (Source: AMH: Varenicline)
Bupropion is chosen when varenicline is unsuitable from the outset. Swapping agents in a patient doing well on one has no evidence and adds seizure and interaction risk. (Source: AMH: Bupropion)

Reactive review is reasonable for a confident ex-smoker with no craving. Scheduled follow-up in the first months after quitting is when most relapse is preventable. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD diagnosis requires DSM-5-TR criteria with onset before age 12, persistence into adulthood, impairment in 2 or more settings, and exclusion of other mental health conditions causing the symptoms. AADPA Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline recommends stimulants (methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine) as first-line for adults without contraindications. Cardiac contraindications include structural heart disease, prior stimulant-induced arrhythmia, uncontrolled hypertension, and concurrent stimulant misuse. Atomoxetine is the first-line non-stimulant. Driving advice and S8 prescribing rules (state-specific authority required) apply. Baseline ECG, BP, HR, and weight are mandatory; follow-up every 3 months in the first year.
key_points: AADPA guidance: stimulants first-line in adults without contraindication
Prior stimulant-induced arrhythmia is a relative contraindication
Atomoxetine is the first-line non-stimulant in adults
Baseline ECG, BP, HR mandatory before starting stimulants
State-specific authority prescription required for S8 stimulants
explanation.pearls: Atomoxetine takes 4-6 weeks to reach full effect; the dose ceiling in adults is 100 mg daily and the gain over stimulants is the absence of abuse liability and cardiac safety in patients with prior stimulant-induced events.

explanation.summary: DSM-5-TR criteria for schizoaffective disorder are: (A) an uninterrupted period of illness during which there is a major mood episode (major depressive or manic) concurrent with criterion A of schizophrenia (delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, grossly disorganised behaviour, or negative symptoms); (B) delusions or hallucinations for 2 or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode during the lifetime duration of the illness; (C) mood-episode symptoms present for the majority of the total illness duration; (D) not attributable to a substance or medical condition. Bipolar type is subtyped when mania has occurred; depressive type when only major depressive episodes have occurred. Treatment combines antipsychotic with mood stabiliser or antidepressant (depending on subtype); long-term prognosis is intermediate between schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.
key_points: DSM-5-TR schizoaffective requires 2 or more weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms
Mood symptoms must be present for the MAJORITY of total illness duration
Bipolar type if mania ever occurred; depressive type if only MDD
Differential from bipolar with psychosis hinges on inter-episode psychosis-only periods
Treatment combines antipsychotic plus mood stabiliser (bipolar type) or antidepressant (depressive type)
explanation.pearls: The 2-week rule (psychosis without mood symptoms) separates schizoaffective disorder from bipolar disorder with psychotic features; missing this transition window causes most diagnostic errors in this differential.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.rationale: Bipolar I with psychotic features requires that psychotic symptoms only occur during mood episodes; the 12-week interval of psychosis in the absence of mood symptoms excludes this. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.rationale: DSM-5-TR requires (a) a major mood episode (manic or major depressive) concurrent with criterion A of schizophrenia, (b) delusions or hallucinations for 2 or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode, (c) mood symptoms present for the majority of total illness duration. All three are met. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

Schizophrenia with comorbid mood disorder requires mood symptoms to be present for a MINORITY of the total illness duration; her mood episodes are prominent and recurrent rather than residual. (Source: DSM-5-TR)
Schizophreniform is defined by total psychotic illness duration of less than 6 months; the 8 year course makes this diagnosis inapplicable. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

Delusional disorder requires criterion A delusions for 1 month or longer without prominent hallucinations or disorganised speech; this patient has clear hallucinations and mood episodes, which rules it out. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Linezolid is a weak reversible MAOI; co-prescription with SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, tramadol, fentanyl, pethidine, dextromethorphan, lithium, triptans, methylene blue, or recreational MDMA can precipitate serotonin syndrome. The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria require ingestion of a serotonergic agent plus one of: spontaneous clonus, inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, tremor with hyperreflexia, hypertonia plus temperature above 38 °C with ocular or inducible clonus. Treatment is removal of all serotonergic agents, benzodiazepines for agitation and clonus, active cooling, and cyproheptadine 12 mg orally followed by 2 mg every 2 hours (max 32 mg/day) for refractory cases. Severe cases require ICU and intubation with non-depolarising muscle relaxants. Recovery is usually within 24-72 hours.
key_points: Hunter criteria diagnose serotonin syndrome clinically
Linezolid is a weak reversible MAOI that combines dangerously with SSRIs
Stop ALL serotonergic agents, supportive care with benzodiazepines, active cooling
Cyproheptadine 12 mg orally for refractory cases
Bromocriptine and dantrolene are NMS, NOT serotonin toxicity, treatments
explanation.pearls: Lower-limb-dominant hyperreflexia, inducible clonus, mydriasis, and hyperthermia in the context of serotonergic co-prescription distinguish serotonin syndrome from NMS; antidote is cyproheptadine 12 mg PO, NOT bromocriptine or dantrolene.

options.rationale: Bromocriptine is used as dopaminergic rescue in neuroleptic malignant syndrome, not serotonin syndrome; the antidote concept here is cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist), not a dopamine agonist. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Dantrolene is used in malignant hyperthermia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome; in serotonin toxicity, benzodiazepines are first-line. Continuing the precipitants is the major management error. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Vancomycin substitution is a sensible eventual antibiotic plan but the IMMEDIATE priority is to stop BOTH serotonergic agents and provide supportive care; sertraline cessation also matters because its half-life is long. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Serotonin toxicity is a clinical diagnosis (Hunter criteria); treatment is removal of serotonergic agents, supportive care with benzodiazepines, active cooling, and cyproheptadine for refractory cases. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology; Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria; UpToDate)

Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist; agitation in serotonin syndrome benefits from benzodiazepines, NOT flumazenil. Flumazenil also lowers seizure threshold and worsens autonomic instability. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Long-term lithium monitoring targets three predictable adverse effects: thyroid dysfunction (5 to 35 percent develop hypothyroidism over years), renal impairment (cumulative tubular and interstitial injury), and primary hyperparathyroidism (raised calcium with inappropriately normal or elevated PTH). RANZCP recommends serum lithium every 6 months once stable (more often if dose changed, dehydration, new interacting medication), TSH and creatinine every 6 months, and calcium with FBC annually. ACE inhibitors, ARBs, NSAIDs, thiazides, and dehydration all raise lithium levels and prompt earlier rechecking.
key_points: Stable maintenance: lithium level + TSH + creatinine 6-monthly
Calcium and FBC annually (detect hyperparathyroidism, marrow effects)
Recheck level promptly if dehydration, NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, or thiazide added
Lithium hypothyroidism affects 5 to 35 percent of long-term users
explanation.pearls: Lithium maintenance monitoring: level + TSH + creatinine every 6 months and calcium annually to detect hypothyroidism, renal decline, and hyperparathyroidism.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Annual lithium and selective biochemistry under-monitors a drug with narrow therapeutic index and predictable renal and thyroid effects, and would miss subclinical change before symptoms develop. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Monthly lithium levels are appropriate during titration and the first 6 months; ongoing maintenance does not require this frequency in a stable patient and over-investigates without clinical benefit. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Reactive-only monitoring misses asymptomatic level drift from dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, and dose-adherence change. RANZCP requires routine surveillance even in stable patients. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: FBC alone misses the key targets of TSH (lithium causes hypothyroidism in 5 to 35 percent over time) and creatinine (cumulative renal injury), and would leave thyroid and renal change undetected. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: RANZCP guidelines for stable maintenance lithium specify level every 6 months, TSH and creatinine every 6 months, and calcium with FBC annually to detect hypothyroidism, renal decline, and hyperparathyroidism. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

explanation.summary: Second-generation antipsychotics (especially olanzapine and clozapine) cause weight gain, dyslipidaemia, and impaired glucose tolerance early in treatment. Australian monitoring per RANZCP and Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic is structured to detect this window. Baseline assessment includes weight, BMI, waist circumference, BP, fasting glucose, fasting lipids, and ECG. Repeat fasting glucose and lipids at 12 weeks (the first checkpoint), then annually thereafter if stable. Weight and BP are checked at every visit. Prolactin is checked if symptomatic.
key_points: Antipsychotic metabolic monitoring schedule: baseline, 12 weeks, then annually
Weight and BP every visit; fasting glucose and lipids per schedule
Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic burden
Switch agent or add metformin if early dyslipidaemia or weight gain
explanation.pearls: Antipsychotic metabolic screen: baseline, 12 weeks, then yearly for fasting glucose and lipids; weight and BP every visit.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: The RANZCP and Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic schedule for second-generation antipsychotic monitoring is baseline, then 12 weeks, then annually for fasting glucose and lipids, with weight at every visit and BP at every visit. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: A 6-week check is not part of the RANZCP or AMH schedule for routine metabolic monitoring; the first repeat is at 12 weeks. Adding a 6-week point does not change management. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: A 6-month first repeat misses the early window for olanzapine-related weight gain and dyslipidaemia, where intervention (switch agent or commence metformin) is most effective. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Annual monitoring alone misses early metabolic side effects that emerge within the first 3 months on olanzapine in particular. RANZCP specifies the 12-week timepoint. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Reactive-only monitoring misses asymptomatic dyslipidaemia and impaired fasting glucose, which are the targets of antipsychotic metabolic screening. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic recommends IM olanzapine 10 mg (5 mg if elderly or frail) as first-line monotherapy for severe acute behavioural disturbance unresponsive to verbal de-escalation. IM droperidol 10 mg is an acceptable alternative (with QT assessment if possible). Combined parenteral antipsychotic plus benzodiazepine carries a respiratory-depression risk and should be separated by at least 1 hour. Continue monitoring including pulse oximetry, BP, and sedation level (RASS) after administration. Physical restraint alone is associated with worse outcomes than appropriate chemical calming.
key_points: First-line: IM olanzapine 10 mg (or IM droperidol 10 mg) monotherapy
Avoid simultaneous parenteral antipsychotic plus parenteral benzodiazepine
Reduce dose in elderly, frail, or naive patients
Continue vital sign and sedation-score monitoring after dose
explanation.pearls: Acute behavioural disturbance first-line in Australia is IM olanzapine 10 mg; never co-administer parenterally with a benzodiazepine because of respiratory depression risk.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Acute behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: Oral diazepam is unlikely to be safely administered to an actively combative patient under physical restraint, and onset is too slow for the immediate safety risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Acute behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: Therapeutic Guidelines recommend IM olanzapine 10 mg as first-line for severe acute behavioural disturbance without contraindication, with strict avoidance of co-administration with parenteral benzodiazepines due to respiratory depression risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Acute behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: Co-administration of IM olanzapine or IM haloperidol with parenteral benzodiazepines is associated with respiratory depression and hypotension; this combination is no longer recommended as first-line in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Acute behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: Oral quetiapine in this dose has slow onset and is impractical to administer to an actively restrained agitated patient; parenteral therapy is needed for immediate safety. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Acute behavioural disturbance)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Acute behavioural disturbance

options.rationale: Prolonged physical restraint without pharmacological calming is associated with rhabdomyolysis, asphyxia, and increased death rate; chemical restraint is part of the standard of care once verbal de-escalation has failed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic - Acute behavioural disturbance

explanation.summary: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose causes fast sodium channel blockade, anticholinergic toxidrome, and alpha-1 antagonism. The cardinal ECG indicator is QRS prolongation; thresholds of more than 100 ms predict seizures and more than 160 ms predict ventricular arrhythmias. A terminal R wave in aVR of more than 3 mm is another marker. IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus, repeated to maintain arterial pH 7.50 to 7.55, reverses sodium-channel block. Avoid class I antiarrhythmics. Hypotension is treated with fluids then noradrenaline (alpha-1 agonist counters the alpha-1 blockade). Lipid emulsion is rescue therapy.
key_points: QRS more than 100 ms after TCA overdose predicts seizures and arrhythmia
Terminal R wave aVR more than 3 mm is another marker of toxicity
IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg, repeat to pH 7.50 to 7.55
Avoid class I antiarrhythmics; flumazenil contraindicated in mixed overdose
explanation.pearls: TCA overdose with QRS more than 100 ms: IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus, titrate to arterial pH 7.50 to 7.55; class I antiarrhythmics and flumazenil are contraindicated.

options.rationale: Two hours post-ingestion with depressed conscious state, charcoal has limited benefit and aspiration risk is meaningful. More importantly, the widened QRS and metabolic acidosis demand active sodium-channel-blockade reversal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology; Murray TCA overdose)
Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose including TCA because it can precipitate seizures, and there is no benzodiazepine indication anyway. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

QRS more than 100 ms after TCA overdose indicates fast-sodium-channel blockade and predicts arrhythmia and seizures. IV sodium bicarbonate (1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus, then infusion or repeat boluses to target arterial pH 7.50 to 7.55) is the antidote and reverses sodium-channel block. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology; Murray TCA overdose)

Magnesium is appropriate for polymorphic VT or torsades but the live problem here is sodium-channel blockade, which responds to sodium bicarbonate not magnesium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Lidocaine is a sodium-channel blocker itself and worsens the TCA toxicity; class IA and IC antiarrhythmics are contraindicated. Sodium bicarbonate is the answer. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate causes major congenital malformation in around 10 percent of exposed pregnancies (especially neural-tube defects) and neurodevelopmental impairment in around 30 to 40 percent. TGA imposes a Pregnancy Prevention Program (PPP) requiring annual risk acknowledgement and effective contraception in all women of childbearing potential. When pregnancy is planned, switching to a safer mood stabiliser before conception is the standard approach. Lithium is the preferred option for bipolar I with risk of Ebstein anomaly approximately 1 in 1000, fetal echo at 18 to 20 weeks. Lamotrigine is an alternative for bipolar depression-predominant illness. Stopping valproate during pregnancy is too late to prevent first-trimester teratogenicity.
key_points: Valproate has 10 percent major malformation rate and substantial neurodevelopmental risk
Switch agent before conception, not at pregnancy confirmation
Lithium preferred for bipolar I (Ebstein risk approximately 1 in 1000) with fetal echo at 18 to 20 wk
TGA Pregnancy Prevention Program requires annual risk acknowledgement
explanation.pearls: Valproate in women of childbearing potential: switch to lithium or lamotrigine before conception; folic acid does not mitigate the 10 percent malformation rate.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Folic acid supplementation does not mitigate valproate's spina bifida and developmental risk; valproate-related neurodevelopmental harm and 10 percent major malformation rate persist despite folate. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG; TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Major teratogenic effects of valproate occur in the early first trimester before pregnancy is often confirmed; stopping at that point is too late to prevent neural-tube defects. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program)

Although risk is dose-related, no dose of valproate is considered safe in pregnancy and the 500 mg dose is also associated with neurodevelopmental harm; switching the agent is preferred. (Source: TGA Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program)

Lithium is the preferred mood stabiliser for bipolar I in women planning pregnancy because of valproate's 10 percent major malformation rate and substantial neurodevelopmental impact. The plan acknowledges Ebstein anomaly risk (approximately 1 in 1000) via fetal echo at 18 to 20 weeks. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline; RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Abrupt valproate cessation risks rapid relapse, and olanzapine 20 mg long-term carries substantial metabolic burden; cross-titration with a mood stabiliser is preferred. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

explanation.summary: Continuing lithium in pregnancy in a woman with severe bipolar I disorder is the default Australian position because the relapse risk after discontinuation (approximately 70 percent within 6 months) substantially outweighs the absolute teratogenic risk. Ebstein anomaly risk increases from background 1 in 20,000 to approximately 1 in 1000 with first-trimester exposure. Management is continuation at the lowest effective dose, divided dosing to limit peak levels, monthly serum levels (increasing in the third trimester as clearance rises), fetal echo at 18 to 20 weeks, and a clear plan around delivery (lithium hold 24 to 48 hours before induction or caesarean to limit toxicity from acute volume shifts).
key_points: Relapse risk after lithium discontinuation: approximately 70 percent in 6 months
Ebstein anomaly risk: approximately 1 in 1000 on first-trimester lithium
Continue at lowest effective dose with divided dosing; fetal echo at 18 to 20 weeks
Lithium hold 24 to 48 hours pre-delivery; monthly levels increasing in third trimester
explanation.pearls: Stopping lithium in pregnancy carries approximately 70 percent relapse risk in bipolar I; continue at lowest effective dose with divided dosing, monthly levels, and fetal echo at 18 to 20 weeks.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Lithium discontinuation in pregnancy carries roughly 70 percent relapse risk in bipolar I; switching to olanzapine alone may not match lithium's efficacy in her established disease and exposes the fetus to two drugs in sequence. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)

Ebstein anomaly risk on first-trimester lithium is approximately 1 in 1000 (background 1 in 20,000); the absolute risk is far outweighed by relapse risk after stopping. RANZCP/COPE recommend continuation at lowest effective dose, divided dosing to minimise peak levels, and fetal echo at 18 to 20 weeks. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline; RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Halving the dose risks subtherapeutic levels and relapse without meaningfully reducing the Ebstein risk, which is most strongly tied to peak rather than trough levels; divided dosing rather than total reduction is preferred. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)

Lamotrigine is preferred for bipolar depression-predominant illness, not the bipolar I with mania-predominant pattern she has. Switching late in the first trimester would expose the fetus to overlapping drugs without justification. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Mood Disorders

options.rationale: Lithium clearance rises as pregnancy progresses, requiring level monitoring monthly then more frequently in the third trimester, plus dose-timing adjustments around delivery. Routine antenatal care alone is inadequate. (Source: COPE Perinatal Mental Health Guideline)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome from a drug-drug interaction between an SSRI and another serotonergic agent (linezolid is a non-selective monoamine oxidase inhibitor, tramadol, fentanyl, MDMA, tryptans) presents within hours to days of the new agent. The Hunter Criteria diagnose toxicity when a serotonergic agent has been taken and any one of: spontaneous clonus, inducible clonus plus agitation or diaphoresis, ocular clonus plus agitation or diaphoresis, tremor plus hyperreflexia, or hypertonia with temperature above 38 degrees with ocular or inducible clonus. Management is cessation of all serotonergic drugs, IV benzodiazepines, active cooling for hyperthermia above 39 degrees, and cyproheptadine 12 mg oral then 2 mg every 2 hours up to 32 mg/24 h as a serotonin antagonist.
key_points: Linezolid plus SSRI causes serotonin syndrome through MAOI activity
Hunter criteria: spontaneous clonus or inducible clonus plus agitation/diaphoresis or ocular clonus combinations
Serotonin syndrome: hyperreflexia + clonus + mydriasis (vs NMS: rigidity + hyporeflexia + diaphoresis)
Cyproheptadine 12 mg oral then 2 mg every 2 hours as serotonin antagonist
explanation.pearls: Linezolid is a non-selective MAOI and precipitates serotonin syndrome with SSRIs; treat with cessation, benzodiazepines, cooling, and cyproheptadine 12 mg orally.

options.rationale: Sustained clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, and short interval after a serotonergic-drug interaction strongly favour serotonin syndrome over NMS, which usually presents with lead-pipe rigidity and hyporeflexia evolving over days. Continuing escitalopram and linezolid would worsen symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria)

This case meets Hunter criteria for serotonin syndrome (spontaneous clonus, or inducible clonus plus agitation plus diaphoresis, or ocular clonus plus tremor plus hyperreflexia). Linezolid is a non-selective MAOI that precipitates serotonin syndrome with SSRIs. Withdraw both agents, support with benzodiazepines and cooling, and add cyproheptadine 12 mg oral as serotonin antagonist. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria)

Both drugs must be ceased because their interaction is causal. Haloperidol can worsen serotonin syndrome by adding dopaminergic blockade and lowering the seizure threshold, and is not first-line for agitation here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Antipyretics alone do not address the cause and continuing escitalopram delays recovery; serotonin-mediated hyperthermia responds poorly to paracetamol. Both drugs need to stop. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Bromocriptine is a dopaminergic agonist used in NMS, not serotonin syndrome; in serotonin syndrome it adds no benefit and risks worsening agitation. Cyproheptadine is the serotonin-specific antagonist. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Severe alcohol withdrawal that does not respond to escalating benzodiazepines (typically defined as more than 200 mg of diazepam in a few hours without response, or CIWA-Ar persistently above 20 despite high doses) is treated by adding a second GABA-A modulator with different binding kinetics. Phenobarbital is the Australian addiction-medicine step (130 to 260 mg IV loading dose, repeated to control, with airway monitoring). Adjuncts include magnesium and phosphate replacement, parenteral thiamine before any glucose, and treatment of co-existing infection. Propofol with intubation is the final escalation when phenobarbital is insufficient. Dexmedetomidine and antipsychotics are adjuncts but do not address the GABA deficit.
key_points: Benzodiazepine-refractory DT escalates to phenobarbital as second GABA-A agent
Phenobarbital IV loading 130 to 260 mg, repeated to symptom control
Continue thiamine, magnesium, phosphate; treat occult infection
Antipsychotics and dexmedetomidine are adjuncts not substitutes
explanation.pearls: Benzodiazepine-refractory delirium tremens: IV phenobarbital 130 to 260 mg loading dose, repeated to control; antipsychotics lower the seizure threshold and are not GABA-active.

options.rationale: Haloperidol does not treat the GABA-deficit driving withdrawal and lowers the seizure threshold; it is not the right next step in benzodiazepine-refractory withdrawal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

Dexmedetomidine reduces sympathetic surge but does not treat the GABA deficit underlying delirium tremens, and is therefore considered adjunctive only after primary GABAergic control. It is not first choice in refractory withdrawal. (Source: ANZICS recommendations)

Baclofen has a role in long-term abstinence support but acute oral baclofen has slow onset and modest effect, and would not control acute delirium tremens in this severity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

Cross-tapering one benzodiazepine for another at higher dose simply repeats the failed mechanism; in benzodiazepine resistance the response is to add a second GABA modulator with different pharmacology, not change the agent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine)

Benzodiazepine-refractory severe alcohol withdrawal requires escalation to a second GABA-A modulator. IV phenobarbital (loading dose 130 to 260 mg, repeated to symptom control with airway watch) is the recognised Australian addiction-medicine step before propofol intubation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Addiction Medicine; ANZICS recommendations)

explanation.summary: RANZCP, the Maudsley Guidelines, and Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic all recommend a structured metabolic monitoring schedule for second-generation antipsychotics: baseline, 12 weeks, then yearly for fasting glucose or HbA1c, fasting lipids, weight, waist circumference, and BP. Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic burden; aripiprazole and lurasidone the lowest. Lifestyle counselling starts at initiation; metformin can be added in established or progressive weight gain or pre-diabetes. ECG is baseline plus reassessment with QT-prolonging agents.
key_points: Baseline, 12-week, then yearly metabolic monitoring is RANZCP standard
Weight checks more frequent (often weekly to monthly) in the first 3 months
Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic burden
Metformin for weight gain or pre-diabetes after lifestyle intervention; not prophylactic
explanation.pearls: Second-gen antipsychotic monitoring: baseline, 12-week, then yearly fasting glucose/HbA1c, lipids, weight, BP, waist. Weight checks more often in first 3 months. Metformin for established weight gain or pre-diabetes after lifestyle intervention.

options.rationale: Weight gain triggers extra review, but routine 12-week metabolic monitoring is scheduled regardless of weight under RANZCP. Many patients develop dyslipidaemia or insulin resistance before substantial weight change. (Source: RANZCP Adult Antipsychotic Monitoring Statement)

RANZCP and the Maudsley Guidelines recommend baseline, 12-week, and then yearly metabolic monitoring (fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipids, weight, BP, waist circumference) for all patients on second-generation antipsychotics, with more frequent weight checks during the first three months. Olanzapine and clozapine have the highest metabolic burden of the second-generation agents. (Source: RANZCP Adult Antipsychotic Monitoring Statement)

Switching is not indicated in a patient stable and responding well after 6 weeks of olanzapine. Monitoring is the next step; switching is reserved for significant or intolerable metabolic decline despite lifestyle intervention. (Source: RANZCP Adult Antipsychotic Monitoring Statement)

Metformin is considered for olanzapine- or clozapine-associated weight gain after it occurs and lifestyle measures fail; it is not routinely prescribed prophylactically at week 6 in a normoglycaemic patient. (Source: RANZCP Adult Antipsychotic Monitoring Statement)

Routine 3-monthly ECG is not required for olanzapine. ECG is checked at baseline and repeated if dose-related QTc concerns arise or with high-QTc agents like ziprasidone. The metabolic profile is the priority for olanzapine. (Source: RANZCP Adult Antipsychotic Monitoring Statement)

explanation.summary: First-line pharmacotherapy for tobacco smoking cessation in Australia includes varenicline, combination nicotine replacement therapy (patch plus short-acting), and bupropion. Varenicline has the highest abstinence effect in network meta-analyses and is now considered safe in stable psychiatric illness following the EAGLES trial. Dose escalates over week 1 with a target quit date in week 2; treatment continues for 12 weeks. Behavioural support (Quitline, brief intervention) doubles efficacy. Bupropion is avoided in eating disorders and uncontrolled epilepsy. NRT alone is appropriate for lighter smokers and where varenicline is contraindicated.
key_points: Varenicline 1 mg twice daily after week-1 escalation; 12-week course
EAGLES trial: no excess neuropsychiatric adverse events in stable psychiatric illness
Bupropion avoided in eating disorders and uncontrolled epilepsy
Combination NRT (patch plus short-acting) is also first-line
explanation.pearls: Smoking cessation first-line: varenicline 1 mg twice daily (after week-1 escalation), combination NRT, or bupropion. EAGLES showed varenicline is safe in stable psychiatric illness. Always pair with Quitline or behavioural support.

options.rationale: Bupropion is effective but carries a seizure risk in eating disorders and uncontrolled epilepsy, and has more drug interactions than varenicline. Varenicline has stronger evidence in stable schizophrenia per EAGLES. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)

Varenicline has the highest abstinence rates in the RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline and is suitable in stable psychiatric illness. The EAGLES trial showed no excess neuropsychiatric adverse events compared with placebo, patch, or bupropion. Dose escalates over week 1 (0.5 mg daily x3 days, 0.5 mg bd x4 days, then 1 mg bd) with a target quit date in week 2. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)

Combination NRT is a reasonable option and is also first-line in RACGP, but in a 25-a-day smoker with prior patch failure and stable psychiatric illness, varenicline has the greatest abstinence effect. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)
Nortriptyline is second-line at best and not registered for smoking cessation in Australia. Side effects (anticholinergic, QT) limit utility. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)
Clonidine has weak evidence for smoking cessation and is not recommended as first-line. Hypotension and sedation limit acceptability. (Source: RACGP Smoking Cessation Guideline)

explanation.summary: Borderline personality disorder is treated primarily with structured psychological therapy under the NHMRC guideline, RANZCP, and NICE. Evidence-based options include dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT), mentalisation-based therapy (MBT), schema-focused therapy (SFT), and transference-focused psychotherapy (TFP). Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive, used for specific comorbidities (depression, psychosis, mood instability) and discontinued if not clearly helpful. Admission is reserved for acute risk that cannot otherwise be managed safely.
key_points: Structured psychological therapy is first-line in BPD (DBT, MBT, SFT, TFP)
Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive, targeting specific symptom clusters only
Avoid valproate in women of reproductive age unless contraception is reliable
Brief planned admissions for crisis only; avoid long inpatient stays
explanation.pearls: BPD first-line: structured psychological therapy (DBT, MBT, schema, TFP). Pharmacotherapy adjunctive only. Avoid valproate in women of reproductive age. Crisis admissions kept brief and planned.

sources.label: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.rationale: Antidepressants help comorbid depression but do not target BPD symptoms specifically. Repeated antidepressant switching in the absence of a clear depressive episode does not address the core problem. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.rationale: Antipsychotics are not first-line in BPD and have modest effects on a narrow symptom range (cognitive perceptual, anger). NHMRC explicitly cautions against using them as a substitute for structured psychotherapy. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.rationale: Sodium valproate has weak and inconsistent evidence in BPD; it is teratogenic and not appropriate for a young woman of reproductive age unless pregnancy is reliably prevented. NHMRC does not endorse it as first-line. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.rationale: Brief crisis-driven admissions can reinforce dependence on inpatient care without addressing core deficits. NHMRC supports community-based structured psychotherapy and only short admissions for acute risk that cannot otherwise be managed. (Source: NHMRC BPD Guideline)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

options.rationale: RANZCP and NHMRC guidance identify structured psychological therapies (dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation-based therapy, schema-focused therapy, transference-focused therapy) as first-line for borderline personality disorder. Pharmacotherapy is adjunctive for specific symptom clusters, never primary. (Source: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder)
source_refs: NHMRC Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Borderline Personality Disorder

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndromic diagnosis recognised across primary psychiatric (mood, psychotic) and medical causes (autoimmune encephalitis, metabolic, infective). The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale is the standard assessment. A lorazepam challenge of 1 to 2 mg IM or IV with reassessment in 30 to 60 minutes is both diagnostic and the first therapeutic step. Maintenance lorazepam (6 to 24 mg per day, occasionally higher) is then titrated. ECT is the second-line treatment for non-responders and the first-line for malignant catatonia (with autonomic instability and hyperthermia). Antipsychotics are avoided until catatonia has resolved.
key_points: Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IM or IV with reassessment at 30 to 60 minutes is the diagnostic challenge
Maintenance lorazepam 6 to 24 mg per day in divided doses for responders
Avoid antipsychotics until catatonia resolves; risk of NMS and worsening
ECT is second-line and first-line for malignant catatonia
explanation.pearls: Catatonia: lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IM or IV challenge, reassess Bush-Francis at 30 to 60 minutes. Responders go to 6 to 24 mg per day in divided doses. ECT is second-line and first-line for malignant catatonia. Avoid antipsychotics until resolution.

options.rationale: Autoimmune encephalitis is on the differential but a primary psychiatric catatonia with a clear precipitant (medication cessation) and normal CT and inflammatory markers does not mandate LP before the lorazepam challenge. LP is considered if challenge fails or red flags emerge. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Statement)

Antipsychotics, particularly typical agents, can worsen catatonia and precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome. They are avoided until catatonia is broken with benzodiazepines or ECT. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Statement)

Restarting lithium is appropriate as a longer-term plan but does not address the acute catatonic state. Catatonia carries risks of dehydration, deep vein thrombosis, and aspiration that need same-day intervention. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Statement)

A lorazepam challenge is the standard diagnostic and initial therapeutic test for catatonia. An improvement of 50% or more on the Bush-Francis scale within 30 to 60 minutes confirms benzodiazepine-responsive catatonia and directs further treatment with scheduled lorazepam, often 6 to 24 mg per day in divided doses. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Statement)
ECT is the next step if the lorazepam challenge fails or for malignant catatonia. Benzodiazepines come first as both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Statement)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome is diagnosed clinically using the Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria: in the setting of a serotonergic agent, the presence of spontaneous clonus, OR inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, OR ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, OR tremor and hyperreflexia, OR hypertonia plus temperature above 38 degrees Celsius with ocular or inducible clonus, is diagnostic. The pattern of hyperreflexia, lower-limb-predominant clonus, mydriasis, and acute onset distinguishes it from NMS (rigidity, bradyreflexia, days to develop). MAOI plus tramadol or other serotonergic agent is a particularly high-risk combination, requiring a 2-week SSRI washout before introducing an MAOI.
key_points: Hunter Criteria use spontaneous or inducible clonus, ocular clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation, diaphoresis, hyperthermia
Serotonin syndrome: hyperreflexia, lower-limb-dominant clonus, mydriasis, acute onset
NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, indolent onset, antipsychotic exposure
MAOI plus tramadol or SSRI without 2-week washout is a high-risk combination
explanation.pearls: Hunter Criteria for serotonin syndrome: spontaneous clonus, OR inducible clonus with agitation/diaphoresis, OR ocular clonus with agitation/diaphoresis, OR tremor and hyperreflexia, OR hypertonia plus T>38 with clonus. Lower limb dominance and mydriasis distinguish from NMS. MAOI plus tramadol is classic.

options.rationale: The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria are met (spontaneous clonus, plus agitation, sweating, and hyperthermia). The combination of phenelzine (irreversible MAOI) plus tramadol (serotonergic) plus an inadequate sertraline washout (less than 2 weeks) is classic. Lower limb hyperreflexia, ocular clonus, and dilated pupils favour serotonin syndrome over NMS. (Source: Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

NMS presents with lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, and an indolent onset over days, typically after antipsychotic initiation or dose increase. This patient has hyperreflexia and clonus and no antipsychotic exposure. (Source: Hunter Criteria; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Anticholinergic toxicity features dry skin and mucous membranes, urinary retention, and a flushed face, not the diaphoresis and clonus here. Tramadol can have anticholinergic effects but the dominant picture is serotonergic. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Thyroid storm causes hypermetabolic state but typically with goitre, atrial fibrillation, and bradyreflexia. The classic combination of agitation, spontaneous clonus, ocular clonus, and diaphoresis points to serotonin syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Stimulant intoxication can produce agitation, hypertension, and tachycardia but does not classically produce lower-limb-dominant clonus or ocular clonus. His recent phenelzine, tramadol and sertraline exposure points to serotonin toxicity instead. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Lithium toxicity occurs by reduced renal clearance (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, dehydration, AKI), dose error, or deliberate overdose. EXTRIP recommendations for haemodialysis are: any lithium level over 4.0 mmol/L, OR over 2.5 mmol/L with significant impaired consciousness, seizures, life-threatening arrhythmia, OR over 2.5 mmol/L with renal impairment that will prevent clearance within 36 hours. Saline IV at 1.5 to 2 times maintenance is given while dialysis is arranged. Rebound rises after dialysis (intracellular shifts) require recheck and may need re-dialysis. The classic clinical triad is coarse tremor, ataxia, and altered mental status.
key_points: Haemodialysis if level over 4.0 mmol/L, OR over 2.5 mmol/L with encephalopathy, seizures, arrhythmia, OR renal impairment
IV 0.9% sodium chloride at 1.5 to 2 times maintenance while dialysis is arranged
Activated charcoal does NOT bind lithium
Expect rebound levels after dialysis from intracellular redistribution
explanation.pearls: Lithium toxicity dialysis (EXTRIP): level over 4.0 mmol/L, OR over 2.5 mmol/L with encephalopathy/seizures/arrhythmia, OR over 2.5 mmol/L with renal impairment. Saline IV at 1.5 to 2 times maintenance bridges to dialysis. Activated charcoal does NOT bind lithium.

options.rationale: Activated charcoal does not bind lithium and has no role in lithium toxicity. It is not recommended in any toxicology guideline for this indication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Saline alone is appropriate for mild toxicity in normal renal function but is insufficient in CKD with AKI, encephalopathy, and a level over 2.5 mmol/L. EXTRIP supports dialysis in this scenario. (Source: EXTRIP)

EXTRIP consensus recommends haemodialysis for lithium toxicity when the level exceeds 4.0 mmol/L, OR exceeds 2.5 mmol/L with significant impaired consciousness, seizures, life-threatening arrhythmia, OR exceeds 2.5 mmol/L with renal impairment that will impair clearance. This patient meets the third criterion: level 3.4 with CKD stage 3 and acute kidney injury, plus altered mental status. IV saline is started while dialysis is arranged. (Source: EXTRIP Workgroup Lithium Recommendations)
Watchful waiting in a patient with encephalopathy, AKI, and a level of 3.4 mmol/L risks deterioration, seizures, and arrhythmia. Active clearance is needed. (Source: EXTRIP)

Sodium polystyrene sulfonate has been investigated for lithium binding but is not endorsed as primary therapy. EXTRIP supports haemodialysis as the definitive extracorporeal removal modality. (Source: EXTRIP)

explanation.summary: The 2022 Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD sets out a structured pathway: GP triage with collateral history and screening (ASRS), then specialist referral for diagnostic confirmation by a psychiatrist, paediatrician, or, in some states, neurologist with stimulant prescribing authority. Stimulant initiation (methylphenidate or dexamfetamine) requires Schedule 8 authority and ECG and cardiovascular screening before initiation. Driving counselling, comorbidity screening (anxiety, depression, substance use), and informed consent on diversion risks are required. GPs continue maintenance under shared-care arrangements.
key_points: Adult ADHD diagnosis requires specialist confirmation by a psychiatrist or paediatrician
Stimulants are Schedule 8 and need state authority before initiation
Cardiovascular screen (history and ECG) before stimulant initiation
GPs continue maintenance under shared-care arrangements
explanation.pearls: Adult ADHD: GP screens (ASRS) and refers; specialist (psychiatrist, paediatrician, sometimes neurologist) confirms diagnosis and initiates stimulant under Schedule 8 authority. CV screen and ECG before initiation; GP shared-care maintenance.

sources.label: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: ADHD is by definition a developmental disorder with symptoms from childhood, and adult presentation reflecting previously unrecognised lifelong difficulty is common. Dismissing the assessment misses a treatable condition. (Source: Australian ADHD Guideline)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: GPs cannot initiate stimulants without specialist authority under state Schedule 8 legislation. Initiation requires specialist diagnosis. (Source: Australian ADHD Guideline)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Atomoxetine is non-stimulant but still requires authority initiation. Adult ADHD diagnosis must be specialist-confirmed before any first-line medication. (Source: Australian ADHD Guideline)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Neuropsychological testing supplements clinical assessment but is not the diagnostic standard. ADHD is a clinical diagnosis based on developmental history, current impairment across settings, and DSM-5-TR criteria. (Source: Australian ADHD Guideline)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

options.rationale: Adult ADHD diagnosis in Australia requires confirmation by an appropriately credentialed specialist (psychiatrist, paediatrician, or in some states neurologist) with stimulant prescribing authority. Stimulants are Schedule 8 and need state authority. GPs co-prescribe under a shared-care plan once initiated. (Source: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD)
source_refs: Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate is associated with up to 10 percent risk of major congenital malformations and 30 to 40 percent risk of neurodevelopmental disorders in exposed children. TGA restrictions require adherence to a Pregnancy Prevention Program for use in women of childbearing potential. Pre-conception planning should switch to a safer agent rather than wait for a positive pregnancy test. Lithium is preferred for bipolar I with manic predominance and has lower (but not zero) teratogenic risk.
key_points: Valproate WCBA risk: around 10 percent major malformations, 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental disorders.
Pre-conception switch should be planned, not at the time of positive pregnancy test.
Lithium is preferred for manic-predominant bipolar I maintenance during pregnancy planning.
Lamotrigine is preferred for bipolar depression prevention.
explanation.pearls: Switch valproate to lithium 400 mg nocte for a woman planning pregnancy with manic-predominant bipolar I disorder; folate does not mitigate the 10 percent malformation and 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental risks of valproate.

options.rationale: Adding folate does not make continued valproate safe before conception; the teratogenicity of valproate extends well beyond neural tube defects and is not mitigated by folate. (Source: TGA valproate-containing medicines safety communications)

Folate supplementation does not abolish the substantial teratogenic risk from valproate. AU regulators have restricted valproate use in WCBA and a pregnancy planning consultation should pivot to a safer agent. (Source: TGA valproate-containing medicines safety communications)

Sodium valproate is contraindicated in women of childbearing potential unless conditions of the AU Pregnancy Prevention Program are met because the absolute risk of major congenital malformations (around 10 percent) and neurodevelopmental disorders (around 30 to 40 percent) is high. Lithium is preferred for relapse prevention in bipolar I disorder with manic predominance, with much lower teratogenic risk and reversible Ebstein anomaly concern weighed against ongoing manic relapse risk. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG; TGA valproate-containing medicines safety communications)

Lamotrigine is recommended for bipolar depression prevention rather than manic relapse prevention. Given her history of manic episodes and absence of depressive episodes on valproate, lithium is the preferred long-term agent. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

Abrupt cessation of valproate without an overlap risks destabilisation. Olanzapine is an option for acute mania but lithium has superior maintenance evidence for bipolar I with manic predominance and is the preferred long-term agent. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

explanation.summary: TCA cardiotoxicity is driven by sodium channel blockade and manifests with QRS widening and a tall terminal R wave in aVR.
