Sodium bicarbonate (1 to 2 mmol/kg, targeting serum pH 7.45 to 7.55 and QRS below 100 milliseconds) is the first-line treatment. Activated charcoal and antiarrhythmics are second-line; class IA agents are contraindicated.
key_points: ECG predictors of TCA toxicity: QRS above 100 ms, terminal R in aVR above 3 mm.
Sodium bicarbonate: 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus, target pH 7.45 to 7.55.
Lidocaine is second-line after bicarbonate; class IA antiarrhythmics are contraindicated.
Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose because of seizure risk.
explanation.pearls: TCA overdose with QRS above 100 ms or terminal R in aVR above 3 mm needs IV sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg titrated to pH 7.45 to 7.55; flumazenil and class IA antiarrhythmics are contraindicated.

options.rationale: Class IB antiarrhythmics are second-line after bicarbonate fails in TCA cardiotoxicity. Class IA agents (procainamide) are contraindicated because they compound sodium channel blockade. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology)

Magnesium sulfate is the antidote for torsades de pointes and refractory ventricular arrhythmias, not for sodium channel blockade-driven QRS widening. The mechanism here is wrong target. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology)

Activated charcoal is reserved for ingestions within 1 to 2 hours in a patient with a protected airway; this patient is drowsy and at risk of aspiration. Cardiotoxicity treatment with bicarbonate is the upstream priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology)

TCA cardiotoxicity is driven by fast sodium channel blockade. ECG features predicting toxicity are QRS above 100 milliseconds and a terminal R wave in aVR above 3 mm. Sodium bicarbonate (1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus, repeat as needed, targeting pH 7.45 to 7.55) overcomes the channel blockade and is the first-line cardiotoxicity treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology; ANZCOR ALS for poisoning)

Flumazenil is contraindicated in mixed overdose because it can precipitate seizures in a patient with sodium channel blockade and low seizure threshold from the TCA itself. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced myocarditis is most likely in the first 4 to 6 weeks of treatment. The Australian protocol monitors troponin and CRP weekly during this window. A rise in troponin to twice the upper reference plus a raised CRP, with or without symptoms, mandates withholding clozapine and urgent cardiology and echocardiographic assessment. Rechallenge after recovery is uncommon and specialist-led.
key_points: High-risk window: first 4 to 6 weeks of clozapine.
Trigger to act: troponin above twice upper reference plus raised CRP.
Withhold clozapine, urgent echocardiogram, cardiology review.
Rechallenge is specialist-led and uncommon.
explanation.pearls: Rising troponin (over twice upper reference) plus raised CRP in the first 4 to 6 weeks of clozapine titration triggers immediate cessation and urgent echocardiogram and cardiology review; do not continue dosing or wait for a second confirmation.

options.rationale: Outpatient stress echo on a non-urgent timeline does not address the acute risk of fulminant myocarditis. The pathway demands urgent inpatient cardiology review. (Source: Clozapine Implementation Tool)

A confirmed troponin and CRP rise during the high-risk window is itself the trigger to act, not to monitor for further worsening. Continued exposure to clozapine while myocarditis is evolving is potentially fatal. (Source: Clozapine Implementation Tool)
Increasing clozapine in the context of biochemical evidence of myocarditis is unsafe and contradicts the cessation pathway. (Source: Clozapine Implementation Tool)

Glucocorticoids are not standard initial therapy for clozapine-induced myocarditis. Cessation of clozapine, supportive care, and cardiology assessment are first. Steroid use is limited to specific eosinophilic or autoimmune subgroups guided by specialist input. (Source: Clozapine Implementation Tool)

Clozapine-induced myocarditis typically presents in the first 4 to 6 weeks of treatment. The Australian protocol monitors troponin and CRP weekly in this window. Rising troponin (over twice the upper reference) plus raised CRP triggers cessation, urgent echocardiogram, and cardiology review. Delaying creates risk of fulminant myocarditis. (Source: Clozapine Implementation Tool; RANZCP psychotropic monitoring guidance)

explanation.summary: Medical instability criteria for admission in anorexia nervosa include heart rate below 50 /min, systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg, QTc prolongation, severe electrolyte disturbance, and BMI below 16. Refeeding starts cautiously (20 to 30 kcal/kg/day) with thiamine prophylaxis and daily electrolytes for the first week to prevent refeeding syndrome. Family-based outpatient treatment is the longer-term framework.
key_points: Medical admission criteria: HR under 50, BP under 90 systolic, QTc prolongation, electrolyte derangement, BMI under 16.
Start refeeding at 20 to 30 kcal/kg/day with thiamine 200 to 300 mg daily.
Daily phosphate, potassium, magnesium for the first week of refeeding.
Cardiac monitoring while bradycardic and QT prolonged.
explanation.pearls: Medical admission for anorexia is triggered by bradycardia under 50, hypotension, QTc prolongation, or electrolyte derangement; refeed at 20 to 30 kcal/kg/day with thiamine and daily electrolytes to prevent refeeding syndrome per ANZAED.

options.rationale: Mental health units may not have cardiac monitoring and electrolyte infusion capability needed for the medical instability. Medical ward admission precedes or runs concurrently with mental health care. (Source: ANZAED Eating disorders guidelines)

Outpatient family-based treatment is the standard psychotherapy for paediatric anorexia, but this patient has multiple medical instability criteria and cannot be safely managed in the community without medical stabilisation first. (Source: ANZAED Eating disorders guidelines)

Discharge in the presence of severe bradycardia, hypotension, QT prolongation, and electrolyte derangement risks sudden cardiac death. Medical admission is required first. (Source: ANZAED Eating disorders guidelines)

Anorexia with bradycardia under 50 /min, hypotension, QTc prolongation, electrolyte derangement, and BMI below 16 meets multiple medical instability criteria for admission per the AU eating disorders MEED-aligned framework. Supervised structured refeeding with phosphate replacement prevents refeeding syndrome. Cardiac monitoring detects arrhythmia driven by hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia. (Source: ANZAED Eating disorders guidelines; MEED-aligned RCH guidance)

Aggressive refeeding precipitates refeeding syndrome (hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, thiamine deficiency, cardiac failure). MEED-aligned AU guidance recommends starting at 20 to 30 kcal/kg/day with thiamine prophylaxis and daily electrolyte monitoring for the first week. (Source: ANZAED Eating disorders guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute on chronic lithium toxicity meets EXTRIP haemodialysis criteria when the level is above 4.0 mmol/L regardless of symptoms, or above 2.5 mmol/L with reduced renal function or severe neurological features. Common precipitants are renal-impairing medications (ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, thiazides) and dehydration. Treatment combines urgent dialysis, volume resuscitation, and identification of the precipitant.
key_points: EXTRIP dialysis criteria: lithium above 4.0 mmol/L OR above 2.5 with renal impairment or severe neurology.
ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, and thiazides reduce lithium clearance.
Dehydration in heat reduces clearance further.
Saline alone is inadequate when dialysis criteria are met.
explanation.pearls: Lithium 2.6 mmol/L with renal impairment and neurological features meets EXTRIP haemodialysis criteria; saline alone is inadequate and ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs are common precipitants.

options.rationale: Activated charcoal does not bind lithium effectively because lithium is a small cation. It also exposes a confused patient to aspiration risk. (Source: EXTRIP recommendations for lithium poisoning)

Saline diuresis alone does not match the clearance achievable with dialysis when there is renal impairment. The patient has neurological signs and a level above 2.5 mmol/L with reduced eGFR, which meet dialysis indication. (Source: EXTRIP recommendations for lithium poisoning)

Acute on chronic lithium toxicity with neurological features and impaired renal function meets EXTRIP haemodialysis criteria: lithium above 4.0 mmol/L regardless of symptoms, or above 2.5 mmol/L with reduced renal function or severe neurological features. The renal impairment from ACE inhibitor introduction and volume depletion precipitated the toxicity. Saline maintains volume status; lithium clears via dialysis. (Source: EXTRIP recommendations for lithium poisoning)
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines; it has no role in lithium toxicity and could precipitate seizures if the patient has unrecognised polypharmacy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology)

Stopping the ACE inhibitor addresses the precipitant but does not address the acute toxicity. The patient has neurological signs requiring active intervention now. (Source: EXTRIP recommendations for lithium poisoning)

explanation.summary: Risk assessment in deliberate self-poisoning follows a fixed sequence: resuscitation, risk assessment from the agent, dose and time, supportive care and monitoring, then investigations. Two investigations are done in everyone regardless of the stated history, an electrocardiogram and a timed paracetamol concentration, because patients under-report and because paracetamol toxicity is both common and completely silent in the first twenty-four hours while it remains fully treatable. Drug concentrations for the agent actually named usually add nothing. In context: this woman also needs serial electrocardiograms for tricyclic cardiotoxicity, a period of observation, and a mental state and risk assessment once she is medically clear, with the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26 available for advice on the observation period.

sources.label: Toxicology Handbook (Murray, Little, Cadogan, Daly), Elsevier Australia

options.rationale: Every deliberate self-poisoning gets a timed paracetamol concentration, because paracetamol is the commonest co-ingestant, the early course is silent, and the antidote works only if given before hepatotoxicity develops.
Tricyclic concentrations are not available quickly enough to guide care and correlate poorly with severity. The QRS duration on serial electrocardiograms is the measure that drives management.
source_refs: Toxicology Handbook (Murray, Little, Cadogan, Daly), Elsevier Australia

options.rationale: A urine screen rarely changes acute management because it detects past use rather than current toxicity. It has a role in forensic work and in unexplained coma where no history is available.
source_refs: Toxicology Handbook (Murray, Little, Cadogan, Daly), Elsevier Australia

options.rationale: An ethanol concentration helps when the conscious state is depressed out of proportion to the history, or when a falling level fails to match improving conscious state. This patient is alert and denies alcohol.
source_refs: Toxicology Handbook (Murray, Little, Cadogan, Daly), Elsevier Australia

options.rationale: Salicylate is measured when the history suggests aspirin, or when there is tinnitus, hyperventilation or a mixed acid-base picture. It is not part of the universal screen the way paracetamol is.
source_refs: Toxicology Handbook (Murray, Little, Cadogan, Daly), Elsevier Australia

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD treatment in Australia combines stimulant pharmacotherapy (dexamfetamine, methylphenidate, lisdexamfetamine) with psychoeducation and CBT. Stimulants are Schedule 8 drugs and prescribing is restricted to psychiatrists or paediatricians under state and territory authority. Atomoxetine and guanfacine are non-stimulant options. Under Austroads 'Assessing Fitness to Drive', a commercial driver with a new ADHD diagnosis is required to notify the driver licensing authority; private drivers are not generally required to notify but the doctor is expected to advise the patient on safe driving and impairment. Stable treatment with documented response usually allows return to commercial driving.
key_points: Stimulants (methylphenidate, dexamfetamine, lisdexamfetamine) are first line
Atomoxetine, guanfacine are non-stimulant options
S8 medicines: psychiatry / paediatric authority prescribing in Australia
Austroads: commercial drivers must notify; private drivers advised by doctor
Baseline ECG, BP, weight monitoring during titration
explanation.pearls: Lisdexamfetamine has a smoother pharmacokinetic profile than dexamfetamine because it is a prodrug requiring red cell hydrolysis to release dexamfetamine - this caps the rate of release and reduces euphoric peak, supporting once daily dosing.

options.rationale: Bupropion is not first line for ADHD in Australia and the driving notification requirement is triggered by the diagnosis, not by the drug class. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline)

Notification of a new ADHD diagnosis is mandatory for commercial driver licence holders under Austroads regardless of medication choice. Atomoxetine is a non-stimulant second line option, not first line. (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive)

CBT is adjunctive but does not match the effect size of stimulants in adult ADHD. Withholding pharmacotherapy from a symptomatic adult on the basis of driving risk is paternalistic and not supported by guideline. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline)
Modafinil is not recommended for ADHD in Australian guidelines and is approved for narcolepsy and shift work sleep disorder. Stimulants remain first line. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline)

Long acting or short-acting psychostimulants (dexamfetamine, methylphenidate, lisdexamfetamine) are first line for adult ADHD; in Australia they are S8 medicines requiring psychiatry-led prescription. Under Austroads 'Assessing Fitness to Drive', a commercial driver with a new ADHD diagnosis must notify the licensing authority and is generally fit to drive only on stable treatment with documented benefit. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline)

explanation.summary: Differentiating substance induced from primary psychosis in a young person with cannabis use and a positive family history is clinically difficult and often requires longitudinal observation. The RANZCP and Orygen early psychosis pathway favours treating as first episode psychosis if symptoms persist beyond a month of abstinence (or earlier if a clear primary disorder is suspected) using low dose oral second generation antipsychotic, integrated substance use treatment, and assertive case management. About one in three cannabis induced psychoses convert to schizophrenia within three years.
key_points: Persistence of psychosis beyond one month of cannabis abstinence supports primary psychosis
Around 30 percent of cannabis induced psychoses convert to schizophrenia within 3 years
Low dose oral second generation antipsychotic is first line (e.g. risperidone, aripiprazole, olanzapine)
Integrated substance treatment within early psychosis service
Family history of schizophrenia roughly doubles conversion risk
explanation.pearls: Among cannabis users with a first episode psychosis, around 30 percent meet criteria for schizophrenia within three years on Australian early psychosis cohort follow up - assertive engagement during this window predicts long term function.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Even if cannabis induced psychosis is the working diagnosis, three weeks of fixed persecutory beliefs, second person auditory hallucinations, and thought disorder in a 21-year-old with family history warrant assertive specialist follow up rather than GP review. Premature discharge risks treatment dropout and decompensation. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Voluntary admission should be offered first if the patient has capacity and agrees. Involuntary admission is reserved for refusal in a person at risk of harm to self or others. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistance (failure of two adequate trials of other antipsychotics). High dose olanzapine in a stimulant naive young man exposes him to weight gain, metabolic syndrome, and sedation. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: First episode psychosis with persistent positive symptoms beyond a few days of abstinence cannot be reliably labelled cannabis induced until at least one month of cannabis abstinence shows symptom resolution. Early Psychosis Prevention and Intervention Centre (EPPIC) model favours assertive specialist follow up, low dose oral second generation antipsychotic, and integrated substance use treatment. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia

options.rationale: Three weeks of psychotic symptoms after presentation already exceeds the two week abstinence window that would support a substance induced diagnosis. Withholding antipsychotic medication delays symptom resolution. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia

explanation.summary: People with severe mental illness die around fifteen to twenty years earlier than the general population, and most of that gap is cardiovascular rather than suicide, so metabolic effects are a treatment outcome rather than a side issue. Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest risk of weight gain and dyslipidaemia, and gain in the first twelve weeks predicts the longer-term trajectory, which is why baseline and three-monthly weight, waist, blood pressure, lipids and glucose are recommended. When lifestyle measures have been tried and the gain continues, switching to a lower-risk agent comes before adding a second drug, with metformin reserved for the patient whose antipsychotic cannot be changed. In context: schizoaffective disorder requires long-term antipsychotic treatment, so the choice of agent has to balance control of psychosis and mood against decades of metabolic exposure, and cardiovascular risk needs active management in primary care alongside psychiatric follow-up.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders
RACGP: Handbook of Non-Drug Interventions and preventive activities

options.rationale: Where weight gain is substantial and lifestyle measures are already in place, Australian guidance is to change to an antipsychotic with a lower metabolic liability, and aripiprazole has efficacy in both psychotic and mood domains with the least weight gain.
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.rationale: Metformin attenuates antipsychotic-associated weight gain and is the option when the current antipsychotic cannot be changed, for example when only clozapine has controlled the illness.
Dose reduction is worth considering when the dose is above the effective range, but a halved dose risks relapse and weight gain is not reliably dose related.

Dietary and exercise support belongs in the plan for everyone on an antipsychotic, and would be the whole answer if no lifestyle change had yet been made. He has already made them and continues to gain.
source_refs: RACGP: Handbook of Non-Drug Interventions and preventive activities
RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.rationale: Annual review suits a patient whose weight and metabolic profile are stable. This trajectory over 12 weeks predicts diabetes and needs action now.
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines: Schizophrenia and Related Disorders
RACGP: Handbook of Non-Drug Interventions and preventive activities

explanation.summary: Long term lithium use carries cumulative renal risk through chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Surveillance every six months should include eGFR, lithium level, thyroid stimulating hormone, calcium and parathyroid hormone (lithium induced hyperparathyroidism), and urinalysis. eGFR below 60 prompts shared care with renal medicine; below 45 prompts active discussion of cessation versus continuation, weighing 50 percent twelve month relapse risk if stopped abruptly. Lithium induced hyperparathyroidism is treated by lithium cessation where possible or parathyroidectomy.
key_points: 6 monthly: eGFR, Li level, TSH, calcium/PTH, urinalysis
eGFR < 60: shared care with renal medicine
eGFR < 45: actively discuss cessation versus continuation
Slow taper over 3 to 6 months reduces relapse risk
Lithium induced hyperparathyroidism: high calcium with high or inappropriately normal PTH
explanation.pearls: Hypercalcaemia plus inappropriately normal or high PTH in a patient on long term lithium is lithium induced hyperparathyroidism - around 10 percent prevalence after 10 years of lithium therapy, and the parathyroid hyperplasia often does not reverse on lithium withdrawal.

options.rationale: Progressive eGFR decline through stage 3b CKD on a known nephrotoxin warrants psychiatric and renal multidisciplinary review with a documented plan to switch or taper, not passive monitoring. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guideline)

Dose reduction below 0.6 mmol/L generally loses prophylactic efficacy and does not reliably halt renal decline. Multidisciplinary planning toward alternative agents is preferred. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guideline)
Abrupt cessation of lithium after long term use carries up to 50 percent risk of mood relapse within 12 months. A planned slow taper is preferred. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guideline)

Volume loading does not reverse established chronic interstitial nephritis from lithium and may risk hyponatraemia. The dose should not stay the same in CKD stage 3b without weighing alternatives. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guideline)

Australian psychiatric guidance advises planned multidisciplinary review when eGFR falls under 60 and especially under 45, weighing relapse risk against renal benefit; a slow taper over 3 to 6 months with an alternative mood stabiliser is preferred. Abrupt cessation risks relapse and may not reverse renal decline beyond stage 3b. (Source: RANZCP Bipolar Guideline)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a clinically diagnosed syndrome (Bush Francis Catatonia Rating Scale: 3 or more of 14 features) that complicates schizophrenia, mood disorders, and a range of medical conditions including autoimmune encephalitis. First line treatment is the lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV or IM with assessment at 15 minutes); around 70 percent improve dramatically. If lorazepam fails or malignant catatonia develops (hyperthermia, autonomic instability), ECT is the next step. Antipsychotics are relatively contraindicated because they may precipitate NMS. Always look for an underlying cause: autoimmune encephalitis (NMDA receptor), HIV, encephalitis, lupus.
key_points: Bush Francis Catatonia Rating Scale: 3 or more of 14 features
Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV or IM (diagnostic and therapeutic - 70 percent response)
ECT for refractory catatonia or malignant catatonia
Avoid antipsychotics first line (precipitate NMS)
Screen for autoimmune (NMDA receptor encephalitis), HIV, lupus, metabolic
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia (catatonia with hyperthermia, autonomic instability, and rigidity) is clinically indistinguishable from neuroleptic malignant syndrome - the differentiator is dopamine antagonist exposure history; treatment is electroconvulsive therapy and supportive ICU care regardless.

options.rationale: Antipsychotics are relatively contraindicated as first line in catatonia because of the risk of precipitating neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) and worsening catatonic features. Benzodiazepines are first line. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guideline)

Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV or IM is both diagnostic and therapeutic in catatonia: around 70 percent of cases show measurable improvement in Bush Francis catatonia rating score within 15 to 30 minutes. Lack of response prompts urgent consideration of electroconvulsive therapy. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guideline)

ECT is second line after lorazepam (and may be first line in life-threatening malignant catatonia with autonomic instability), but trialling lorazepam first is standard in non-malignant catatonia. ECT is also indicated when there is no response within 24 to 48 hours. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guideline)

Flumazenil is contraindicated when a seizure risk exists, may precipitate seizures, and addresses a different clinical picture from catatonia. The urinary drug screen excludes benzodiazepine intoxication here. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guideline)

NMS requires recent exposure to dopamine antagonists, hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability, and a raised creatine kinase - none of which are present here. Dantrolene has no role in non-malignant catatonia. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Guideline)

explanation.summary: Lithium toxicity is precipitated commonly by dehydration, NSAID use (reduced renal prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation), ACE inhibitor or thiazide initiation, and acute kidney injury. Management is immediate cessation of lithium and precipitating drug, intravenous saline for volume expansion, and consideration of haemodialysis for severe toxicity (level above 4, or 2.5 to 4 with severe symptoms or renal failure, or 1.5 to 2.5 with significant neurological signs). Coarse tremor and ataxia indicate moderate toxicity.
key_points: Common precipitants: NSAID, ACE inhibitor, thiazide, dehydration, AKI
Symptoms: coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, vomiting, dysarthria, seizures (severe)
Haemodialysis if level > 4, or 2.5-4 with severe symptoms or renal failure
Stop lithium plus precipitating drug, give intravenous saline
Long-term follow-up: thyroid, parathyroid, and renal function monitoring
explanation.pearls: Ibuprofen reduces lithium clearance by around 25 percent through prostaglandin-mediated renal vasoconstriction and can push a previously therapeutic patient into toxicity within days; routine paracetamol is the preferred analgesic on lithium.

options.rationale: Lithium level 1.8 with neurological features and impaired renal function meets criteria for moderate-to-severe lithium toxicity. NSAIDs reduce renal lithium clearance through prostaglandin-mediated vasoconstriction. Haemodialysis is indicated for level greater than 4 mmol/L, or 2.5 to 4 with severe symptoms or renal failure, or 1.5 to 2.5 with significant neurological involvement. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

Continuing lithium at this level with neurological involvement risks deterioration including seizures, arrhythmias, and irreversible neurological injury. Immediate cessation is required. (Source: AMH: Lithium)
Dose reduction without cessation does not address acute toxicity, and continued NSAID exposure will perpetuate the renal clearance impairment. (Source: AMH: Lithium)
Premature restart before level clears risks rebound toxicity. Switching to valproate is a longer-term consideration rather than acute management of a toxic level. (Source: AMH: Lithium)
Sustained-release lithium does not reduce toxicity; it changes the kinetics. The acute step is to remove lithium, not to reformulate it. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

explanation.summary: Clozapine is regulated through a national TGA risk management plan because of the risk of agranulocytosis and other haematological events. Australian protocol requires weekly full blood count for the first 18 weeks of treatment (highest risk window), then four-weekly indefinitely while the patient remains on clozapine. Trigger thresholds use the absolute neutrophil count: green zone (>= 2.0) continue, amber (1.5-1.99) twice weekly, red (< 1.5) cease and admit.
key_points: Weekly FBC for first 18 weeks of clozapine
Then four-weekly indefinitely
Green: ANC >= 2.0; amber: 1.5-1.99; red: < 1.5
Red zone: cease clozapine, admit, haematology referral
Also monitor for myocarditis (first 4 weeks): troponin, CRP, ECG
explanation.pearls: Agranulocytosis risk on clozapine peaks within the first 18 weeks (around 0.8 percent cumulative incidence) then falls; this is why the Australian registry steps weekly monitoring down to four-weekly only after week 18.

options.rationale: Counts of 2.0 are at the lower limit of the green zone and do not trigger increased monitoring frequency. Twice weekly is not a routine clozapine monitoring interval. (Source: TGA Clozapine Risk Management Plan)

The Australian clozapine registry protocol requires weekly haematological monitoring for the first 18 weeks (highest risk period for agranulocytosis), then four-weekly thereafter for the duration of therapy. (Source: TGA Clozapine Risk Management Plan)
Monthly monitoring is not appropriate before 18 weeks because the highest risk of agranulocytosis is within the first 18 weeks of treatment. (Source: TGA Clozapine Risk Management Plan)

Absolute neutrophil count of 2.0 is at the lower border of the green zone and does not require cessation. The red zone (cease clozapine and admit) is below 1.5. (Source: TGA Clozapine Risk Management Plan)
Weekly indefinite monitoring is not the registry protocol and over-burdens the patient. Frequency steps down after 18 weeks of stable counts. (Source: TGA Clozapine Risk Management Plan)

explanation.summary: SSRI discontinuation syndrome presents with FINISH features (Flu-like symptoms, Insomnia, Nausea, Imbalance, Sensory disturbances including brain zaps, Hyperarousal). It is most common with short half-life agents (paroxetine, venlafaxine) and is differentiated from depressive relapse by onset within days, sensory symptoms, and rapid response to reinstatement. Management is restart at the original dose and taper gradually (25 percent reduction every 2 to 4 weeks) over months.
key_points: FINISH mnemonic for discontinuation symptoms
Highest risk: paroxetine, venlafaxine (short half-lives)
Onset within days of stopping; resolves within hours of reinstatement
Slow taper: 25 percent reduction every 2-4 weeks for at-risk agents
Fluoxetine has long half-life and rarely causes discontinuation syndrome
explanation.pearls: Paroxetine's discontinuation syndrome is the worst of the SSRIs because of its short half-life and lack of active metabolites; tapering by 5 to 10 mg every 2 to 4 weeks is appropriate.

options.rationale: Untreated paroxetine discontinuation syndrome usually persists for one to three weeks (paroxetine has a short half-life and high discontinuation rate). Reassurance alone is inadequate. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

Bridging with fluoxetine is sometimes used for severe discontinuation syndrome but seven days is too short, increases fluoxetine accumulation, and does not address the underlying need for a gradual taper. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)
Switching antidepressant class is not the answer to discontinuation symptoms and venlafaxine has a similar or worse discontinuation profile than paroxetine. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

The recommended approach is to restart at the original dose and then taper slowly (typically 25 percent reduction every 2 to 4 weeks) over months. Paroxetine has the worst discontinuation profile of common SSRIs and requires the slowest taper. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)
Benzodiazepines do not treat SSRI discontinuation syndrome and risk dependence in this 35-year-old. The underlying need is to restart paroxetine and taper. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is a syndrome of motoric, behavioural, and autonomic features (mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, mitgehen, mannerisms, echolalia, echopraxia) seen with mood, psychotic, and general medical conditions. Diagnosis is by Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale plus a positive lorazepam challenge (2 mg intravenous or intramuscular yielding meaningful response within minutes). Treatment is scheduled lorazepam (titrated up to around 8 to 24 mg per day) or electroconvulsive therapy for benzodiazepine non-responders or malignant catatonia.
key_points: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale screens for the syndrome
Lorazepam 2 mg IV is diagnostic and therapeutic
Avoid typical antipsychotics: risk of NMS and worsened catatonia
Electroconvulsive therapy if lorazepam fails or for malignant catatonia
Always exclude medical causes (infection, drugs, autoimmune encephalitis)
explanation.pearls: A positive lorazepam challenge in catatonia is a meaningful response within 5 to 10 minutes of a 2 mg dose; failure to respond after 4 mg IV is the trigger for urgent ECT planning.

options.rationale: Antipsychotics, particularly typical agents, can precipitate or worsen catatonia and may also trigger neuroleptic malignant syndrome which clinically overlaps. They are not first-line in confirmed catatonia. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position Statement)

Atypical antipsychotics are safer than typicals but still not first-line in catatonia. The first step is benzodiazepine challenge, then electroconvulsive therapy if no response. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position Statement)

Lorazepam 2 mg intravenous or intramuscular is the recommended first-line diagnostic and therapeutic challenge for catatonia; a meaningful response within 5 to 10 minutes both confirms diagnosis and is initial treatment. Non-response prompts urgent electroconvulsive therapy. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position Statement)

Standard antidepressant titration does not address acute catatonia; the syndrome requires immediate benzodiazepine challenge or electroconvulsive therapy. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position Statement)

Valproate is not first-line for catatonia and MRI is not required when CT brain is unremarkable and there are no focal neurological signs. Time-critical lorazepam challenge should not be delayed. (Source: RANZCP Catatonia Position Statement)

explanation.summary: DSM-5 differentiates primary psychotic disorders by duration: brief psychotic disorder is less than 1 month with full return to baseline; schizophreniform disorder is 1 to 6 months; schizophrenia is 6 months or more. Schizoaffective disorder requires concurrent major mood episodes overlapping with active psychosis for at least half the illness duration. Bipolar I with psychotic features requires a manic episode. About one third of schizophreniform diagnoses convert to schizophrenia within six months of follow-up.
key_points: Brief psychotic disorder: < 1 month, full return to baseline
Schizophreniform: 1-6 months total duration
Schizophrenia: >= 6 months total duration
Schizoaffective: major mood episode + psychosis concurrent
Antipsychotic taper trial after first-episode psychosis: not before 12 months symptom-free in Australian practice
explanation.pearls: Schizophreniform disorder is provisional - around one third convert to schizophrenia by six months and two thirds remit; the diagnosis is reviewed after the six month mark.

options.rationale: DSM-5 schizophrenia requires symptoms (active and prodromal/residual) for at least 6 months. Total illness duration is 16 weeks here, below threshold. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

Brief psychotic disorder requires duration less than 1 month with full return to baseline. His symptoms lasted around six weeks before treatment plus four further weeks on treatment, exceeding one month. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

Schizoaffective disorder requires concurrent major mood episodes (manic or depressive) overlapping with active psychotic symptoms for the majority of the illness duration; he has had neither. (Source: DSM-5-TR)
Bipolar I with psychotic features requires a manic episode at some point with associated psychotic symptoms. He has had no documented mood elevation or major depressive episode. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

DSM-5 schizophreniform disorder requires symptoms for 1 to 6 months. His total duration of approximately 10 weeks (6 weeks before plus 4 weeks of residual on treatment) sits squarely in this window; the diagnosis converts to schizophrenia if symptoms persist beyond 6 months. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Bipolar depression is differentiated from unipolar major depression by a personal history of mania (bipolar I) or hypomania (bipolar II). Antidepressant monotherapy risks switch to mania, rapid cycling, and worsening course; mood stabiliser cover is essential. RANZCP first-line agents for bipolar depression are quetiapine, lurasidone, lithium, and lamotrigine. Olanzapine-fluoxetine combination is also evidence-based.
key_points: Past mania = bipolar I; past hypomania = bipolar II
Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar depression: risk of switch and rapid cycling
First-line: quetiapine, lurasidone, lithium, lamotrigine
Olanzapine-fluoxetine is evidence-based combination
Always screen unipolar-appearing depression for past hypomania/mania
explanation.pearls: Atypical depressive features (hypersomnia, weight gain, leaden paralysis) plus a past episode of decreased sleep need with grandiosity is bipolar I depression and quetiapine has the strongest RANZCP evidence as monotherapy.

options.rationale: Her past episode (sustained two-week mood elevation with grandiosity, decreased sleep need, and impulsivity requiring hospitalisation) was a manic episode, making her current presentation bipolar I depression. Quetiapine has the strongest evidence as first-line monotherapy for bipolar depression per RANZCP. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)
SSRI monotherapy in bipolar depression risks switch to mania or rapid cycling and is contraindicated as first-line. Mood stabiliser cover is required. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)
Venlafaxine carries the highest switch-to-mania risk among antidepressants in bipolar disorder and should be avoided as monotherapy. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

Tricyclic antidepressants are second-line in unipolar depression and carry significant switch risk in bipolar disorder. They are not first-line for bipolar depression. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)
ECT is reserved for severe, psychotic, melancholic, treatment-resistant, or actively suicidal depression. First-line pharmacotherapy is offered first. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia results from dopamine D2 antagonism in the tuberoinfundibular pathway. Risperidone, paliperidone, amisulpride, and the typical antipsychotics are the highest-risk agents. Clinical consequences include amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, sexual dysfunction, reduced bone mineral density, and possibly increased breast cancer risk. First-line management is switching to a prolactin-sparing agent (aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine), with aripiprazole most effective at normalising prolactin.
key_points: High prolactin risk: risperidone, paliperidone, amisulpride, typical antipsychotics
Low prolactin impact: aripiprazole (often lowers prolactin), quetiapine, olanzapine
Switch antipsychotic is first-line management
MRI pituitary only if prolactin > 4000 mU/L, persistent after switch, or neurology
Dopamine agonists (cabergoline) risk psychotic relapse
explanation.pearls: Aripiprazole is a partial D2 agonist and can paradoxically lower prolactin below baseline, making it both the preferred switch and a possible adjunct for women who must remain on a high-prolactin antipsychotic.

options.rationale: Dopamine agonists in patients with psychotic disorders can precipitate relapse of psychosis through dopaminergic stimulation; they are not first-line for antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

Risperidone causes the highest rate of hyperprolactinaemia among second-generation antipsychotics. Switching to a prolactin-sparing or prolactin-lowering agent (aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine) is first-line, with aripiprazole the most effective at normalising prolactin. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)
Hormone replacement does not address the underlying cause and combined oestrogen carries thrombotic risk. Switching antipsychotic addresses the root mechanism. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

When the prolactin elevation is plausibly attributable to a known dopamine antagonist, the standard step is antipsychotic switch first; MRI is reserved for prolactin above 4000 mU/L, persistence after switch, or focal neurology. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)
Progestogen-only contraception suppresses menstruation without addressing prolactin or restoring physiological oestrogen, leaving bone density at risk. (Source: RANZCP Schizophrenia CPG)

explanation.summary: Lithium use in pregnancy involves balancing absolute teratogenic risk (Ebstein anomaly around 1 in 1000, around 10 to 20 times baseline but absolute risk low) against high relapse risk if discontinued in severe bipolar I disorder. RANZCP guidance supports continuation in women with severe disease and documented lithium responsiveness, with TID dosing to flatten peaks, fetal cardiac ultrasound at 18 to 20 weeks, lithium monitoring every 2 to 4 weeks with adjustment for rising clearance, and a planned peripartum dose reduction. Valproate is contraindicated.
key_points: Lithium teratogenicity: Ebstein anomaly absolute risk around 1 in 1000
Lithium clearance rises 30-50 percent in pregnancy; dose adjustment needed
TID dosing flattens peaks and may reduce teratogenicity
Fetal cardiac ultrasound at 18-20 weeks screens for Ebstein
Valproate is contraindicated; lamotrigine has weak mania prevention evidence
explanation.pearls: Continuing lithium in severe bipolar I disorder during pregnancy is supported because the absolute Ebstein anomaly risk (around 1 in 1000) is much smaller than the relapse-driven risk to mother and baby of stopping; switch to TID dosing to flatten peaks.

options.rationale: Lithium clearance increases by 30 to 50 percent during pregnancy, so dose adjustment and more frequent level monitoring are required. Once daily dosing also produces higher peaks linked to teratogenicity risk. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

Lithium cessation in a woman with severe bipolar I disorder and two prior manic episodes (one with psychosis) carries very high relapse risk during pregnancy and postpartum, with risks to maternal and fetal wellbeing exceeding the absolute teratogenic risk. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

Severe bipolar I with documented lithium responsiveness and failed alternatives justifies lithium continuation. Risk mitigation includes TID dosing to flatten peaks, fetal cardiac ultrasound at 18 to 20 weeks for Ebstein anomaly screening (absolute risk around 1 in 1000), and lithium monitoring every 2 to 4 weeks (more frequent in third trimester) with peripartum dose reduction. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

Sodium valproate is the most teratogenic mood stabiliser (fetal valproate syndrome, neural tube defects up to 10 percent, and lasting neurodevelopmental impairment) and is contraindicated in women of childbearing potential without a pregnancy prevention program. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

Lamotrigine is reasonable for bipolar depression maintenance but has weaker evidence for mania prevention. This patient already had a manic relapse on lamotrigine alone; switching now is not safer than continuing lithium. (Source: RANZCP Mood Disorders CPG)

explanation.summary: Partial-response clozapine-treated schizophrenia (persisting positive symptoms despite 14 months of clozapine at therapeutic trough) requires augmentation. The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists CPG and the CLO-ECT evidence base list electroconvulsive therapy as the augmentation strategy with the strongest evidence; approximately 50 per cent of clozapine-resistant patients respond to ECT. The failed sodium valproate trial at therapeutic trough over 3 months rules out continuing the current regimen or increasing valproate. Of the options, ECT has the strongest evidence, antipsychotic augmentation is weak for positive symptoms, a mood-stabiliser switch is modest, and waiting is not evidence-based. In context, partial-responders to clozapine should be offered ECT augmentation in line with the AU evidence base.
key_points: Clozapine at therapeutic trough (350 to 600 ng/mL) plus partial response: next step is augmentation, not dose increase.
ECT is the AU evidence-based augmentation with the strongest effect on positive symptoms in clozapine partial-responders.
Sodium valproate adjunct does NOT have evidence for positive-symptom augmentation in clozapine.
Aripiprazole augmentation is for metabolic / weight; lamotrigine has modest effect; CBT for psychosis is an adjunct not a substitute.
Therapeutic clozapine trough varies with smoking status; current trough is in range and ratio 1.98 suggests adherence.
explanation.pearls: Clozapine partial-responders with persisting positive symptoms have an approximately 50 per cent response rate to ECT augmentation per the CLO-ECT meta-analysis; offer it before further pharmacological augmentation.

options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is the augmentation strategy with the strongest evidence in partial-response clozapine-treated schizophrenia. The CLO-ECT meta-analysis and the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists clinical practice guideline on schizophrenia both list ECT as a Level A or B recommendation for clozapine-augmentation in patients with persisting positive symptoms despite adequate clozapine dosing and trough level. Bilateral or right unilateral ECT 8 to 12 sessions twice weekly while continuing clozapine produces approximately 50 per cent response in this population. Sodium valproate adjunct does NOT have evidence for positive-symptom augmentation (it is added in clozapine for seizure prophylaxis or mood targets) and has not added benefit here. The failed valproate adjunct of 3 months at therapeutic trough rules out continuing the current regimen or increasing valproate. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists CPG: Schizophrenia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; CLO-ECT meta-analysis)

Trough clozapine of 387 ng/mL is already within the target range (350 to 600) and the clozapine-to-norclozapine ratio of 1.98 is within typical bounds. Further dose increase without a low trough is not the evidence-based next step and adds toxicity risk (seizures, sedation, metabolic). Smoking cessation is an appropriate parallel intervention but is not the strongest evidence-based augmentation. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)

Aripiprazole augmentation of clozapine has been studied for clozapine-induced metabolic effects and shows weight and lipid benefit; it has weak evidence for positive-symptom augmentation. The CLOZ-AUG meta-analyses rank aripiprazole below ECT for positive-symptom response. Would be the correct first augmentation choice if the dominant unmet need were metabolic side-effects rather than persisting positive symptoms. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)

Lamotrigine adjunct has small-to-moderate effect for positive-symptom augmentation in clozapine in some meta-analyses but the effect size is below ECT. It is reasonable when ECT is declined or contraindicated. The slow titration (8 weeks to therapeutic dose) plus 12-week review delays response in a patient with distressing persistent symptoms. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)

CBT for psychosis is an evidence-based adjunct but is not a substitute for pharmacological or somatic augmentation when positive symptoms remain distressing after 14 months of clozapine at therapeutic trough plus 3 months of valproate adjunct. The patient is already engaged in psychosocial rehabilitation. Continued waiting is not the strongest evidence-based next step. (Source: RANZCP CPG: Schizophrenia)
